pg047_n0004: Production and social organisation in pre-colonial Africa
pg047_n0008: Pre-colonial African societies interacted with one another in various ways.
pg047_n0009: The interactions enabled them to produce the basic needs and other necessities of their life.
pg047_n0010: The interactions and production of their necessities influenced social and economic development.
pg047_n0011: In this chapter, you will learn about the concepts used in social organisation and economic production.
pg047_n0012: You will also learn about communal, slave, and feudal modes of production in pre-colonial Africa and their characteristics.
pg047_n0013: The competencies developed will enable you to differentiate pre-colonial social organisations from contemporary African social organisations so as to maintain good practices and discourage inhuman social relations.
pg047_n0017: The ownership of the major means of production
pg047_n0019: Concepts of social organisation and economic production
pg047_n0021: In order to explain the socio-economic development that Africa attained before colonialism, it is essential to understand some key concepts.
pg047_n0022: One such concept is social organisation, which is about how people and groups in the society interact in the process of material production.
pg047_n0023: In this kind of organisation, people are assigned duties according to their positions in the society.
pg047_n0024: Another concept is economic production, which refers to the process of producing goods and services to meet human needs.
pg047_n0025: It also includes the creation of economic value from raw products.
pg047_n0026: Examples of activities related to economic production are crop cultivation and cloth-making.
pg047_n0027: Thus, with economic production, social organisation is how people are organised and related to each other in the process of producing goods or services.
pg047_n0029: Human beings need to produce various types of goods and services to survive.
pg047_n0030: They use tools such as hand hoes, machetes, spears, axes, arrows, tractors and computers to produce goods and services.
pg047_n0031: The tools are collectively called instruments of labour.
pg048_n0003: Thus, instruments of labour mean all tools used by human beings in the production process.
pg048_n0004: The tools range from simple to complex, depending on the level of technology a particular society attains.
pg048_n0005: These instruments extend human’s natural organs, such as hands, legs, eyes and the brain.
pg048_n0006: Means of labour help human beings to simplify work.
pg048_n0009: Instruments of labour are organised around human labour.
pg048_n0010: Human labour is people’s physical and mental energy to produce what they want.
pg048_n0011: Physical labour refers to the energy people use to produce what they want.
pg048_n0012: Mental labour is to do with the knowledge and skills that people utilise during production.
pg048_n0013: When labour and instruments of labour have been combined, they are called productive forces.
pg048_n0014: In production, productive forces act upon resources such as land and forests.
pg048_n0015: These resources are called objects of labour.
pg048_n0017: An object of labour refers to anything on which human labour is applied in order to produce goods.
pg048_n0018: Such resources are primarily found in natural environments, such as land, rivers and forests.
pg048_n0019: That means human beings need objects of labour to work.
pg048_n0021: For example, one may have a good fishing instrument, but one will not fish unless there is a river, an ocean, a lake or a water pond in which fish are found.
pg048_n0022: When human labour, instruments of labour and objects of labour have been combined, they are called means of production.
pg048_n0024: Means of production comprises the combination of means of labour, human labour and objects of labour.
pg048_n0025: They are necessary for the production of goods and services.
pg048_n0027: When left alone, the means of labour have no value in life.
pg048_n0028: Therefore, human labour must act on objects of labour to produce goods and services.
pg048_n0030: People enter into certain kinds of relations in order to produce goods and services.
pg048_n0031: Relations are either exploitative or non-exploitative, Relation is exploitive when the producers of goods and services are not paid accordingly and the vice versa.
pg048_n0032: A combination of productive forces and relations of production constitutes a mode of production.
pg048_n0033: A mode of production of a particular society is meant to meet people’s needs.
pg048_n0037: Visit one of the economic production or service provision centres to study production relations, then write a report.
pg049_n0005: Pre-colonial African societies passed through three modes of production, namely communalism, slavery and feudalism.
pg049_n0006: However, not all societies passed through all the three modes of production.
pg049_n0007: The transition from one mode of production to another was largely influenced by the environment and the development of productive forces.
pg049_n0011: Communalism was the first mode of production which all human societies passed through.
pg049_n0012: This mode was also known as primitive communalism.
pg049_n0013: It was called primitive communalism because of the low level of technological development attained by societies.
pg049_n0015: Communalism was based on collective ownership of the means of production and equal distribution of the gains.
pg049_n0016: In Africa, communalism existed for a much longer time than any other mode of production.
pg049_n0017: It developed when people began to live in communities many years ago.
pg049_n0019: Some African societies that are still practising communal life include hunter-gatherers such as the Mbuti of the Ituri Forest of Eastern Congo, the San of the Kalahari Desert, the Sandawe and Hadzabe of Northcentral Tanzania, and the Khoikhoi of South Africa.
pg049_n0020: Other examples include pastoralist communities like the Fulani of Northern Nigeria in West Africa, the Galla and Somali of northeastern Africa, the Teso of Uganda and Kenya, the Karamojong of Uganda, and the Ndorobo of Tanzania and Kenya.
pg049_n0021: Some of these societies have adopted new modes of production as a result of their interaction with other societies.
pg049_n0025: Communalism had a number of characteristics as follows.
pg049_n0027: The major means of production such as land, forests and water bodies were owned by the whole society.
pg049_n0028: The production of goods was done by all people on the basis of gender and age.
pg049_n0029: As a result, the products of labour were shared according to people’s needs.
pg049_n0030: There was no exploitation among people.
pg049_n0031: This was because no one was allowed to own the resources individually since all people worked together for a common goal.
pg049_n0032: For example, activities such as hunting, farming and fishing were done collectively.
pg049_n0033: Communalism did not produce classes of people.
pg049_n0034: Instead, people respected each other and were equal in principle.
pg049_n0037: This means that communal societies produced only for survival.
pg049_n0038: That was because the tools of production were crude as a result of low level of technology and the small population that needed little food.
pg049_n0039: For instance, communal hunters would kill animals and consume them, and then would go
pg050_n0004: Similarly, gatherers would collect food for a day’s consumption.
pg050_n0005: After they had finished the food, they would go back to the forest to collect food again.
pg050_n0007: The division of labour was simple and based on gender.
pg050_n0008: Gender is a social division of labour and responsibilities between men and women, especially when considered with reference to cultural perceptions and constructions.
pg050_n0009: The role men and women play in the production process is an aspect of gender.
pg050_n0010: For example, men hunted wild animals, looked after livestock and built huts while women gathered vegetables, fruits and edible insects.
pg050_n0011: Women also cooked food and cared for children.
pg050_n0013: Transition from communalism to other modes of production
pg050_n0016: The transition from communal to slave mode of production began when societies had improved in iron technology.
pg050_n0017: Technology facilitated the increase in production, hence the rise of private ownership of properties, such as land.
pg050_n0018: This shift marked a significant step in human history from depending on hunting and gathering to depending on agriculture and animal domestication and from scattered dwellings of hunter-gatherers to permanent farming villages.
pg050_n0020: The ways of living were transformed as some people became pastoralists and others crop cultivators.
pg050_n0021: For example, after people had discovered the use of iron tools, they began to produce surplus.
pg050_n0022: The production of surplus wealth led to the development of trade and the rise of states.
pg050_n0023: The states were characterised by the emergence of classes, namely slave masters and slaves in the slave mode of production.
pg050_n0024: Later, land owners and peasants or serfs emerged as classes under the feudal mode of production.
pg050_n0028: Read various reliable online and library sources and identify features of primitive communalism that are still found in the present society.
pg050_n0032: Slavery was the second mode of production and the first exploitative mode of production in human history.
pg050_n0033: It was a socio-economic system based on private ownership of the means of production, including slave labour.
pg050_n0034: African societies which experienced slavery included Ancient Egypt and some East African coastal societies as indicated in Figure three point one.
pg050_n0035: These societies owned slaves and used slave labour in income generating activities.
pg051_n0003: Ways by which people became slaves
pg051_n0005: People became slaves if they failed to pay their debts.
pg051_n0007: Involvement in criminal offences was also another way through which people became slaves.
pg051_n0008: An individual could be sold into slavery after committing a serious crime such as stealing, beating a master or murdering.
pg051_n0010: War captives could also be turned into slaves.
pg051_n0011: Some war captives were killed, some were turned into slaves, and some women were made wives of the warriors.
pg051_n0013: In addition, inheritance of the slave status was another way through which a person could become a slave.
pg051_n0014: A child could become a slave because the parents were slaves.
pg051_n0016: Furthermore, entering into a contract between a slave and a slave master was another way through which a person became a slave.
pg051_n0017: In this case, a person volunteered to be a slave for a certain period of time because of reasons such as poverty.
pg051_n0018: Sometimes, a person could sell a child into slavery in exchange for land, food or money.
pg051_n0022: As a mode of production, slavery was characterised by the following features:
pg051_n0024: Under the slave mode of production, the population was divided into free and enslaved people.
pg051_n0025: Free people had civil, property and political rights while the enslaved were deprived of all these rights and could not join the ranks of free people.
pg051_n0026: Free people included large landowners who were also slave owners.
pg051_n0028: The existence of classes of slaves and slave owners characterised the slave mode of production.
pg051_n0029: Slave labour became the main means of production where slave masters exploited slaves.
pg051_n0030: The masters were economically powerful because they owned property, especially the slaves.
pg051_n0031: They also controlled the society’s economic, political and cultural institutions.
pg051_n0032: The rise of the states also characterised this mode of production.
pg051_n0033: In Africa, states emerged when societies could produce surplus.
pg051_n0034: People who were separated from the production processes at this stage became rulers.
pg051_n0035: The elders and military clan leaders became kings and princes, while others, especially people with low income, were subjected to slavery.
pg051_n0036: Moreover, the slave mode of production was characterised by the improvement of productive forces, which later facilitated the production of surplus and the division of labour.
pg051_n0041: What are the limitations of social classes in the society?
pg052_n0005: Feudalism was the third mode of production based on land and cattle ownership.
pg052_n0006: It was the second exploitative mode of production after the slave mode of production.
pg052_n0007: Under this, there were two classes of people.
pg052_n0008: The first class consisted of feudal lords who owned the major means of production and appropriated the surplus.
pg052_n0009: The other one comprised serfs and tenants who were given pieces of land to cultivate.
pg052_n0010: In return, they paid rent to the feudal lords.
pg052_n0012: Origins and development of feudalism in pre-colonial Africa
pg052_n0014: Feudalism developed among the African societies which had undergone political centralisation.
pg052_n0015: Powerful kings owned and controlled all the land.
pg052_n0016: They gave some of it to chiefs.
pg052_n0017: The chiefs provided services to the kings in return for the land.
pg052_n0018: They rented some of it to peasants for farming and grazing purposes.
pg052_n0019: The peasants provided certain services to the chiefs in return for the land.
pg052_n0020: They also gave part of their farm produce to the rulers so that they could be protected from all kinds of threats.
pg052_n0022: The nature of rent which tenants or peasants paid changed as feudalism developed.
pg052_n0023: Initially, peasants paid rent in the form of labour.
pg052_n0024: Later, as feudalism evolved, landlords demanded rent in the form of products from peasants.
pg052_n0025: This form of rent is called rent in kind.
pg052_n0026: Thus, peasants would give some of their produces to landlords as rent.
pg052_n0027: As feudalism developed and the money economy took shape in the societies, landlords started to demand rent in the form of cash.
pg052_n0028: This is also known as money rent.
pg052_n0030: Some of the feudal states which emerged in Africa included Egypt, Axum, Nubia and Ethiopia in north-eastern Africa, Mwenemutapa and Lunda in central Africa.
pg052_n0031: In the interlacustrine region there were Buganda, Karagwe, Buhaya, and Bunyoro kingdoms.
pg052_n0032: In the East African coast, feudalism existed on the Zanzibar Island.
pg052_n0033: In West Africa there were states such as Ghana, Mali and Songhay, Asante, Oyo, Benin and Dahomey.
pg052_n0035: Areas that practised the feudal mode of production in pre-colonial Africa
pg052_n0037: The following are areas that practised the feudal mode of production in pre-colonial Africa.
pg052_n0041: The interlacustrine region is the area located between the Great Lakes of East Africa.
pg052_n0042: The lakes are Victoria, Tanganyika, Kivu, Albert, Edward, and Kyoga.
pg052_n0043: The kingdoms found in this region were Bunyoro, Busoga, Ankole, Buganda, Rwanda, Burundi, Buhaya, and Karagwe.
pg052_n0044: In these areas feudalism started after the fall of Bunyoro-Kitara about fifteen hundred C.E.
pg052_n0045: The main economic activities were farming and livestock keeping.
pg052_n0046: The people in these kingdoms grew various types of cereals and bananas.
pg052_n0047: They mainly kept the long-horned cattle, goats, and sheep.
pg053_n0003: The interlacustrine region developed feudal relations, which appeared in two main forms.
pg053_n0004: The first form of feudalism was based on land ownership.
pg053_n0005: Land was needed for banana cultivation.
pg053_n0006: The areas where this form of feudalism existed included Buganda, Buhaya, Uzinza, and Ukerewe.
pg053_n0007: The second form was based on cattle keeping.
pg053_n0008: The areas which developed feudal relations on the basis of cattle keeping were Burundi, Rwanda, Karagwe, and Ankole.
pg053_n0012: In Buganda, feudalism was connected with the coming into power of Kabaka in the seventeenth century.
pg053_n0013: Initially, Kabaka faced strong opposition from the indigenous clan rulers.
pg053_n0014: In order to consolidate his political power in the kingdom, Kabaka decided to take a number of steps.
pg053_n0015: First, he confiscated and controlled all land.
pg053_n0016: Being the controller of land and being in charge of politics in the kingdom, he distributed land to the nobilities, who were known as the Balangira, and to his own favourites known as the Batongore.
pg053_n0017: By appointing his own assistant chiefs, Kabaka gradually succeeded in weakening the powers of the clan heads.
pg053_n0018: By controlling large tracts of arable land which was offered to a few people, Buganda developed feudalism.
pg053_n0020: At the same time, many people were landless.
pg053_n0021: As a result, there were two classes of people in Buganda, the class of landowners and that of the landless.
pg053_n0022: The landless were tied to feudal relations, on the basis of which they had to pay feudal rent.
pg053_n0023: Akasanvu was one of the types of rent they paid.
pg053_n0024: This was a system which required the tenants to provide labour for government projects.
pg053_n0025: The other form of rent was Obusulu, which was paid in the form of labour or goods in return for protection by the chief.
pg053_n0026: Envunjo was the third type of rent.
pg053_n0027: This was a gift of one-tenth of a person's produce given to the chief as a sign of respect for the chief.
pg053_n0028: By the onset of colonialism in the late nineteenth century, Buganda had completely changed into a feudal society.
pg053_n0032: Buhaya developed feudal relations like those of the Buganda Kingdom.
pg053_n0033: The feudal system of production that evolved in Buhaya was known as Nyarubanja, which was based on land ownership.
pg053_n0034: The Bahaya society developed feudalism when it started to transform itself into elaborate political chiefdoms.
pg053_n0035: The Bahaya called their king Omukama.
pg053_n0036: The Omukama controlled all the land and used it as he wished.
pg053_n0037: He distributed land to the lesser kings called the Bakungu and the nobility called the Balangira.
pg053_n0038: The peasants were the majority and possessed land on behalf of the Omukama.
pg053_n0039: The new form of land ownership created two main classes in Buhaya, landowners and peasants.
pg053_n0041: The class of landowners consisted of the Omukama, the Bakungu, and the Balangira.
pg053_n0042: These formed the landed-ruling class called Batwazi.
pg053_n0043: The peasants formed the class of serfs called Batwarwa.
pg053_n0044: The Batwazi imposed certain feudal obligations on the
pg054_n0003: Batwarwa such as the payment of rent in the form of labour, kind, and cash.
pg054_n0004: Up to the time of establishing colonialism in the late nineteenth century, feudal relations were still quite evident in Buhaya.
pg054_n0008: The feudal relations in Urundi and Ruanda, nowadays Burundi and Rwanda, were shaped by cattle ownership.
pg054_n0009: Cattle owners formed the class of feudal lords.
pg054_n0010: In the cattle culture, two dominant economies were practised, namely agricultural and pastoral economies.
pg054_n0011: In Urundi and Ruanda the Tutsi were pastoralists.
pg054_n0012: The Hutu formed the class of peasants in both Urundi and Ruanda.
pg054_n0013: The Tutsi pastoralists exploited the Hutu agriculturalists by imposing feudal obligations on them in the form of payment of rent in return for protection.
pg054_n0014: In Ruanda, two forms of feudal relations existed.
pg054_n0015: These were known as Umuheto and Ubhuhake.
pg054_n0016: In Urundi, the feudal relations were known as Ubugabire.
pg054_n0017: Rent payment was established in both kingdoms.
pg054_n0018: The payment of rent was known as Kutonja or Kugaba.
pg054_n0022: The feudal system that developed on the coast of East Africa was known as Umwinyi.
pg054_n0023: This system existed along the coast for many years.
pg054_n0024: Umwinyi was largely practised in Zanzibar, and it existed side by side with slavery.
pg054_n0026: In the hierarchical structure of coastal feudalism, the overall control of the feudal lords was exercised by Mwinyi Mkuu.
pg054_n0027: He enjoyed unquestionable political, social and economic privileges.
pg054_n0032: Determining and imposing feudal obligations on his subjects;
pg054_n0035: Exercising overall political power in his dominion;
pg054_n0041: Charging and controlling the fees paid by his subjects; and
pg054_n0046: Under Mwinyi Mkuu were his vassals.
pg054_n0047: The first group of the vassals was known as the Sheha or Diwani.
pg054_n0048: They assisted Mwinyi Mkuu in administering the dominion.
pg054_n0049: For example, they administered the villages and ensured law and order in their respective villages.
pg054_n0050: The Sheha was also called Sheha wa Mji or Mjumbe.
pg054_n0051: He ensured that all the people in his area paid their rent and fees.
pg054_n0052: He retained part of the feudal fees paid and submitted the surplus to Mwinyi Mkuu.
pg054_n0054: He did that because he controlled the village fund known as Koba la Mji.
pg054_n0055: The Sheha appointed officials who assisted him in collecting taxes in the village.
pg055_n0003: Under the Sheha or Diwani were tax collectors known as the Shakua.
pg055_n0004: The taxes collected by the Shakua were usually in the form of millet and mangrove poles.
pg055_n0005: People also paid feudal rent in the form of labour.
pg055_n0006: They worked for Mwinyi Mkuu for a number of days in return for food and protection.
pg055_n0007: Below the Shakua were some religious leaders known as Wavyale or Wazale.
pg055_n0008: They performed various religious functions and duties such as leading prayers and burials.
pg055_n0009: They also functioned as traditional healers, countered witchcraft and presided over rituals.
pg055_n0010: Moreover, they blessed the land and economic activities in the villages.
pg055_n0011: They survived by appropriating part of the surplus wealth produced by peasants.

pg056_n0020: The feudal mode of production permitted private ownership of the major means of production, especially land.
pg056_n0023: There were two classes under the feudal mode of production.
pg056_n0027: As a mode of production, feudalism had the following features:
pg056_n0029: The feudal mode of production permitted private ownership of the major means of production especially land.
pg056_n0030: Therefore, land was privately owned and controlled by feudal lords.
pg056_n0031: Those who owned land were economically and politically powerful as they could do anything to get their interests without the consent of the landless, serfs.

pg056_n0034: There were exploitative relations through which the feudal lords exploited the serfs and peasants who paid various kinds of rent such as labour rent and rent in kind.
pg056_n0035: With respect to labour rent, for example, peasants and serfs were given plots of land by the landlords and were supposed to work on their plots and on those of their landlords using their own implements.
pg056_n0037: Feudalism was characterised by the presence of classes, namely landlords and serfs or tenants.
pg056_n0038: The landlords were the ruling class.
pg056_n0039: The ruling class in these states had political power and collected tributes from peasants.
pg056_n0040: The feudal system also permitted the division of labour and specialisation.
pg056_n0041: People specialised in different activities like agriculture, fishing, pastoralism and industries.
pg056_n0042: This division of labour and specialisation were the result of surplus production.
pg057_n0003: The productive forces in the feudal mode of production were more advanced than those in communal and slave modes of production.
pg057_n0004: In the feudal mode iron tools were widely used.
pg057_n0005: That is why there was relatively high production of grains and other items.
pg057_n0006: Therefore, advancement in productive forces created surplus which supported other economic sectors such as trading, mining, agriculture and handcraft industries.
pg057_n0007: Although other economic activities were also carried out during feudalism, agriculture was the major activity.
pg057_n0008: For example, in the western Sudanic states yams and cassava were grown as major food crops.
pg057_n0009: Likewise, in the Buganda Kingdom and in other parts of the interlacustrine region, banana and cassava were cultivated as food crops.

pg059_n0005: Development of agriculture in pre-colonial African societies
pg059_n0009: Iron technology in pre-colonial African societies brought significant changes in agriculture.
pg059_n0010: Iron tools enabled communities to clear forests, break up soils and increase production.
pg059_n0011: Farmers could cultivate large plots of land efficiently by using iron tools such as hoes.
pg059_n0012: In this chapter, you will learn about the agriculture, pastoralism and mixed farming in pre-colonial African societies.
pg059_n0013: The competencies developed will enable you to cherish agricultural innovations and practises of the pre-colonial African societies that laid the foundation for modern agriculture.
pg059_n0017: On benefits of engaging in agriculture
pg059_n0021: Agriculture is an activity involving cultivating crops and keeping livestock.
pg059_n0022: It started at the end of the Late Stone Age after human beings had improved their tools of production.
pg059_n0023: The kind of crops cultivated or animals kept in an area depended on the environment and the efficiency of the tools used.
pg059_n0024: Examples of crops cultivated in pre-colonial Africa were maize, sorghum, millet, finger millet, yams, and wheat.
pg059_n0025: Domesticated animals included cattle, goats, sheep, camels and donkeys.
pg059_n0027: Agricultural practices were influenced by environmental factors such as conducive weather conditions, free from diseases, and vegetation cover.
pg059_n0028: These factors worked hand in hand with the level of technology attained by a particular society.
pg059_n0029: The term environment refers to the natural world in which human beings live.
pg059_n0030: It includes fellow human beings, land, water bodies, forests, mountains, and many other physical features.
pg060_n0003: In addition, the environment includes other man-made features such as dams, buildings, and harbours.
pg060_n0004: As mentioned earlier, environmental factors such as weather conditions, free from diseases and vegetation cover largely determined the types of economic activities undertaken in a given place.
pg060_n0005: For example, crops like bananas and wheat were cultivated in areas that received relatively high amounts of rainfall.
pg060_n0006: In contrast, crops such as sorghum and millet were cultivated in areas that received moderate or low amounts of rainfall in savannah areas.
pg060_n0008: Technology refers to the practical application of science in making tools.
pg060_n0009: It helps improve human lives in a given environment.
pg060_n0010: For example, the discovery of ironworking enabled human beings to develop tools for agricultural production, defence, and hunting.
pg060_n0011: Our ancestors invented tools which enabled them to control their environment.
pg060_n0012: They continued to improve their technology as they faced new life challenges throughout history.
pg060_n0013: For example, African societies started using stone tools and later invented iron tools.
pg060_n0014: These remarkable achievements led to the development of various economic activities, including agriculture.
pg060_n0016: Types of agricultural practices in pre-colonial Africa
pg060_n0018: Pre-colonial African societies developed three types of agricultural practices by seventeen hundred C E.
pg060_n0019: These were crop cultivation, pastoralism, and mixed farming.
pg060_n0023: Crop cultivation is a type of agriculture involving the use of land to grow different types of crops.
pg060_n0024: There were two types of crop cultivation practiced during the pre-colonial period, namely, shifting and permanent crop cultivation.
pg060_n0028: Shifting cultivation involves the movement of farmers from one place to another.
pg060_n0029: This type of crop cultivation was common in grassland areas with long dry seasons and scattered trees.
pg060_n0030: An area with such natural vegetation is known as savannah.
pg060_n0032: In the savannah areas, soils were light and fertile.
pg060_n0033: However, soil fertility in these areas exhausted quickly after a few years of cultivation.
pg060_n0034: Human settlements in these areas were usually temporary.
pg060_n0035: People lived in an area for a short time and shifted when their land was exhausted.
pg060_n0036: They moved on to open new agricultural land and settled there to begin crop cultivation again.
pg060_n0037: This could be close to the old farmland or far away from it.
pg060_n0038: The old farmland was left to fallow.
pg060_n0039: Sometimes, shifting cultivation involved the use of a particular area for more than one growing season.
pg060_n0041: Under shifting cultivation, people cleared and burned bushes and trees.
pg060_n0042: Planting and sowing began when rainy season started.
pg060_n0043: The crops grown were mainly the
pg061_n0003: drought-resistant ones such as cassava, millet, sorghum, pumpkins, and cowpeas.
pg061_n0004: This type of agriculture produced little harvest that could only support a small population.
pg061_n0005: Thus, little surplus food produced could not support strong centralised states in these areas.
pg061_n0008: Shifting cultivation involved livestock keeping as well.
pg061_n0009: Shifting cultivators kept animals such as cattle, sheep, and goats.
pg061_n0010: These animals provided them with milk, meat, blood, manure, and hides.
pg061_n0011: In East Africa, such societies lived in central, southern, and western Tanzania.
pg061_n0012: They also lived in most parts of central and north-eastern Kenya.
pg061_n0013: The presence of tsetse flies infected both people and animals with trypanosomiasis, sleeping sickness.
pg061_n0014: In West Africa, Mandinka and Bambara were among the societies that practised shifting cultivation.
pg061_n0016: Shifting cultivation had the major disadvantage of intensive labour power because it needed much labour to clear the vegetation before planting crops.
pg061_n0020: This was a form of farming where people cultivated the same land for a long period without moving to another area.
pg061_n0021: Pre-colonial African societies in the eastern, western, southern, central, and northern parts of the continent practised permanent crop cultivation.
pg061_n0022: In Central Africa, the Shona and Bemba were among the ethnic groups that practised permanent crop cultivation.
pg061_n0023: The crops grown included millet, sorghum, and beans.
pg061_n0024: In West Africa, some of the ethnic groups that participated in permanent crop cultivation were the Ashanti, Yoruba, Akan, and the Edo.
pg061_n0025: Some of the crops grown included millet, yams, cassava, groundnuts, bambara nuts, and palm oil.
pg061_n0027: In addition, permanent crop cultivation was also practised in the central and southern regions in pre-colonial Africa.
pg061_n0028: The Shona, Bemba, Sotho, and Zulu were among the ethnic groups that practised permanent crop cultivation.
pg061_n0029: The crops grown in these regions are maize, sorghum, millet, and beans.
pg061_n0030: In Northern Africa, the Berbers cultivated crops such as wheat, barley, and olives.
pg061_n0031: However, it is important to note that societies developed a unique agricultural system in a particular region, depending on the available resources, climatic condition, and traditional beliefs.
pg061_n0035: The following were the advantages of permanent crop cultivation.
pg061_n0036: It led to an increase in agricultural production.
pg061_n0037: Also, it stimulated population growth, since there was adequate food.
pg061_n0038: Moreover, it stimulated the exchange of goods or trade. The long-distance trade routes in Eastern Africa and West Africa show that exchange of agricultural and mineral goods took place.
pg062_n0003: It also led to the development of permanent settlements which rose to urban centers that served as trading towns.
pg062_n0004: In addition, it led to the emergence and growth of centralised political systems like chiefdoms and kingdoms.
pg062_n0005: Likewise, it encouraged the improvement of farming technology.
pg062_n0006: People needed better tools in order to simplify their work and increase production.
pg062_n0007: The main disadvantage of permanent crop cultivation is that it led to increase of conflicts in society.
pg062_n0009: These conflicts resulted from the scarcity of resources, especially the control of fertile land and iron ore sites caused by the increase in population.
pg062_n0011: Both shifting and permanent cultivators invented and used various techniques for improving crop yields.
pg062_n0012: The Nyakyusa, Shambaa, Sukuma, and Nyamwezi, for example, terraced hillsides.
pg062_n0013: This technique conserved water and prevented soil erosion.
pg062_n0014: Similarly, water canals were dug in the gardens to keep rainwater.
pg062_n0015: The Buganda, Ankole, Buhaya, and Ufipa grew various crops in their farms to conserve moisture.
pg062_n0016: They also made banks on which they planted crops such as yams and potatoes.
pg062_n0017: Such banks kept rainwater and prevented soil erosion.
pg062_n0018: Plant remains were buried, decayed, and became composite manure.
pg062_n0019: People who lived in the highlands, such as the Chagga, Pare, and Shambaa, dug irrigation furrows into their farms.
pg062_n0020: They also made and used composite manure as well as manure produced by cattle and goat.
pg062_n0021: The people of Ukerewe and Ukara Islands enriched the soil with composite and animal manure.
pg062_n0022: They also kept cattle, which provided milk, meat, and manure.

pg063_n0005: Pastoralism refers to keeping and grazing livestock.
pg063_n0006: People who practised pastoralism were called pastoralists.
pg063_n0007: Ancient pastoral communities kept animals such as cattle, sheep, camel, donkeys, and goats.
pg063_n0009: For example, they provided meat, milk, blood, manure, and hides or animal skins.
pg063_n0010: In some societies, animals like camels and donkeys were used for transportation, for carrying people and goods.
pg063_n0011: In many societies, livestock was a source of wealth.
pg063_n0012: People who owned huge stock of livestock were the richest in the society.
pg063_n0013: They felt prestige and enjoyed privileges because of their wealth.
pg063_n0014: They could loan their cattle to poor people in exchange for labour, loyalty, and patronage.
pg063_n0017: Cattle, goats and sheep were used for paying dowry.
pg063_n0018: In Zulu, Xhosa, Swazi, Shona and Ndebele livestock were paid as Lobola.
pg063_n0019: Lobola is a property in livestock or kind which a prospective husband or head of his family undertakes to give to the head of prospective wife’s family in gratitude of letting the husband marry their daughter.
pg063_n0020: Black cattle and sheep were slaughtered in traditional ceremonies such as wedding, burial, rainmaking, initiation and coronation of a chief or king onto the throne.
pg063_n0021: Pastoralism was common in arid, semi-arid, and savannah or tropical grassland areas in pre-colonial Africa.
pg063_n0024: There were two types of pastoral societies, namely nomadic and sedentary or settled pastoralists.
pg063_n0028: These pastoralists often moved from one place to another in search of water and pasture for their livestock.
pg063_n0029: They lived on milk, meat, and blood.
pg063_n0030: They also ate vegetables and food grains such as maize and sorghum.
pg063_n0031: These were obtained through exchange with neighbouring agricultural communities, which needed livestock products.
pg063_n0032: Nomadic pastoralists were also war-like people; they were always ready to fight in defence of their wealth.
pg063_n0033: They raided their neighbours for livestock from time to time.
pg063_n0034: Examples of nomadic pastoralists were the Tuaregs of North Africa, the Fulani of northern Nigeria, the Somali of Somalia and Kenya, the Karamajong of northern Uganda, and the Maasai of Tanzania and Kenya.
pg063_n0038: Sedentary pastoralism was a form of animal husbandry in which livestock were kept in one location.
pg063_n0039: The livestock kept include cattle, goats, sheep, camels and donkeys.
pg063_n0040: Herders with knowledge of local environment and the needs of the animals tended the livestock.
pg063_n0041: Sedentary pastoralism enabled pre-colonial African societies to build settled communities while depending on their livestock for food and economic development.
pg064_n0003: These communities were purposely located near water sources and grazing areas.
pg064_n0004: Livestock in pre-colonial African societies remained important resources, providing not only food but also materials for clothing and shelter.
pg064_n0005: Some of the societies that practised sedentary pastoralism were Khoikhoi and the San in the southern part of Africa.
pg064_n0006: In the savannah regions of East Africa, the Maasai and Samburu practised sedentary pastoralism.
pg064_n0007: In West Africa, some groups of the Fulani were nomadic; others adopted a settled lifestyle that included pastoral activities.
pg064_n0008: Some animals kept were cattle, goats, sheep, camels and donkeys.
pg064_n0009: Both nomadic and sedentary pastoralists were able to identify various herbs to treaty their diseased animals.
pg064_n0014: How did nomadic pastoralists in pre-colonial African societies adapt to their environment?
pg064_n0016: Explain how sedentary pastoralists in pre-colonial African societies structure their communities.
pg064_n0020: Some societies combined animal keeping and crop cultivation.
pg064_n0021: This type of agriculture is known as mixed farming.
pg064_n0022: It was practised in areas with heavy rainfall as well as in grasslands with seasonal rainfall and woodland savannah.
pg064_n0023: It was practised by people such as the Gogo, Nyaturu, Nyiramba, Sukuma, Nyamwezi, Hutu, Ankole, Pare and Kimbu.
pg064_n0024: These people grew both permanent and seasonal crops such as bananas, yams, beans, and cereals.
pg064_n0025: They also kept livestock such as cattle, sheep, goats and donkeys.
pg064_n0026: The long-horned Ankole types of cattle were kept in the interlacustrine region.
pg064_n0027: The short-horned cattle known as zebu were kept in the drier woodland savannah and wooded steppes.
pg064_n0028: Other societies that practised mixed farming in pre-colonial Africa were Rwozi in Central Africa.
pg064_n0029: They applied irrigation and terracing methods.
pg064_n0030: In West Africa the Hausa, Yoruba, Ewe, Ashanti, Nupe and Igbo practised mixed farming.
pg064_n0031: These societies cultivated variety of cash crops and raised livestock.
pg064_n0032: They grew crops such as millet, sorghum, yams, maize, and raised livestock like cattle, sheep and goats.

pg066_n0003: Ways in which pre-colonial agriculture changed the lives of human beings
pg066_n0005: Agriculture led to increased food production.
pg066_n0006: This, in turn, contributed to population increase.
pg066_n0007: As the population grew, social conflicts emerged.
pg066_n0008: This gave rise to the need for leadership to solve conflicts.
pg066_n0009: Leadership also became increasingly responsible for protecting important sources of wealth such as salt mines, pastoral lands, and iron ore.
pg066_n0010: Similarly, leadership became responsible for the distribution and utilisation of resources such as land, water, and pastures.
pg066_n0012: Moreover, agricultural activities contributed to the rise of specialisations.
pg066_n0013: For examples, while some community members engaged in agriculture, others made iron tools or engaged in fishing, basketry, or pottery.
pg066_n0014: Specialisation emerged because of two main reasons: Firstly, not every member of society engaged in crop cultivation or animal keeping.
pg066_n0015: Secondly, there was surplus food to feed non-food producers who specialised in skilled craft works.
pg066_n0016: Hence, some people weaved baskets and mats while others made and repaired iron tools.
pg066_n0017: Others specialised in trade and exchanged their surplus products in order to obtain commodities that they did not produce.
pg066_n0019: The combination of population growth and raise of specialisation led to exchange relations which later on created trading posts.
pg066_n0020: These posts grew to become urban centres which functioned as trading, cultural and administrative centres.
pg066_n0021: Examples of these centres were Taghaza, Bilma, Taoden and Niamey in West Africa.

pg067_n0007: Three. Identify the features of pre-colonial agricultural systems that still exist in present-day societies.
pg067_n0008: Four. How did environmental factors determine crop selection and farming methods in pre-colonial agriculture?

pg068_n0004: Handcraft and mining industries in pre-colonial Africa
pg068_n0009: Pre-colonial African societies underwent various transformations in economic aspects such as handcraft and mining.
pg068_n0010: These transformations were largely a result of human’s struggle to improve technology to manage the environment.
pg068_n0011: In this chapter, you will learn about types of industries that existed in pre-colonial Africa.
pg068_n0012: You will also learn different types of minerals extracted in pre-colonial African societies.
pg068_n0013: The competencies developed will enable you to appreciate the efforts our ancestors made to improve their standard of living and sustain life.
pg068_n0017: Handcraft industries that are available in your society
pg068_n0021: An industry is a place where transformation of raw materials into finished goods is carried out.
pg068_n0022: In pre-colonial Africa, the natural resources that existed in a given society determined the nature of industries found in that area.
pg068_n0023: For example, in iron smelting industry, iron ore was smelted and forged into iron goods such as knives and hoes.
pg068_n0024: Similarly, people moulded and baked clay into pots, bowls and bricks in areas rich in suitable clayey soil.
pg068_n0026: Besides, handcraft refers to an art of using skills and hands to design and fashion things.
pg068_n0027: Handcraft industries were a type of industries in which humans used hands, skills and knowledge to produce different products such as baskets, pots and mats.
pg068_n0028: Handcraft industries enabled people to make and obtain tools and other objects.
pg068_n0029: In pre-colonial Africa, different handcraft industries emerged as people specialised in other activities apart from agriculture.
pg068_n0030: These included iron making industries, basketry, spinning, weaving, cloth making, carving and canoe making.
pg069_n0005: Cloth making was an art of making clothes from local cotton species, barks of trees and animal skins.
pg069_n0006: A number of communities in pre-colonial Africa specialised in cloth making.
pg069_n0007: Clothes were made by pounding the bark of certain trees.
pg069_n0008: They also decorated clothes using dyes.
pg069_n0009: This way of making clothes was common among the Haya, Nyakyusa and Ganda of East Africa who used appropriate tree barks to make clothes.
pg069_n0010: Other societies used skins of animals such as sheep, goats and camels to make clothes.
pg069_n0011: This was common in Madagascar, Northern Africa, Sudan and the Sahel belt of West Africa, as well as among the Yoruba and people from Malawi and Mozambique.
pg069_n0013: Moreover, cotton cloth making was common in many African societies of Aksum-Sudan, Iwelen-Nigeria, Takrur-Ghana, Ufipa, Unyamwezi and Unyiha in East Africa.
pg069_n0014: Other societies were the Shire Valley in Malawi and Igombe-Ilede in South Africa.
pg069_n0015: Figure five point one shows cloth making in pre-colonial Africa.
pg069_im001: Decorated cloth panels and two people weaving fabric on a simple outdoor loom, showing cloth making in pre-colonial Africa.
pg069_n0017: Figure five point one: cloth making in pre-colonial Africa.
pg069_n0021: People wore clothes in order to cover their bodies from nakedness, to decorate themselves, or keep themselves warm.
pg069_n0022: Clothes were also worn on special occasions such as during religious, traditional and funeral ceremonies.
pg069_n0023: Colours of clothes were also important, for example in some societies.
pg069_n0024: For example, rainmakers wore black clothes as a symbol of dark clouds which pour rains.
pg069_n0025: In other societies twins were not allowed to wear read clothes during raining seasons.
pg069_n0026: Clothes became important commodities that stimulated the development of trade in the pre-colonial period.
pg070_n0005: Pottery is an art of making pots and other items from clayey soils.
pg070_n0006: This skill was common in areas with suitable clayey soil.
pg070_n0007: In pre-colonial Africa, people who specialised in pottery made items such as pots, pipes, and bowls for domestic use and exchange.
pg070_n0008: Pottery was common among the Pare of North-Eastern Tanzania, the Kerewe of the Ukerewe Island in Lake Victoria, and the Kisi on the shores of Lake Nyasa.
pg070_n0009: It was also common in the Nok area in Northern Nigeria.
pg070_n0013: Pottery was useful for making objects for cooking and storing water, beer, milk, and grains.
pg070_n0014: Pottery objects also became important commodities in both local and regional trade.
pg070_n0015: For example, Pare potters traded their objects with neighbouring societies such as the Chagga, Taveta and the Maasai.
pg070_n0016: Kisi potters traded their objects with the Nyakyusa, Ndali, Kinga, Pangwa, Ngoni, and other neighbouring societies.
pg070_n0017: The Lozi of Zambia traded pots among themselves and with their neighbours, the Lunda and Bisa.
pg070_n0021: Basketry is the art of weaving palm leaves and other special reeds to make items like fish traps, mats, hats, baskets and ropes.
pg070_n0022: Basketry was practised by many societies in pre-colonial Africa including the Nyamwezi, Gogo, Zaramo, Yao and Ganda.
pg070_n0023: Basketry was also common among the Chokwe, Lozi, and Tonga of Zambia, Buga of Guinea and Liberia.
pg070_n0024: Others included Sara of Chad, Zulu of South Africa, Barotse and Twana of Botswana and Bamileke of Cameroon.
pg070_n0025: The materials used in basketry were mostly obtained from palm trees, reeds, bamboos and various types of grass that were found in many places.
pg070_n0026: Figure five point two shows basketry products in pre-colonial Africa.
pg070_im001: Various basketry products from pre-colonial Africa, including a large round woven mat, a hat, a lidded basket, a shallow tray, two handled baskets, and a decorated woven container.
pg070_n0028: Figure five point two: basketry products in pre-colonial Africa.
pg071_n0005: Baskets were used in different ways.
pg071_n0006: Some of them were used for collecting and carrying agricultural products from farms while others were using for storing grain and seeds for later use.
pg071_n0007: Basketry also produced fish traps which were used for catching fish in rivers, lakes and oceans.
pg071_n0008: Mats were used for sitting, sleeping and drying foodstuff.
pg071_n0009: Moreover, they were used for wrapping human dead bodies for burial.
pg071_n0013: Carpentry involved working on wood logs and poles to make wooden products.
pg071_n0014: This art was common in many African communities living in woodland environment.
pg071_n0015: For example, artisans carved wood to make stools, mortars, pestles, doors, canoes, beehives, and wooden basins.
pg071_n0019: Canoes were used for transporting people and commodities and fishing.
pg071_n0020: The Makonde of Southern Tanzania and Northern Mozambique carved wood to make figurines, masks, earrings and bracelets.
pg071_n0021: Other people made mortars to pound grains into flour and crash herbs into usable medicine.
pg071_n0025: Your school has an arranged inter-school debate on the motion, “Handcraft industries are still important in today's world”.
pg071_n0026: Prepare the points that you would give to support or oppose the motion
pg071_n0030: Mining is the extraction of minerals from the ground.
pg071_n0031: It was practised in different parts of Africa by people who had knowledge and skills in mineral extraction.
pg071_n0032: Examples of such minerals in pre-colonial Africa were iron, salt, gold, copper, silver and tin.
pg071_n0036: Ironworking started in some of the African communities in the first millennium B C E.
pg071_n0037: In East Africa, this technology started around five hundred B C E and widely spread in the region by around one thousand seven hundred C E.
pg071_n0038: The production of iron tools passed through the following main stages: firstly, iron ore was mined from the ground.
pg071_n0039: Secondly, the ore was smelted in furnaces in order to purify it.
pg071_n0040: Thirdly, pure iron was left to cool and
pg072_n0004: Fourthly, the solidified iron was heated until it became red hot.
pg072_n0005: Then it was hammered into different shaped tools or weapons.
pg072_n0006: The process of hammering iron into tools is known as forging.
pg072_n0007: People who specialised in processing iron into iron tools and weapons were called ironsmiths.
pg072_n0008: Figure five point three shows a kiln for iron extraction among the Fipa of Tanzania.
pg072_im001: Traditional clay kiln used for iron extraction among the Fipa, shown partly broken open with a dark interior and a measuring rod beside it in a grassy field.
pg072_n0010: Figure five point three: Kiln for iron extraction among the Fipa
pg072_n0012: In East Africa, ironworking developed among the Meru, Kerewe, Haya, Fipa, and Baganda.
pg072_n0013: Among the Pare, ironsmiths came from the royal Shana clan.
pg072_n0014: Among the Zinza of Geita, iron smelting was taught to anyone who paid a fee to learn that skill.
pg072_n0015: Similarly, iron technology developed among the Venda people of Southern
pg073_n0003: Transvaal in South Africa and the Teso of Eastern Uganda.
pg073_n0004: Others were the Mashona of Zimbabwe, the Mang’anja of Malawi, and societies around Kalambo Falls in Zambia.
pg073_n0005: In West Africa, ironworking societies were found in the Futa Djalon plateau in present-day Guinea.
pg073_n0006: In North-eastern Africa, examples included societies in Nubia and Meroe in present-day Sudan as well as Axum in present-day Ethiopia.
pg073_n0010: The use of iron tools and weapons had many advantages.
pg073_n0011: It led to the improvement of tools, which in turn facilitated the expansion of agriculture and increased food production.
pg073_n0012: Iron tools also simplified the mining of iron and non-iron minerals and the making of other handcrafts.
pg073_n0013: Moreover, communities were able to increase production of different items.
pg073_n0014: This led to the rise and development of trade.
pg073_n0015: In some African areas, people used iron bars as currency.
pg073_n0016: Iron technology consolidated sedentary or settled life.
pg073_n0017: This was because the technology enabled people to establish homes and use iron weapons to defend their families and properties against enemies.
pg073_n0018: It also contributed to the rise of states in some parts of Africa, such as Fipaland, Buganda, and Karagwe.
pg073_n0019: Similarly, the use of iron weapons made great changes in warfare.
pg073_n0020: Societies with iron weapons became stronger.
pg073_n0021: They conquered weaker ones, which were still using stone and wooden weapons.
pg073_n0022: These conquests led to the expansion of chiefdoms or kingdoms.
pg073_n0023: It also increased the frequency of wars among rival communities.
pg073_n0027: Salt making was among the earliest industries in pre-colonial Africa.
pg073_n0028: There were four main methods of obtaining and processing salt.
pg073_n0029: These were salt extraction from salty reeds, leaching of rocky soils, salt mining from rocks, and evaporating salty water.
pg073_n0032: Salty reeds were burnt and the ash was dissolved in water.
pg073_n0033: The solution was filtered and boiled until all the water evaporated.
pg073_n0034: The remaining residue was used as salt.
pg073_n0035: This method was common among the Mang’anja people along Lake Nyasa, also around Lake Victoria and Lake Albert in East Africa.
pg073_n0036: It was also commonly practised among the people of the interlacustrine region.
pg073_n0039: Leaching is a method by which water was drained through rocky soils that had a high content of salt.
pg073_n0040: It was sieved and boiled to obtain salt crystals.
pg073_n0041: The method was practised at Uvinza and Ivuna in Tanzania and at Bilma in West Africa.
pg073_n0044: In this method, people directly mined salty rocks.
pg073_n0045: Then, the rock crystals were used as salt.
pg073_n0046: This method was used by people around Bangwelo and Luapula rivers in Central Africa and Lake Chad in Western Sudan.
pg073_n0047: In West Africa, the method was used at Bilma, Taghaza, Idjil, and Taoudeni.
pg074_n0003: Evaporation. In the evaporation method, salty ocean water was trapped in pans and left to dry under the heat of the sun.
pg074_n0004: After drying, salt crystals remained in the pans.
pg074_n0005: This method was and is still common along the East African coast.
pg074_n0006: For example, salt pans are found along the coastline of Tanga, Bagamoyo, Dar es Salaam and Lindi.
pg074_n0009: Read different reliable online and library sources on the methods used to extract salt, uses of salt and economic opportunities available around salt extraction areas.
pg074_n0010: Then write a report and share it for discussion.
pg074_n0014: Salt had many uses in the pre-colonial period.
pg074_n0015: It served as a food ingredient and preservative.
pg074_n0016: Foodstuff, such as beef and fish lasted longer when salted.
pg074_n0017: Salt was also used as a medium of exchange because it was a rare commodity in many societies.
pg074_n0018: Therefore, it became an important commodity in trade.
pg074_n0019: For example, salt from Uvinza was a commodity of exchange all over the Great Lakes region.
pg074_n0020: In addition, the people of Ethiopia and the merchants of Timbuktu in the Sahara Desert used salt as a medium of exchange.
pg074_n0021: Likewise, salt was used for the treatment of wounds.
pg074_n0022: In some societies, people used salt as medicine for curing wounds.
pg074_n0023: Sodium bicarbonate was used as antacid to treat indigestion and upset stomach as it reduces stomach acid.
pg074_n0024: Salt was also used for preserving dead bodies from decaying.
pg074_n0025: This was common among ancient Egyptians.
pg074_n0026: This practice of body preservation using salt is called mummification.
pg074_n0029: Briefly explain how handcraft industries led to the development of other sectors of the economy, like trade and agriculture.
pg074_n0033: In pre-colonial Africa, gold was mined and processed in different parts of Africa.
pg074_n0034: In Southern Africa, it was mined along River Sabi and River Zambezi.
pg074_n0035: In West Africa, it was mined in areas such as Bambuk, Bure, Lobi and the forest area of Asante.
pg074_n0036: The common methods used to obtain gold differed from one place to another.
pg075_n0005: In this method, people collected alluvial gold found along the streams or river beds.
pg075_n0006: They used pans to separate gold from sand or rocks.
pg075_n0007: The method was mainly practised along the tributaries of Rivers Sabi and Zambezi which flow across Mozambique and Zimbabwe.
pg075_n0011: Some areas contained underground gold veins.
pg075_n0012: In order to obtain gold, people dug out rocks containing gold.
pg075_n0013: The rocks were then taken to furnaces where they were burnt to obtain pure gold.
pg075_n0014: This method was used in the Mashonaland of Zimbabwe and Asante in Ghana.
pg075_n0018: In pre-colonial Africa, gold was used as a commodity or trade item.
pg075_n0019: It was also used as a medium of exchange or a form of currency.
pg075_n0020: Gold was used for making symbols of power and authority for African rulers.
pg075_n0021: For example, among the Asante of Ghana, the King’s stool was made of gold.
pg075_n0023: In addition, gold was used for making jewelry, ornaments and decorative materials.
pg075_n0024: Furthermore, gold was used to make golden utensils, like cups and plates as well as handles of knives and swords.
pg075_n0025: Likewise, gold served as symbol of wealth and power for those who possessed it.
pg075_n0029: Copper was produced mainly through smelting of copper ores.
pg075_n0030: Ores containing copper were smelted and made into pieces of pure metal shaped like a brick.
pg075_n0031: Mining of copper took place in many areas of pre-colonial Africa.
pg075_n0032: These included Kafue in Zambia, Gwai River in Zimbabwe and Katanga in Congo.
pg075_n0033: Others included the Sinai Peninsula in Egypt and the land of Igbo and Yoruba in Nigeria.
pg075_n0035: Copper had various uses during the pre-colonial period.
pg075_n0036: It was used for making items like ornaments, bowls, copper wire, daggers, and helmets.
pg075_n0037: It was also used as a medium of exchange especially in West Africa.
pg075_n0038: Moreover, copper was used for making fish hooks.
pg075_n0039: This was done mainly in Egypt.

pg077_n0004: Social, political and education systems in pre-colonial Africa
pg077_n0008: Pre-colonial African societies displayed dynamic characteristics and reached different levels of socio-political development.
pg077_n0009: Such development demonstrates their ability to rule themselves, manage conflicts and select their leaders.
pg077_n0010: By fifteen hundred C.E., African societies had developed different social and political systems.
pg077_n0011: In this chapter, you will learn about the concepts of social, political and education systems.
pg077_n0012: You will also learn about the non-centralised political systems that include clan or kinship organisation and the age-set system.
pg077_n0013: You will also learn about the type of education provided in pre-colonial Africa.
pg077_n0014: The competencies developed will enable you apply the positive elements of pre-colonial systems in family and society.
pg077_n0017: A political authority without central government
pg077_n0019: Concepts of social, political and education systems
pg077_n0021: The term “system” refers to a set of objects or things arranged in such a way that they are interrelated to perform a specific function.
pg077_n0022: Each part has a fixed place and a definite role to play.
pg077_n0023: A good example is the digestive system of a human being.
pg077_n0025: Political system describes power relations among people and societies.
pg077_n0026: It includes the governing institutions, how leaders make decisions and how they deal with internal and external matters.
pg077_n0028: A social system is a set of rules, structures and beliefs guiding human interactions and relations in a society.
pg077_n0029: Besides, education is the pattern of knowledge and skills the society transfers from one generation to another to achieve a common goal.
pg078_n0003: In pre-colonial African societies, the development of social, political and educational systems was not similar in all parts of the continent.
pg078_n0004: It varied from one society to another due to factors like geographical location and technological development of a particular society.
pg078_n0005: Some societies practised non-centralised political systems and others had reached centralised political systems.
pg078_n0006: The two political systems differed on how power was shared among the society members and the nature of social relations that existed.
pg078_n0009: Read Sections thirty-three through thirty-six of Chapter Two of the nineteen seventy-seven Constitution of the United Republic of Tanzania, then provide your views on how the Government would perform its functions without the central authority.
pg078_n0013: Non-centralised or decentralised social and political systems were a form of organisation with no central authority.
pg078_n0014: Some of the common characteristics of non-centralised political system included:
pg078_n0016: They did not have a central ruler known as a king; their political leaders were mainly clan heads, assisted by councils of elders; political power and authority were shared among the council of elders and clan heads.
pg078_n0017: There were two forms of non-centralised social and political systems in pre-colonial Africa, namely clan or kinship organisation and the age-set system.
pg078_n0021: A kinship or clan organisation is a type of social and political organisation involving closely related families with the same or common ancestor.
pg078_n0022: This was the most common form of kinship practised worldwide, including pre-colonial Africa.
pg078_n0023: A clan consisted of several families, which are closely related together.
pg078_n0024: Such families consisted of the husband, wife or wives, children, grandparents and extended relatives.
pg078_n0025: The family was the basic unit of production.
pg078_n0026: Some examples of pre-colonial African societies that practised clan or kinship organisation were the Igbo of West Africa, Sukuma of Tanzania and the Kikuyu of Kenya.
pg078_n0027: There were two main types of kinship in pre-colonial Africa.
pg078_n0029: These groups were created for various reasons but served the same goals.
pg079_n0005: This is the most common form of kinship practised worldwide, including Africa.
pg079_n0006: People who practise it trace their kin through their fathers.
pg079_n0007: When a woman is married, she moves to her husband’s clan and becomes part of his kin group.
pg079_n0008: Children in this social system take and follow the names of their father’s clan.
pg079_n0009: Examples of societies that followed the patrilineal system included the Luo of Kenya and Tanzania, the Zulu of South Africa, the Ndebele of Zimbabwe, and the Ngoni and Tumbala of Northern Zambia.
pg079_n0010: One of the characteristics of the patrilineal kinship was that men on the father’s line dominated social, economic and political decisions.
pg079_n0011: They made important decisions concerning the welfare and interests of the family or clan.
pg079_n0012: They also owned and determined the use of the major means of production, like land.
pg079_n0013: They decided on the amount and distribution of the bridewealth and oversaw marriage transactions.
pg079_n0017: Under the matrilineal social system, a married man moves from his father’s family and clan to live with his wife’s family.
pg079_n0018: He may live within the wife’s family compound or nearby.
pg079_n0019: Children take and follow the names of their mother’s clan.
pg079_n0020: Thus, clan inheritance is based on the mother’s clan.
pg079_n0021: In pre-colonial Africa, fathers had no power over children in matrilineal societies.
pg079_n0022: Maternal uncles made all important decisions concerning their nephews and nieces, including deciding on bride wealth.
pg079_n0023: Some societies that followed the matrilineal system were the Luguru of Morogoro, the Yao and the Makonde of Lindi and Mtwara, the Bemba of Zambia, the Mbundu of the Kingdom of Ndongo in Angola, the Herero of Namibia and Botswana, as well as the Ashanti and Akan of Ghana.
pg079_n0026: Read various reliable digital and non-digital sources on patrilineal and matrilineal social systems, then write an essay on social-economic advantages and disadvantages of each system in modern African societies.
pg079_n0029: Characteristics of clan or kinship organisation
pg079_n0031: The following were the characteristics of the clan or kinship organisation.
pg079_n0033: A clan or kinship had common rituals, taboos, and customs.
pg079_n0034: These cultural characteristics helped create stability, strength, and uniqueness of each clan from other clans.
pg079_n0035: They helped to bind members of the clan together and forge a sense of community.
pg080_n0003: Clans or kinships were self-governing but had no rulers or kings.
pg080_n0004: The absence of rulers meant that clans had neither centralised political administration nor state instruments of power.
pg080_n0006: Because of these characteristics, clan or kinship systems are regarded as non-centralised or stateless in nature.
pg080_n0007: It was a social and political organisation without a central government to enforce laws.
pg080_n0008: Clan leaders had limited political and military powers.
pg080_n0010: Clan or kinship communities were small and simple.
pg080_n0011: The populations of clan or kinship communities were small and their levels of economic and technological development were relatively low.
pg080_n0012: They relied on simple activities such as hunting, gathering, fishing and cropping.
pg080_n0013: They also used simple tools made of stone and wood.
pg080_n0014: Some of these communities acquired simple iron tools from neighbouring societies through barter trade.
pg080_n0016: Clans had sufficient land and lived in closely spaced clan units.
pg080_n0017: There was less competition for basic resources such as livestock, agricultural land, minerals, and water.
pg080_n0018: Therefore, there were no marked differences related to wealth or property ownership.
pg080_n0020: Social, political and economic organisation of clans or kinships
pg080_n0022: In clan or kinship organisations, the family was the basic unit of production.
pg080_n0023: Land, which was the major means of production, belonged to the whole clan.
pg080_n0024: However, the tools or instruments of labour belonged to the individual families.
pg080_n0025: The clan head and elders did not own the major means of production.
pg080_n0026: Their responsibility was to allocate the land for use to other clan members.
pg080_n0027: The elders also guided clan members in the production process.
pg080_n0028: Each family in the clan was given as much land as it could utilise.
pg080_n0029: They shared most of the products of labour according to the needs of each member.
pg080_n0030: The basic means of production and product of labour were shared among the members of a given clan.
pg080_n0032: Politically, clan organisation revolved around the position of the clan heads who provided leadership for the group.
pg080_n0033: Clan heads were responsible for regulating political, economic and social relations in the community.
pg080_n0034: They settled disputes in the community, arranged marriages for members, and performed clan rituals.
pg080_n0035: In addition, they allocated land to members of the clan or immigrants; gave names to newly born babies; and acted as guardians of all communal properties such as land, forests, and water sources.
pg080_n0038: The closeness of family units ensured the existence and sustenance of a clan.
pg080_n0039: This closeness was enhanced by cultural elements
pg081_n0003: such as rituals, values, customs, and taboos.
pg081_n0004: These connected individuals and bonded them together as members of the clan.
pg081_n0008: What were the roles of the family in pre-colonial African societies?

pg081_n0016: The age-set system is another form of social and political organisation that existed in pre-colonial Africa.
pg081_n0017: Under this form of organisation, the division of labour and social responsibilities was based on age and sex.
pg081_n0018: This form of socio-political organisation was common among pastoral, agro-pastoral and some agricultural societies.
pg081_n0020: Social, political and economic organisation under age-set system
pg081_n0022: There was no central authority under the age-set system.
pg081_n0023: Instead, the role of leadership and decision-making were made by council of elders.
pg081_n0024: In this system, children of the same age were initiated together and taught the values of their community.
pg081_n0025: They were taught about culture, history, and social responsibilities.
pg081_n0026: After initiation, they were given a group name.
pg081_n0027: From then onwards, they would perform special duties and responsibilities together as an age-set unit.
pg081_n0029: Each age-set consisted of members who belonged to a particular generation.
pg081_n0030: Age groups were determined by initiation, rituals and cultural ceremonies.
pg081_n0031: Seniority in each age group depended on age, wisdom and good character.
pg081_n0032: Leaders in each age group were older than the rest, more hardworking and more reliable.
pg081_n0033: Obedience was an important aspect of life in an age group.
pg081_n0034: The members of an age group made decisions on day-to-day matters concerning their lives.
pg081_n0038: Pastoral communities lived in areas with little rain covered by short grass.
pg081_n0039: These areas were mainly arid and semi-arid.
pg081_n0040: Such environment allowed them to engage in pastoralism as a major economic occupation.
pg081_n0041: They kept moving from one place to another with their herds of cattle in search of good pasture and water.
pg081_n0042: They did not live in large communities but in small and simple ones.
pg082_n0003: streams, and rain to get drinking water for people and livestock.
pg082_n0004: They also depended on the surrounding vegetation for pastures.
pg082_n0005: Furthermore, pastoralists required safe places for both people and their livestock.
pg082_n0006: Examples of pastoralists in pre-colonial Africa were the Berbers and Tuaregs of North Africa, the Fulani and Hausa of West Africa, the Somali of North-Eastern Africa, the Karamojong of Uganda, the Maasai of Tanzania and Kenya, and the Khoikhoi of Southern Africa.
pg082_n0008: Division of labour in pastoral societies
pg082_n0010: Members of pastoral societies fulfilled various responsibilities at the family and community levels.
pg082_n0011: However, most responsibilities were assigned according to age-sets and gender.
pg082_n0012: Therefore, men, women, children, youth and elders carried out different responsibilities.
pg082_n0014: Duties and responsibilities of various groups
pg082_n0016: Women and children: Women stayed and worked at home.
pg082_n0017: They cooked food, milked cows, grazed calves, and cared for the children.
pg082_n0018: Children assisted women in fulfilling such duties.
pg082_n0020: Youth: The responsibilities of the youth were distributed according to their age groups.
pg082_n0021: The youth aged nine to eighteen years were involved in livestock grazing during the afternoon and assisting their mothers in household duties when they returned home.
pg082_n0022: The youth aged about fifteen to twenty-five consisted of the middle-aged youths, who among the Maasai, were called the Moran.
pg082_n0023: The Moran had six responsibilities, namely defending the community from enemies; protecting livestock against thieves and wild animals; raiding herds of neighbouring communities to obtain more livestock; driving cattle to new grazing land; collecting tribute from traders who passed through Maasai territory; and surveying neighbouring areas for pastures and sources of water.
pg082_n0025: Elders: This age group comprised elderly men in society.
pg082_n0026: This group consisted of elders aged forty and above.
pg082_n0027: They were the senior age group, so they were respected by other members of society.
pg082_n0028: The elders were also owners of cattle in their respective households.
pg082_n0029: The most senior member of the elderly group was called laibon.
pg082_n0030: He commanded special respect as the highest cultural, political, and religious authority in the community.
pg082_n0031: The laibon also presided over major cultural and religious ceremonies.
pg082_n0032: He was seen as the link between his people and the gods.
pg082_n0033: The head of a council of laibons among the Maasai was known as Laigwanan.
pg082_n0034: He was chosen from among the laibons representing different Maasai communities.
pg083_n0005: The Maasai are among the societies that practised age-set organisation.
pg083_n0006: Draw a tree diagram indicating different age groups and their respective roles.
pg083_n0010: The Nyakyusa were among the agricultural communities that practised the age-set system.
pg083_n0011: The Nyakyusa population tended to rise very rapidly, which led to a dense concentration of people in small areas.
pg083_n0012: They owned vast areas of fertile land that could be used for agricultural production activities.
pg083_n0013: They did not move from one place to another.
pg083_n0014: They settled in one area and undertook their economic activities there.
pg083_n0015: To prevent overpopulation in small areas, they adopted the age-set system.
pg083_n0016: In this case, the youth of a specific age group were allocated a new piece of land to occupy and establish their settlement.
pg083_n0017: The heads of respective age groups, called amafumu, headed each age village.
pg083_n0018: A ceremony called ubusoka was held to mark the passage of a new age group into adulthood.
pg083_n0020: Another agricultural community that practised the age-set organisation was the Rendile of northern Kenya.
pg083_n0021: Age-set organisation among the Rendile involved grouping people with similar age into separate age-sets.
pg083_n0022: Each age-set was given specific responsibilities.
pg083_n0023: Some of these responsibilities involved managing and taking care of community resources.
pg083_n0024: Age-set organisation among the Rendile community served as an important element in maintaining their agricultural practices and promoting unity within the community.
