pg084_n0003: Education system in pre-colonial African societies.
pg084_n0005: Pre-colonial education is defined as a lifelong process of transmitting and imparting knowledge, skills, values, norms, and experiences from one generation to another in a given society.
pg084_n0006: Pre-colonial education was delivered through active participation and observation.
pg084_n0007: Each clan had ways of transmitting knowledge, skills, values, and cultural norms, including taboos, to its young generation.
pg084_n0008: Each adult participated in transmitting knowledge.
pg084_n0009: Youth training depended on the experience of the trainer in a specific field.
pg084_n0010: For example, the knowledge of midwifery could be imparted to some women, who would later train young girls to assist each other during pregnancy.
pg084_n0011: They were also taught how to become acceptable wives and mothers.
pg084_n0013: Likewise, adults taught young men and women parental and marital responsibilities.
pg084_n0014: For example, girls were taught a wide range of household and agricultural duties at an early age, including cooking, cultivation, and attending children.
pg084_n0015: Boys were taught to be responsible husbands and fathers.
pg084_n0016: They also herded cows and looked after goats and other livestock.
pg084_n0017: Children helped with minor household tasks and performed light duties for relatives.
pg084_n0019: Taboos were taught to younger generations to instill proper morals and protect natural resources like water, forest, and land.
pg084_n0020: For example, children in some societies were prohibited from going into the forest alone, claiming that they would meet dangerous creatures that would harm them.
pg084_n0021: Young generations inherited knowledge, values, and wisdom from their parents and relatives, especially those related to the prosperity of society.
pg084_n0025: The pre-colonial education aimed at imparting knowledge, skills and values to young members of the society through word of mouth and direct involvement in activities like fishing, carpentry and painting.
pg084_n0026: In most cases, it was learning by doing.
pg084_n0027: It also imparted social values and transmitted good morals and norms to younger generations to prepare them for their future careers.
pg084_n0028: For example, the youth were taught to do various economic activities such as fishing, farming and hunting.
pg084_n0029: This went hand in hand with equipping them with the basic knowledge and skills related to particular economic activities.
pg084_n0030: In that way, pre-colonial education developed a sense of belonging in learners and encouraged them to participate actively in performing family responsibilities.
pg084_n0032: The pre-colonial education was intended to develop children’s character, physical strength and intellectual abilities.
pg084_n0033: Children were taught practical skills and self-dependence.
pg085_n0003: Moreover, this kind of education aimed at promoting peace and security in the society.
pg085_n0004: The education trained the youth to defend their societies against enemies.
pg085_n0005: For instance, in the Maasai society the Morans were responsible for peacekeeping.
pg085_n0006: They were also taught how to defend their community, protect their livestock from thieves and wild animals, and raid their neighbouring communities to expand their herds of cattle.
pg085_n0008: Furthermore, it aimed at preparing the youth to take over after the end of the existing phase of leadership in their societies.
pg085_n0009: This duty was important because administrative knowledge was at the very heart of social, political and economic development.
pg085_n0010: Well-prepared young leaders could enhance the stability of society across generations.
pg085_n0012: Additionally, pre-colonial education aimed at making the youth patriotic.
pg085_n0013: It was the duty of elders to impart a sense of patriotism to the youth so that they might be proud of their people, environment and resources.
pg085_n0014: In pre-colonial societies, there were different conflicts among states.
pg085_n0015: Therefore, a sense of patriotism was very important among the youth to discourage conspiracy against the welfare of their societies.
pg085_n0019: Pre-colonial education was practical in nature.
pg085_n0020: For example, the youth were taken to the seas, oceans, rivers and lakes, where they were taught how to fish.
pg085_n0021: A similar practice was done among the agricultural communities, who taught young people how to farm.
pg085_n0022: Moreover, those interested in iron smithery or industries were practically taught how to make iron or other industrial goods.
pg085_n0025: It varied from one society to another, depending on a given society’s economic, social and environmental conditions.
pg085_n0026: Each society had its customs and traditions.
pg085_n0027: For example, the customs and traditions of the societies that lived in the arid and semi-arid environments differed from those found around rivers and lakes.
pg085_n0031: You are among the students chosen to participate in the debate on the motion “Pre-colonial education was better than formal education”.
pg085_n0032: Provide clear arguments to support or oppose the motion.
pg086_n0003: The pre-colonial education was valuable and relevant to the societies where it was practised.
pg086_n0004: It contained positive elements which helped to shape the culture of societies at that particular time.
pg086_n0005: The education was not class-biased, thus, not discriminatory.
pg086_n0006: It was provided to all members of the society, regardless of one’s wealth or status.
pg086_n0007: The only difference was that sometimes boys were taught military techniques, while girls were not.
pg086_n0008: This was influenced by the way informal education was given.
pg086_n0009: As a result, the education provided did not create classes in the society.
pg086_n0010: Instead it promoted specialisation as reflected in diviners’ or healers’ activities.
pg086_n0012: This type of education was not financially motivated.
pg086_n0013: During the pre-colonial era, every member of the society considered themselves as having significant responsibilities to fulfil in the society.
pg086_n0015: To motivate instructors, the community gave them gifts in the form of domestic animals or crops, depending on what was available at the time.
pg086_n0017: Pre-colonial education emphasised good morals and good social conduct.
pg086_n0018: The learners were taught good character.
pg086_n0019: Elders ensured that good values and behaviour, such as hardwork were imparted successfully, while undesirable behaviour like theft or prostitution were strongly condemned.
pg086_n0021: The pre-colonial education showed a few weaknesses.
pg086_n0022: For instance, the content of the education included certain customs and traditions that were unnecessary.
pg086_n0023: In many cases, it undermined the rights of women.
pg086_n0024: For example, a woman who lost her husband was not allowed to inherit the wealth left behind by her husband.
pg086_n0025: In some societies, women were not allowed to eat certain types of food such as eggs, milk, and some parts of animal flesh, such as the liver.
pg086_n0026: Similarly, women were not allowed to learn iron-working in the iron-working societies.

pg088_n0008: The process of state formation in pre-colonial Africa varied across regions and time.
pg088_n0009: While some regions developed into centralised states, others remained decentralised.
pg088_n0010: This chapter extends the discussion on state organisation from Chapter Six.
pg088_n0011: In this chapter, you will learn about the centralised states in western, central, southern, and eastern Africa.
pg088_n0012: The competencies developed will enable you to value and maintain good African historical processes of establishing and maintaining good governing institutions.
pg088_n0020: A state is a centralised political organisation that imposes and enforces rules over resources and people within a territory.
pg088_n0021: The important elements that make up a state include people, territorial boundaries, sovereignty, that is, freedom from foreign rule, and government.
pg088_n0022: The development of centralised states in pre-colonial Africa was gradual and influenced by different factors.
pg088_n0023: In the history of Africa, political centralisation started with Ancient Egypt from about the third millennium B C E.
pg088_n0024: However, the process became more widespread and consistent from about the fifth century and continued through the nineteenth century.
pg088_n0025: Pre-colonial African states in eastern, western, central, and southern Africa had different characteristics and organisational structures.
pg088_n0029: Several centralised states developed in East Africa.
pg088_n0030: They included Buganda, Bunyoro, Karagwe, and Ruanda-Urundi.
pg088_n0031: Other states like Nyamwezi, Chagga, Hehe, Sangu, Sukuma, Pare, Shambaa, and Kamba were semi-centralised.
pg088_n0032: Figure seven point one shows some centralised and semi-centralised states in Esat Africa.
pg088_n0033: Among the aforementioned states, Buganda and Bunyoro are taken as case study.

pg090_n0005: The Bunyoro Kingdom is traced back to the kingdom of Bunyoro-Kitara founded by the Bachwezi people in the thirteenth century.
pg090_n0006: By the sixteenth century, Bunyoro-Kitara had started to decline and gave rise to new and smaller kingdoms.
pg090_n0007: One of the new kingdoms, which emerged, was Bunyoro.
pg090_n0008: The title of the king of Bunyoro was Omukama.
pg090_n0010: Factors for the rise of Bunyoro Kingdom
pg090_n0012: There were specific factors for the rise of the Bunyoro Kingdom.
pg090_n0015: Influence of traditions: Traditions had great influence on choosing the Omukama.
pg090_n0016: The Omukama was chosen from among the chiefs who came from the ruling family or the royal dynasty of Babito.
pg090_n0017: This practice helped reduce disputes over power succession among the provincial chiefs who were called Saza.
pg090_n0019: Role of strong kings: The Bunyoro Kingdom needed strong leadership in order to maintain its position.
pg090_n0020: Such leadership was provided by famous kings like Omukama Kabarega who helped Bunyoro to grow into a powerful kingdom in the nineteenth century.
pg090_n0021: Kabalega Kamurasi created the Bunyoro’s standing army, which consisted of about twenty thousand soldiers.
pg090_n0023: He divided his army into ten divisions, each under a commander.
pg090_n0024: These were then deployed in the provinces to defend the empire against external invasions.
pg090_n0025: They also checked the internal revolts against the central government.
pg090_n0026: Apart from ensuring law and order, the army was also used to raid neighbouring states of Toro, Ankole, and Busoga during the wars of conquest and expansion.
pg090_n0028: Influence of the geographical conditions: Bunyoro was one of the most fertile areas in the Great Lakes region.
pg090_n0029: Its climate was good, and enabled the people of Bunyoro to grow various crops and raise livestock.
pg090_n0030: They produced enough food, which supported their society including rulers and soldiers.
pg090_n0032: Strong and efficient political system: The kingdom was divided into provinces.
pg090_n0033: These provinces were ruled by provincial chiefs known as Saza who were appointed by the Omukama.
pg090_n0034: The Saza controlled land on behalf of the Omukama.
pg090_n0035: These chiefs were loyal to the king.
pg090_n0036: In their provinces, they distributed land to peasants and cattle herders in return for loyalty, services, and tributes.
pg090_n0037: They helped to promote peace and unity among the people of Bunyoro.
pg090_n0041: The Bunyoro Kingdom declined in the sixteenth century due to a number of factors, including the following:
pg091_n0003: Expansion in the size of the kingdom: The increased geographic coverage of the kingdom made it difficult for the king to control it efficiently.
pg091_n0004: Sometimes, provincial chiefs, especially those along the borders, revolted against the central government and broke away.
pg091_n0005: Examples of the provinces that broke away were Buddu, Toro, Busoga, and Koki.
pg091_n0006: This led to the decline of Bunyoro since it lost important provinces which produced grain and iron tools.
pg091_n0008: Disputes in the ruling family: Members of the ruling family sometimes quarrelled over kingship succession.
pg091_n0009: A good example of disputes and conflicts over succession occurred during the rule of Omukama Kyebambe Nyamutukura the third.
pg091_n0010: One of his sons called Kaboyo Omuhanwa rebelled against his father and established the Toro kingdom.
pg091_n0012: Limited control over regional chiefs: Provincial chiefs had a certain degree of independence from Omukama.
pg091_n0013: For example, they could raise their own provincial armies.
pg091_n0014: This was dangerous to the unity of the Kingdom as some of the leaders build their own armies to revolt against the central government.
pg091_n0018: The Buganda Kingdom was situated in the southwest of modern Uganda.
pg091_n0019: It started as a small political unit in the sixteenth century and began to expand from the seventeenth century.
pg091_n0020: It reached its peak of prosperity in the mid-nineteenth century.
pg091_n0021: The Buganda Kingdom was one of the highly centralised states in East Africa.
pg091_n0022: The title of the king was Kabaka.
pg091_n0023: Buganda came into existence after the collapse of the Bunyoro-Kitara Kingdom.
pg091_n0024: By the second half of the nineteenth century, Buganda became one of the strongest and largest kingdoms in the interlacustrine region.
pg091_n0025: It increased its size by conquering and controlling small neighbouring kingdoms.
pg091_n0026: The conquered territories were placed under the leadership of chiefs called Batongole.
pg091_n0027: These were responsible to the Kabaka as the territorial leader.
pg091_n0031: The Buganda Kingdom was among the best political systems in the interlacustrine region.
pg091_n0032: At the top of the leadership structure there was the Kabaka.
pg091_n0033: He was the overall political leader and the final decision maker.
pg091_n0034: Below him was an administrative hierarchy with a number of chiefs.
pg091_n0035: The chiefs helped him to spread his authority throughout the kingdom.
pg091_n0036: Kabaka governed his kingdom with the assistance of his advisory council called Lukiiko.
pg091_n0037: The council was made up of the prime minister called Katikiro, the treasurer general called Omuwanika, and the chief justice called Mugema.
pg091_n0038: Members of the Lukiiko were appointed by Kabaka.
pg091_n0039: The Lukiiko did not make laws, but gave advice to Kabaka.
pg092_n0003: Factors for the rise of Buganda Kingdom
pg092_n0005: There were various factors that led to the rise of Buganda Kingdom.
pg092_n0008: Development of agriculture: Buganda evolved in an area with good climate and fertile soils favourable for agriculture.
pg092_n0009: People grew banana as the main food crop.
pg092_n0010: The kingdom produced surplus food that favoured the growth of population that had to be governed.
pg092_n0011: There was also a clear division of labour among the Baganda.
pg092_n0012: While women concentrated on food production, men performed other duties including warfare to expand the size of the kingdom.
pg092_n0014: Formation of a strong and stable army: At its peak, Buganda had one of the strongest armies in pre-colonial African societies.
pg092_n0015: This enabled the Baganda to strengthen and expand their kingdom.
pg092_n0016: The army was also used to protect the wealth of the society and conquer neighbouring societies.
pg092_n0018: Clear system of leadership succession: Buganda’s administration was centralised.
pg092_n0019: Kabaka and his subordinate leaders practised a hereditary system.
pg092_n0020: In this system, leadership passed from the father to the son.
pg092_n0021: This helped to prevent and resolve disputes over succession.
pg092_n0022: The situation was different in the Bunyoro and Ankole states where succession disputes were common.
pg092_n0024: Control of trade: Buganda participated in the East and Central African long-distance trade.
pg092_n0025: This trade enabled Kabaka to collect tributes that were used to strengthen his kingdom.
pg092_n0026: Trade also provided the kingdom with weapons, especially guns.
pg092_n0028: Strong link between the state and clans: The political system of Buganda reduced conflicts and maintained peace within the state.
pg092_n0029: Kabaka married wives from several clans.
pg092_n0030: The marriage alliance from different clans helped him to create unity and harmony within the kingdom.
pg092_n0032: Religious beliefs and practices: Religious beliefs and practices contributed to the growth and expansion of the Buganda Kingdom.
pg092_n0034: As a clan head, Kabaka was a spiritual leader who presided over religious functions, and was regarded as a semi-divine person.
pg092_n0035: As a spiritual leader, Kabaka was surrounded by religious leaders from different clans.
pg092_n0036: Thus, religion was one of the pillars that encouraged socio-political unity and maintained power relations within the kingdom.
pg092_n0038: Development of iron technology: Iron was used to make weapons and tools that enabled Buganda to conquer weaker states as well as to engage in production activities.
pg092_n0039: Both conquest and high production enabled the expansion of the kingdom.
pg093_n0003: Factors for the weakening of Buganda Kingdom
pg093_n0005: Despite all the factors that led to the rise of Baganda Kingdom, it finally became weak.
pg093_n0006: The following were the factors for the weakening of the Buganda Kingdom.
pg093_n0008: Establishment of colonialism: The establishment of the colonial rule undermined political power and authority of Kabaka.
pg093_n0009: The Buganda Agreement of nineteen hundred allowed the Governor to control Buganda.
pg093_n0010: Under this agreement, Kabaka Mwanga unwillingly submitted to British control and became part of the British protectorate.
pg093_n0011: As part of the British protectorate, the Kingdom was no longer free.
pg093_n0012: This greatly reduced the power of Kabaka, and led to the weakening of the Kingdom.
pg093_n0014: Religious differences and conflicts: There were three conflicting religious groups, namely Christianity, Islam, and the indigenous religion.
pg093_n0015: These conflicts occurred during the second half of the nineteenth century.
pg093_n0016: These groups divided the Buganda Kingdom into conflicting religious ideologies.
pg093_n0017: Buganda gradually lost its internal unity and stability as a socio-political entity, and led to its weakening.
pg093_n0019: Introduction of colonial economy: The introduction of a peasant economy by British colonial officials changed the production system in Buganda and brought in the disintegration of the kingdom.
pg093_n0020: People started to produce cash crops, which reduced the production of food crops.
pg093_n0021: As a result, the food available could not sufficiently feed the entire population in the kingdom.
pg093_n0023: Conflicting administrative interests: Since many Batongole ruled Buganda, some provincial chiefs tried to gain absolute power and authority over their subjects.
pg093_n0024: These efforts resulted in administrative misunderstandings and conflicts between Batongole and Kabaka.
pg093_n0025: The situation brought the whole kingdom into administrative problems that finally led to its weakening.

pg094_n0007: The empire of Ghana was located in the southern border region of modern-day Mauritania and Mali, between the bend of the Niger and Senegal rivers.
pg094_n0008: This empire rose in the fifth century after several small states were brought together through war.
pg094_n0009: The founders of the empire were the Soninke people.
pg094_n0010: The capital of the Ghana Empire was Kumbi Saleh and the title of the king was Tunka or Ghana.
pg094_n0011: The towns located near the Ghana Empire were Walata, Awdaghust, also known as Audoghast, Timbuktu, Tichitt, and Jenne.
pg094_n0013: Factors for the rise of Ghana Empire
pg094_n0015: The factors that led to the rise of the Ghana Empire were not different greatly from those of Buganda, in East Africa.
pg094_n0016: The following were the factors which led to the rise of Ghana Empire.
pg094_n0018: Good geographical position: Ghana was at the intersection of many Trans-Saharan trade routes.
pg094_n0019: It played an intermediary role in this trade.
pg095_n0003: southern, northern, and eastern regions passed through Ghana.
pg095_n0004: Its position also encouraged agricultural production, which ensured sufficient food to feed people.
pg095_n0006: Availability of gold: Ghana produced a lot of gold, which was the main item of trade and a form of currency.
pg095_n0007: Trade in gold made the empire politically strong and economically rich.
pg095_n0009: Efficient administrative system: The empire of Ghana was divided into provinces.
pg095_n0010: The king appointed provincial chiefs in each province.
pg095_n0011: Those chiefs provided support to the king in their respective areas.
pg095_n0012: In this way, he managed to control the entire kingdom.
pg095_n0014: Military strength: The king of Ghana established a strong standing army of about two hundred thousand soldiers.
pg095_n0015: The army had the duty of fighting weaker chiefdoms and defending the kingdom from external attacks.
pg095_n0017: Development of iron technology: Iron technology produced farming tools.
pg095_n0018: Such tools helped to improve agricultural activities, increase food production, and enhance food security.
pg095_n0019: Food security led to population growth, which strengthened the empire.
pg095_n0020: Weapons made of iron also improved military power, and state security led to the expansion of the territory.
pg095_n0022: Factors for the decline of the Ghana Empire
pg095_n0024: The Ghana Empire declined and eventually collapsed in the eleventh century due to the following factors:
pg095_n0026: Attacks by Almoravids: Ghana was frequently attacked by the Almoravids from North Africa from ten seventy-six to ten seventy-seven.
pg095_n0027: These attacks aimed at reclaiming Awdaghust, which was a major source of salt and gold.
pg095_n0028: These attacks weakened the empire and led to its decline.
pg095_n0030: Dissatisfaction of traders: Gold traders in Ghana were complaining about the king’s monopoly of gold trade and heavy taxes, hence making trading activities unprofitable.
pg095_n0031: Thus, many traders diverged their activities to other growing states such as Mali.
pg095_n0032: This weakened the empire and contributed to its decline.
pg095_n0034: Dissatisfaction of vassal states: Different vassal states refused to pay tributes while others declared themselves independent of the kingdom.
pg095_n0035: This weakened the empire and contributed to the decline.
pg095_n0037: Vastness of the empire: The Ghana Empire was too large to control.
pg095_n0041: The Mali Empire rose after the decline of the Ghana Empire.
pg095_n0042: It began as a small Mandinka kingdom at the upper bend of River Niger.
pg095_n0043: Between the eleventh century and twelfth century, Sundiata Keita and some of the rulers of Mali brought a number of
pg096_n0004: In the thirteenth century, Sundiata led a Malinke army against the Sumanguru of Sosso whom he defeated at the Kirina battle near the modern city of Bamako.
pg096_n0005: With the defeat of Sumanguru, Sundiata took control of all the Soninke people.
pg096_n0006: Sundiata built up a large empire of Mali with its capital located at Niami.
pg096_n0007: The title of the kings of Mali was Mansa.
pg096_n0008: The most famous ruler of the Empire was Mansa Kankan Musa.
pg096_n0010: Factors for the rise of Mali Empire
pg096_n0012: Factors that led to the rise of Mali Empire included the following:
pg096_n0014: Strong standing army: Mansa Musa kept a large standing army under a battalion of commanders.
pg096_n0015: The army was used to protect the empire from outside attacks.
pg096_n0016: It was also used to patrol trading routes and to ensure that district chiefs paid tribute to the king.
pg096_n0018: Role of Islam: Mansa Musa used Islam as a state religion.
pg096_n0019: He used Islam as a unifying factor and commanded respect among his people.
pg096_n0020: Islamic laws, Sharia, were used to control the behaviour and attitudes of people.
pg096_n0021: This brought discipline and unity among them.
pg096_n0023: Development of agriculture: Mali had rich agricultural land.
pg096_n0024: The fertile land enabled people to produce a wide variety of grains and other crops.
pg096_n0025: They also kept livestock such as cattle, goats, and sheep.
pg096_n0026: Farming and cattle keeping ensured availability of food.
pg096_n0029: Control of gold mines and trade routes: The empire controlled gold mines at Bambuk, Bundu, and Wangara.
pg096_n0030: It also controlled gold trade routes passing through its territory.
pg096_n0031: Because of this trade, Niami, Jenne, Timbuktu, and Gao developed into major commercial centres in the empire.
pg096_n0032: Gold trade linked the empire with Morocco, Tripoli, and Egypt.
pg096_n0033: Trade also attracted traders from Europe and the Middle East.
pg096_n0034: This development was a major stimulus for the rise of Mali.
pg096_n0036: Strong leadership: Sundiata Keita and Mansa Musa were good leaders.
pg096_n0037: They divided the empire into provinces and appointed leaders in charge of each province.
pg096_n0038: They did not want to exercise total power.
pg096_n0039: They left the administration of the region to loyal chiefs whom they appreciated.
pg096_n0040: This leadership style promoted loyalty and mutual understanding between the king and his vassals.
pg096_n0042: Factors for the decline of Mali Empire
pg096_n0044: The Mali Empire started to decline in the second half of the fourteenth century.
pg096_n0045: Several factors led to the decline of the empire.
pg096_n0047: Internal struggles for succession: The empire faced many succession conflicts and struggles.
pg096_n0048: These struggles created divisions and separations, which weakened the state.
pg097_n0003: Attacks from trade competitors: The Mosi Kingdom from the south and the Tuaregs from the north attacked the Mali Empire to get control of the Trans-Saharan Trade routes as well as items of trade such as gold, slaves, and salt.
pg097_n0004: These attacks weakened the empire and led to its collapse.
pg097_n0006: The rise of the Songhay Empire: The empire of Songhay was created by Sunni Ali.
pg097_n0007: His soldiers attacked and destroyed Jenne and robbed its wealth.
pg097_n0008: This weakened the Mali Empire because Jenne was the backbone of its economy.
pg097_n0009: The attack and plunder contributed to the decline of the Mali Empire.
pg097_n0013: The Songhay Empire was the largest empire of all the western Sudanic states.
pg097_n0014: Gao was the capital city of the empire.
pg097_n0015: This city was also one of the great centres of trade during the Trans-Saharan Trade.
pg097_n0016: The title of the king was Sunni.
pg097_n0017: Under the leadership of Sunni Ali, Gao conquered neighbouring kingdoms.
pg097_n0018: By the fifteenth century, it had become the centre of a vast empire called Songhay.
pg097_n0019: Another prominent leader of the Songhay Empire, apart from Sunni Ali, was Askia Mohamed.
pg097_n0021: The factors for the rise of the Songhay Empire
pg097_n0023: Factors that led to the rise of Mali Empire did not differ so much from those of Mali Empire.
pg097_n0025: The following factors led to the rise of the Songhay Empire.
pg097_n0027: Control of trade routes: Some of the important Trans-Saharan Trade routes passed through Gao.
pg097_n0028: Gao used this opportunity to tax traders who passed through the areas.
pg097_n0029: The wealth collected from taxes enabled the empire to create and support a large permanent army.
pg097_n0031: Strong leadership of Sunni Ali and Askia Mohamed: Sunni Ali and Askia Mohamed led to the successful expansion of the empire.
pg097_n0032: By the late fifteenth century, the empire had expanded to cover the whole area between Kebbi in the east and Jenne in the west.
pg097_n0033: In the north, the empire had reached Timbuktu while, in the south, it had reached Hombori.
pg097_n0035: The role of Islam: Another important factor was the adoption of Islam as a state religion.
pg097_n0036: Rulers used Islam to unify the people and to justify wars of conquest, jihads.
pg097_n0037: In addition, they used Islam to justify the enslavement of non-Islamic believers.
pg097_n0039: Strength of the army: Sunni Ali had a strong army that helped him to protect and expand the empire.
pg097_n0040: His army was comprised of well-armed horse-riding forces that were used to conquer and defend the kingdom.
pg098_n0003: Development of agriculture and industry: Increased agricultural production assured the civilians and soldiers of sufficient food.
pg098_n0004: Industries produced tools that led to an increase in the production of different goods and weapons.
pg098_n0005: All these activities were vital to the growth of the empire.
pg098_n0007: Factors for the decline of Songhay Empire
pg098_n0009: The Songhay Empire reached the peak of its power in the early sixteenth century.
pg098_n0011: The following were the reasons that led to the decline of the Songhay Empire:
pg098_n0013: Succession disputes after the death of Askia Mohamed: The death of Askia Mohamed created some misunderstandings in the ruling family.
pg098_n0014: After his death, a period of weak and unskilful leadership followed.
pg098_n0015: This led to frequent unrests which in turn undermined the stability of the Songhay Empire.
pg098_n0017: Resistance to heavy tributes: Peasants and artisans resisted the heavy tributes demanded by the king.
pg098_n0018: They disobeyed the king and refused to implement decisions made by him.
pg098_n0021: Change of trade routes: During the sixteenth century, the direction of trade routes shifted towards the Atlantic coast where European merchants had established themselves.
pg098_n0022: This shift resulted in the decline of the Trans-Saharan Trade, which was the backbone of the Songhay Empire.
pg098_n0024: Moroccan invasion in the sixteenth century: The Sultan of Morocco wanted to monopolize the West African gold trade.
pg098_n0025: His army attacked and conquered the Songhay Empire.
pg098_n0026: This invasion weakened the Songhay Empire and led to its collapse.
pg098_n0030: How did trade and commerce facilitate state formation in the Western Sudanic States?
pg098_n0034: In pre-colonial Africa, a number of states also developed in the Forest Zone of West Africa.
pg098_n0035: The most important forest states were Asante, Oyo, Benin, and Ife.
pg098_n0036: Most of these states were found by the Yoruba people.
pg098_n0037: State formation among the Yoruba began in the eleventh century.
pg098_n0038: Figure seven point three shows Forest States
pg099_im001: Map of Africa showing the West African forest zone shaded along the Gulf of Guinea and red dots marking the locations of forest states such as Asante, Dahomey, Oyo, and Benin.
pg099_n0003: Figure seven point three: Forest States
pg099_n0007: The Asante Kingdom was founded by the Oyoko people, one of the Akan clans, in the seventeenth century.
pg099_n0008: The Oyoko first founded five small chiefdoms which later on united into one powerful kingdom of Asante.
pg099_n0009: Those chiefdoms were Kumasi, Nsuta, Kokofu, Bwekai, and Dwaben.
pg099_n0010: By sixteen seventy, Kumasi was the greatest and the most powerful kingdom.
pg099_n0011: Obiri Yeboa was the first ruler of the Asante Kingdom.
pg099_n0012: He made Kumasi the unifying centre of the Asante Kingdom.
pg099_n0013: He also made Kumasi the capital of the kingdom.
pg099_n0014: The title of the king of the Asante Kingdom was Asantehene.
pg099_n0016: Factors for the rise of the Asante Kingdom
pg099_n0018: Factors for the rise of the Forest Zone states were not different from those of the other areas.
pg099_n0019: The following were the reasons for the rise of the Asante Kingdom:
pg099_n0021: Soil fertility: The Asante Kingdom evolved from an area that was endowed with soil fertility.
pg099_n0022: Soil fertility supported agriculture, which was the main economic activity in the kingdom.
pg099_n0023: The development of agriculture ensured the availability of sufficient food for the people, rulers, and soldiers.
pg099_n0024: The Asante people cultivated crops such as grains and palm.
pg100_n0003: Military strength: The kingdom developed a strong military force which was formed by a well-disciplined army equipped with modern weapons such as guns.
pg100_n0004: These were obtained from the Trans-Saharan Trade and the Atlantic Slave Trade.
pg100_n0005: The army fought wars of conquest and expanded the size of the kingdom.
pg100_n0006: It also ensured peace and security in the kingdom.
pg100_n0008: Long-distance trade: The kingdom actively participated in the West African long-distance trade and established trading centres along the Atlantic coast.
pg100_n0009: Trade was mainly based on the export of slaves and gold from the forest region.
pg100_n0010: The kingdom imported beads, clothes, and firearms.
pg100_n0011: Such firearms were used for security and warfare.
pg100_n0012: In some cases, warfare generated slaves who were important commodities of trade.
pg100_n0013: The wealth collected from this trade was, therefore, used for strengthening the kingdom.
pg100_n0015: Strong leadership: The rise and growth of the Asante Kingdom benefited from the strong leadership of Asantehene Obiri Yeboa, Osei Tutu and Opokwu Ware.
pg100_n0016: Yeboa unified the rulers of Nsuta, Kokofu, Bwekai, and Dwaben states into a single Oyoko clan.
pg100_n0017: This ensured unity among the people of the kingdom.
pg100_n0018: Obiri Yeboa used this unity to conquer the surrounding states.
pg100_n0019: Those states recognized Yeboa as the Asantehene of Asante.
pg100_n0020: Obiri Yeboa died in the late sixteen seventies, but had laid down the foundation of the Asante Kingdom.
pg100_n0022: He became a key factor for the growth of the kingdom.
pg100_n0023: Osei Tutu was a charismatic, strong and courageous leader.
pg100_n0024: He expanded and built a highly centralised kingdom.
pg100_n0025: He used the Golden Stool as a symbol of unity, which was respected by all the Asante people.
pg100_n0026: He introduced a royal lineage family that Asante rulers were to come from descendants of Obiri Yeboa and Osei Tutu.
pg100_n0027: He also established Kumasi as the capital of the empire.
pg100_n0028: He introduced a traditional annual religious festival known as Odwira.
pg100_n0029: Also, he demanded payment of tribute from every adult member of the empire.
pg100_n0030: Therefore, all these measures helped to strengthen political unity and the economy of the empire.
pg100_n0032: Military conquest of neighbouring states: Osei Tutu and his successors successfully conquered neighbouring states.
pg100_n0033: He created a federation that conquered Denkyira and other Akan states.
pg100_n0034: By the eighteenth century, he controlled most goldfields of the Forest zone.
pg100_n0035: His successors, Opukwu Ware and others expanded the boundaries of Asante, covering areas from the coast to the Savannah in the North.
pg100_n0037: Traditions belief: With the onset of Osei Tutu’s administration, Okomfo Anokye, a traditional priest, made Osei Tutu the occupant of the Golden Stool.
pg100_n0038: This action strengthened the Asante Kingdom in different ways.
pg100_n0039: Osei Tutu now became a religious and political leader.
pg100_n0040: He became a link between the people and the gods.
pg100_n0041: The Golden Stool replaced all previous symbols of authority.
pg100_n0042: It became the symbol of unity and soul of the people of Asante.
pg101_n0003: Factors for the fall of Asante Kingdom
pg101_n0005: By the first half of the nineteenth century, the Asante Kingdom had begun to decline.
pg101_n0006: This was due to a number of factors, including the following:
pg101_n0008: British imperial activities: The British frequently attacked the kingdom between eighteen seventy-one and nineteen oh one.
pg101_n0009: This undermined peace and security of the kingdom as well as trading activities in the region.
pg101_n0010: The imperial activities affected the prosperity of the Asante Kingdom.
pg101_n0013: Abolition of the slave trade: From around the mid nineteenth century, the British led a campaign to abolish the slave trade.
pg101_n0014: This campaign led to the end of the trade in West Africa, which ruined most of the forest states, including the Asante Kingdom.
pg101_n0015: This is because the power of these states depended on the slave trade.
pg101_n0016: With the abolition of the slave trade, the Asante Kingdom lost important sources of revenue hence it declined.
pg101_n0018: Vastness of the kingdom: In the first half of the nineteenth century, the size of the Asante Kingdom grew bigger.
pg101_n0019: This growth partly caused the decline of the Asante.
pg101_n0020: The conquered territories of Gonja, Kong, Bonchiku, Baule, and Anyi gradually rebelled against the central government in Kumasi and developed into self-governing states.
pg101_n0024: Investigate the role of influential leaders in state formation in the Forest States of West Africa.
pg101_n0028: This was a Yoruba state which was formed around the fourteenth century.
pg101_n0029: Its founder was Oduduwa, whose origin is explained by two myths.
pg101_n0030: The first myth is that of creation.
pg101_n0031: According to this myth, Oduduwa was brought on earth from heaven by his father, Olorun, who was regarded as the supreme god of the Yoruba.
pg101_n0032: The second myth claims that Oduduwa came to Ife from the eastern part of the region.
pg101_n0036: Good climatic conditions, revenues and good leadership were the factors that influenced the rise of the Ife Kingdom.
pg101_n0038: Good climatic conditions: The Ife Kingdom was located in an area with good climatic conditions.
pg101_n0039: This enabled its people to produce surplus food.
pg101_n0040: Accordingly, it was possible for the kingdom to support rulers and officials who were not directly engaged in productive activities.
pg102_n0003: Collection of revenues: Ife rulers managed to collect taxes from traders and tributes from peasants.
pg102_n0004: The people of Ife had trade links with the Sahel people who were famous for copper and salt mining.
pg102_n0005: The Kingdom collected tax from copper and salt traders from the Sahel.
pg102_n0006: In addition, it collected tributes from its peasants who exchanged their food and kola nuts with copper and salt from the Sahel region.
pg102_n0008: Good leadership: Good leadership of Oduduwa was another important factor for the rise and growth of this state.
pg102_n0009: He managed to unite his people and formed a strong and well-organized state.
pg102_n0010: In addition, Oduduwa was highly respected by his subjects partly because he was regarded as the son of Olorun.
pg102_n0014: Ife Kingdom declined following the growing influence of the Oyo Kingdom in the Yorubaland.
pg102_n0015: The Oyo Kingdom invaded Ibadan, an important town in Yorubaland, which was by then controlled by Ife.
pg102_n0016: After the invasion, Ife lost control of Ibadan and became weak.
pg102_n0017: Later, Oyo invaded Ife and settled in its territory.
pg102_n0018: This marked the total collapse of Ife.
pg102_n0022: Benin was found in the southern part of Ife near the Niger Delta.
pg102_n0023: It was located deep into the forest.
pg102_n0024: The area occupied by the Kingdom is modern southwestern Nigeria.
pg102_n0025: Therefore, the present-day country of Benin has no connection with the ancient Benin Kingdom.
pg102_n0026: The state was developed by Edo-speaking people in the thirteenth century.
pg102_n0027: The tittle of the King of Benin was Oba.
pg102_n0028: The kings, oba, of Benin claimed to have descended from Oduduwa, the founding ancestor of the Yoruba.
pg102_n0029: The first Oba of Benin was Oranmiyan, the son of Oduduwa, who is said to have been brought to Benin by the early inhabitants in order to solve conflicts among the chiefs.
pg102_n0030: By the fifteenth century, Benin had grown into a huge centralised state enclosed with a wall.
pg102_n0031: When Europeans came to Benin, they described it as the Great City of Benin for its size and decorative buildings.
pg102_n0033: Factors for the rise of the Benin Kingdom
pg102_n0035: Factors for the rise of Benin Kingdom were similar to those of other states.
pg102_n0036: The only difference was the context.
pg102_n0037: The following thus, were the factors for the rise of the Benin Kingdom.
pg102_n0039: Strong leadership: The Kingdom had some strong leaders such as Ewuare, also known as Ewuare the Great.
pg102_n0040: He was responsible for turning the city-state of Benin into a kingdom.
pg102_n0041: Under his leadership, the kingdom was well organised and strengthened.
pg102_n0042: Oba Ewuare appointed his royal district chiefs who ensured the stability of the empire.
pg102_n0043: He established a good oba succession system, whereby his oldest son was recognized officially as the successor of the kingdom.
pg103_n0003: Strong army: The leaders of Benin built a powerful army in the mid-fifteenth century.
pg103_n0004: The army defended the state against external threats.
pg103_n0005: It ensured peace, security, and stability within the state.
pg103_n0006: It also facilitated the expansion of the territory by conquering weaker neighbouring states.
pg103_n0008: Involvement in trade: The oba of Benin and some of the people in the empire participated in trade with the Portuguese.
pg103_n0009: They took trade items such as ivory, gums, pepper, and cotton cloth from Benin to the coast.
pg103_n0010: They sold those goods to Portuguese traders.
pg103_n0011: In addition, Benin artists made saltcellars, ivory carvings, and bangles, which were sold to the Europeans.
pg103_n0015: The empire declined in the eighteenth century due to a number of factors.
pg103_n0016: The following are some of them:
pg103_n0018: Civil wars and dynastic disputes: The kingdom of Benin was later faced with civil wars and dynastic disputes.
pg103_n0019: These disputes were sometimes caused by conflicts over succession.
pg103_n0020: The disputes finally resulted in wars, which weakened the state.
pg103_n0021: Internal disputes were, therefore, an important factor for the decline of the Benin Kingdom.
pg103_n0023: Slave trade: The obas sold their people and war captives to the Portuguese as slaves.
pg103_n0024: Despite the fact that the slave trade was one of the sources of Benin’s wealth, it had negative effects on the production capacity of the empire.
pg103_n0025: This was because slave trade removed productive people from their respective areas.
pg103_n0027: In the end, this led to the decline of the state.
pg103_n0029: British invasion: British troops invaded Benin in eighteen ninety-seven and robbed brass, bronze, and copper sculptures, which were symbols of power in the kingdom.
pg103_n0030: The invasion also resulted in the signing of several treaties with the people of the Niger Delta.
pg103_n0031: These treaties declared the whole region of the Niger Delta as a British protectorate.
pg103_n0032: With this declaration, Benin lost its independence and autonomy.
pg103_n0037: The Oyo Kingdom was established in the fourteenth century.
pg103_n0038: Like other Forest states, it originated from the Ife Kingdom.
pg103_n0039: The founders of the Oyo Kingdom are believed to have been descendants of Oduduwa, the founder of the Yoruba states.
pg103_n0040: Unlike other Forest states in Yorubaland, which were situated to the south, Oyo was located north of the tropical forests in the Savannah.
pg103_n0041: It occupied the southwestern corner of present-day Nigeria.
pg103_n0042: The title of the ruler of the Oyo state was Alaafin.
pg104_n0003: Factors for the rise of Oyo Kingdom
pg104_n0005: There were several factors that contributed to the rise of Oyo Kingdom.
pg104_n0008: Invasion by the Bariba and Nupe: The Oyo Kingdom rose because of the invasion of the Ife Kingdom by the Bariba and Nupe.
pg104_n0009: This invasion caused the people to move from Ife Kingdom to Oyo Ile, Old Oyo.
pg104_n0010: In Oyo Ile, they established outlying towns that formed the new Oyo Kingdom.
pg104_n0012: Military strength: The rulers of Oyo built a centralised state using a standing army.
pg104_n0013: In addition, the Kingdom was located in a tsetse fly-free zone, which made the use of horses possible.
pg104_n0014: During this period, horses were important for the efficiency of the army, since soldiers used them during warfare.
pg104_n0016: Involvement in trade: The Kingdom participated in the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade and in other trade interactions with its neighbours.
pg104_n0017: It gained access to the trade after invading the coastal kingdom of Allada.
pg104_n0018: The Kingdom was one of the sole protectors of the trade between the coast and Hausa land, which benefited the Kingdom largely.
pg104_n0019: Through this trade, Oyo rulers managed to collect a lot of tributes and taxes from villages and towns, as well as from transit traders.
pg104_n0020: These revenues benefited rulers and the state in general.
pg104_n0022: Strong and organised leadership: The kingdom had strong leaders like Alaafin Orompoto and Abiodun.
pg104_n0023: They managed to organise the state well and stabilise its economy.
pg104_n0024: These leaders were chosen by the council of seven chiefs, Oyo Mesi, from the lineage that traced its origin to Oduduwas or Oduduwas’ son, Oronyan.
pg104_n0025: Oyo Mesi was headed by the Basorun.
pg104_n0026: The system of checks and balance also ensured the presence of good leaders.
pg104_n0027: Oyo Mesi also had the ability to force the Alaafin to renounce the throne and commit suicide when he did not perform well.
pg104_n0031: The Oyo Kingdom collapsed in the nineteenth century.
pg104_n0032: The following were some of the reasons for its decline.
pg104_n0034: Leadership problems: The decline of the Oyo Kingdom started when some of its leaders failed to rule the state effectively.
pg104_n0035: Some of them lacked wisdom and governed contrary to the established norms of the kingdom.
pg104_n0036: One such leader was Aole, also known as Awole, who took the throne in seventeen eighty-nine.
pg104_n0037: Aole ordered the attack of Apomu, one of the towns of Ife, against the oath he had taken.
pg104_n0038: Since Ife was regarded as the ancestral home of the people of Oyo, the action caused embarrassment and chaos in the kingdom.
pg104_n0039: Following this incidence, the king was forced to commit suicide.
pg105_n0003: who followed Aole brought more problems which caused some of the chiefdoms to break.
pg105_n0004: Egba was one of the break away chiefdoms that got its independence in seventeen ninety-seven.
pg105_n0006: Fall of the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade: The abolition of the slave trade along the coast of West Africa in eighteen oh seven destabilised the economic foundation of the empire.
pg105_n0007: This was the case because Oyo greatly depended on selling slaves as a source of revenues for its own development.
pg105_n0008: With the abolition of the slave trade, the Oyo Kingdom lost this important source of revenues, thus the empire declined.
pg105_n0010: The weakening of the Oyo army: Internal conflicts weakened the Oyo army and undermined its ability to handle subsequent military challenges.
pg105_n0011: For example, when Oyo was invaded by Benin in seventeen eighty-three and Nupe in seventeen ninety-one, the army was too weak to resist; as a result, the empire declined.
pg105_n0013: Disintegration of the central authority: Due to internal conflicts, some of the chiefdoms stopped paying tributes.
pg105_n0014: This deprived the central government of revenues.
pg105_n0015: For example, Dahomey, under king Ghezo, refused to pay tribute in eighteen seventeen.
pg105_n0016: One year later, this chiefdom seized its independence.
pg105_n0018: Conflicts between the council of chiefs, Oyo Mesi, and kings: It has been observed that the council of chiefs played an important role in the rise and growth of Oyo Kingdom by electing the king and oversetting his leadership.
pg105_n0019: However, by the early nineteenth century, conflicts of interest developed between the council and kings.
pg105_n0020: For example, there was a conflict between Gaha, who was the leader, Basorun, of the council of chiefs, and the Alafins between seventeen fifty-four and seventeen seventy.
pg105_n0021: As a result, the leader of chiefs, Basorun, was involved in the murder of four kings during his reign in the council.
pg105_n0022: These conflicts affected the stability of the state and led to its fall.
pg105_n0025: Briefly explain the role of religion in promoting the growth of the Asante Kingdom.
pg105_n0029: Pre-colonial Central African kingdoms included Kongo, Mwenemutapa, Luba, Lunda, Malavi and Lozi.
pg105_n0030: Four kingdoms, namely Kongo, Mwenemutapa, Luba and Lunda, as shown in Figure seven point four, are discussed.
pg106_im001: Map of Africa highlighting the locations of the centralized states of Kongo, Luba, Lunda, Lozi, and Mwenemutapa in Central and Southern Africa.
pg106_n0052: Figure seven point four: Some centralised states in Central Africa
pg107_n0005: The Kongo Kingdom was one of the most important kingdoms in Central Africa.
pg107_n0006: It started towards the end of the fourteenth century.
pg107_n0007: By fourteen eighty-two, when the Portuguese arrived, the kingdom was highly centralised.
pg107_n0008: The title of the king was Mani Kongo.
pg107_n0009: The capital of the kingdom was called Mbanza.
pg107_n0010: The Portuguese later called the capital San Salvador.
pg107_n0011: The first Mani Kongo of the kingdom was Nzinga Nkuwu.
pg107_n0013: Factors for the rise of the Kongo Kingdom
pg107_n0015: The Kongo Kingdom rose to power due to various factors.
pg107_n0016: The following are some of them:
pg107_n0018: Development of arts and crafts: The Bakongo were highly developed in arts and crafts.
pg107_n0019: They were skilled metal workers, potters, and weavers.
pg107_n0020: Fine clothes woven from the fibre of raffia palm were widely traded along the Atlantic coast.
pg107_n0021: They were exchanged for salt and seashells, which were used as local currency.
pg107_n0023: Frequent movement of the people: People frequently moved in and out of the Kongo Kingdom.
pg107_n0024: This led to the emergence of new villages with different clans.
pg107_n0025: Those clans needed a political organisation to unite them.
pg107_n0026: The Kongo state provided strong centralised leadership to those clans.
pg107_n0028: Religious beliefs: The power and authority of the king partly depended on religious beliefs.
pg107_n0029: The Mani Kongo was considered a semi-god by his people.
pg107_n0030: He used spiritual powers to unite the people in his kingdom.
pg107_n0031: These powers made all provinces to pay tribute to the king.
pg107_n0032: The tributes helped him strengthen the central government.
pg107_n0034: Monopoly of trade: The king of Kongo monopolised trade in the kingdom, including the slave trade.
pg107_n0035: He introduced taxes to traders passing through the kingdom.
pg107_n0036: He also collected tributes from vassal states.
pg107_n0037: The taxes and tributes were used for strengthening and consolidating the kingdom.
pg107_n0039: Favourable climatic conditions: The Kongo Kingdom was located in a heavy forest region.
pg107_n0040: The area had sufficient rainfall and fertile soil that supported the development of agriculture.
pg107_n0041: Agriculture, in turn, provided sufficient food to feed the growing population in the Kingdom.
pg107_n0043: Population increase: As people increased in number, it became necessary for them to organise themselves under a strong political authority.
pg107_n0044: This is because there was a need to ensure law and order in the society and security against external threats.
pg107_n0046: Factors for the decline of Kongo Kingdom
pg107_n0048: The Kongo Kingdom declined in the seventeenth century.
pg107_n0049: The reasons that led to the decline include the following:
pg108_n0003: Introduction of Christianity: Christianity was introduced by Portuguese Catholic priests.
pg108_n0004: The priests taught Bakongo Christians that Jesus Christ is the only King of the Earth.
pg108_n0005: This meant that Mani Kongo Nzinga Nkuwu was not the king.
pg108_n0006: This teaching encouraged the Bakongo Christians to stop being loyal to Nzinga Nkuwu.
pg108_n0007: This brought division and conflict between Christians and traditionalists.
pg108_n0008: Consequently, Nzinga Nkuwu and his son Mpanzua Kitima abandoned Christianity.
pg108_n0009: However, his mother and son Nzinga Mbemba remained Christians.
pg108_n0012: Resistance from provincial governors: Divisions in the royal family convinced the provincial governors to declare independence.
pg108_n0013: They refused to pay tribute to the central authority at Mbanza, San Salvador.
pg108_n0014: This forced Mani Kongo to find other means of getting revenues for the government.
pg108_n0015: He established trading relations with the Portuguese, which weakened the kingdom.
pg108_n0017: Introduction of the slave trade: The Portuguese initiated and promoted local wars in order to increase the supply of slaves.
pg108_n0018: However, Nzinga Nkuwu did not want slave trade to take place in his kingdom.
pg108_n0019: Differences in attitude towards the slave trade brought the king into conflicts with the Portuguese slave traders.
pg108_n0020: These conflicts undermined Mani Kongo’s power and led to the fall of the kingdom by the second half of the eighteenth century.
pg108_n0024: The Mwenemutapa Kingdom was founded around the fifteenth century.
pg108_n0025: It was located in the north of Mashonaland in present-day Zimbabwe.
pg108_n0026: The name Zimbabwe comes from the Shona language, to mean stone buildings known as Great Zimbabwe.
pg108_n0027: The founder of the Mwenemutapa Kingdom was Nyatsimba Mutota, who belonged to the Karanga clan of the Mashona ethnic group.
pg108_n0028: The capital of Mwenemutapa was called Great Zimbabwe.
pg108_n0029: Under the leadership of Nyatsimba Mutota, the Mwenemutapa Kingdom fought wars and conquered the Tonga and Tawara of the Zambezi Valley.
pg108_n0030: Mutota’s victories enabled him to acquire the title Mwenemutapa, which meant master of the conquered land.
pg108_n0031: Mutota died in fourteen fifty and his throne was inherited by his son Matope, who also died in fourteen eighty.
pg108_n0032: After Matope’s death, there were succession disputes until fourteen ninety when Changamire took over.
pg108_n0034: Factors for the rise of Mwenemutapa Kingdom
pg108_n0036: The kingdom of Mwenemutapa became powerful due to the following reasons.
pg108_n0038: Trading activities: The Mwenemutapa Kingdom was famous for gold, copper, and ivory.
pg108_n0039: These items attracted many Swahili, Portuguese and Arab traders to visit the kingdom for trading purposes.
pg108_n0040: Mwenemutapa levied duties on all imported goods into the kingdom.
pg108_n0041: The wealth obtained through these levies was used for consolidating the kingdom.
pg109_n0003: Rise of ambitious leaders: Mwenemutapa rose and grew because of ambitious leaders who were eager to expand the kingdom.
pg109_n0004: Among these were Nyatsimba Mutota and his son Matope, and Changamire.
pg109_n0005: They wanted land on which their people could settle, graze livestock and grow crops.
pg109_n0006: Thus, he acquired the area from the Great Zimbabwe to Dande, then from the Zambezi to Limpopo, and from the Kalahari Desert to the Indian Ocean.
pg109_n0008: Role of indigenous religion: The Mashona worshipped a supreme god called Mwari.
pg109_n0009: Their powerful god could only be approached through priests called Svikiro.
pg109_n0010: This powerful religious system made people obey their kings.
pg109_n0011: The Mwari cult was an important spiritual institution that helped the rise and growth of the Mwenemutapa Kingdom.
pg109_n0013: Strong and well-equipped army: The creation of a strong and well-equipped army helped to protect the Kingdom.
pg109_n0014: Moreover, the strength of the army enabled the king to gain the allegiance of village leaders.
pg109_n0015: This ensured that local village leaders paid regular tribute to the king.
pg109_n0017: Factors for the fall of Mwenemutapa Kingdom
pg109_n0019: The Mwenemutapa Kingdom began to decline towards the first half of the sixteenth century.
pg109_n0020: The reasons for its decline included the following:
pg109_n0022: Resistance against payment of tributes: Some of the clans such as Uteve, Barwe, and Manyika started refusing to pay tribute to the king.
pg109_n0023: This weakened the kingdom since it lost one of the most important sources of revenue.
pg109_n0025: Arrival of Portuguese: The participation of Portuguese merchants in gold trade from Mwenemutapa in the Indian Ocean trade partly caused the decline of the Kingdom.
pg109_n0026: Between fifteen oh two and fifteen oh seven C E, the Portuguese attacked and seized Kilwa and Sofala, which were trading centres for gold from Mwenemutapa.
pg109_n0027: The conquest of these centres caused a decline in the volume of gold from the Mwenemutapa Kingdom.
pg109_n0028: Consequently, this led to the fall of the economy of Mwenemutapa.
pg109_n0029: Hence, Mwenemutapa began to lose its strength and eventually declined.
pg109_n0030: Having conquered Kilwa and Sofala, the Portuguese attacked the Mwenemutapa Kingdom in order to be in control of the gold mines.
pg109_n0031: This invasion enabled the Portuguese to overthrow the king of Mwenemutapa and put their appointee on the throne.
pg109_n0032: As a result, the Mwenemutapa Kingdom declined in the seventeenth century.
pg109_n0036: The Luba Kingdom was among the important centralised states in Central Africa.
pg109_n0037: It was located on the upper Lualaba River valley around Lake Kisale in the southeast of the present-day Democratic Republic of Congo, D R C.
pg109_n0038: By thirteen hundred C E, people in the
pg110_n0003: Lake Kisale region had organized themselves in many farming and trading chiefdoms.
pg110_n0004: These chiefdoms united into a single centralised kingdom between thirteen hundred C E and fourteen hundred C E under a dynasty called Nkongolo.
pg110_n0005: Later, in the fifteenth century, Ilunga Kalala, a heroic hunter who was believed to possess magical powers, overthrew the Ngongolo dynasty.
pg110_n0006: Ilunga Kalala introduced the Ilunga dynasty, which centralised the government power and expanded the kingdom to the west of Lake Kisale.
pg110_n0008: Factors for the rise of Luba Kingdom
pg110_n0010: Several factors contributed to the emergence and expansion of the Luba Kingdom.
pg110_n0011: The following are some of them:
pg110_n0014: The kingdom was located in a favourable environment.
pg110_n0015: The area was conducive for agricultural production because of its fertile soil and sufficient rainfall.
pg110_n0016: This environment supported the production of cereal crops.
pg110_n0017: Moreover, woodlands had many animals, including elephants, which were hunted for ivory.
pg110_n0018: All these activities encouraged the development of the state.
pg110_n0020: Development of iron and copper technology:
pg110_n0021: Another important reason for the rise and expansion of the Luba Kingdom was the development of technology in iron and copper.
pg110_n0022: Iron and copper were not mined in the Luba region, but were imported from the north.
pg110_n0023: Yet, peasants around Lake Kisale developed knowledge and skills in metalworking.
pg110_n0024: They processed iron to make tools such as hoes and axes for agricultural production.
pg110_n0025: They also made iron weapons, which were used for strengthening the army.
pg110_n0026: Copper was imported from the present-day Zambia and Congo border, the Copper belt.
pg110_n0027: The people around Lake Kisale used copper to forge items such as fine wire for rings, bracelets, and necklaces.
pg110_n0028: They also cast copper into cross-like bricks.
pg110_n0029: All these items were exchanged for other goods from neighbouring societies.
pg110_n0030: Consequently, wealth increased in the area, leading to state formation and expansion.
pg110_n0033: Fishing was another factor for the emergence of the Luba Kingdom.
pg110_n0034: The land was endowed with lakes and rivers that were rich in fish.
pg110_n0035: The people of Luba developed important tools used for fishing.
pg110_n0036: Such tools included fishing nets, harpoons, and dugout canoes.
pg110_n0037: They also developed different methods of drying fish.
pg110_n0038: A substantial amount of fish was sold to other societies in the region and beyond.
pg110_n0039: The wealth obtained from this trade was used for developing and expanding the kingdom.
pg110_n0042: Good leadership also facilitated the emergence and expansion of the Luba Kingdom.
pg110_n0043: Luba Kings developed a well-organized structure of leadership.
pg110_n0044: They appointed provincial governors who were often from the royal family.
pg110_n0045: These governors were responsible for collecting tributes from the chiefs under them.
pg111_n0003: central court was dominated by the royal family.
pg111_n0004: Although the kingdom had a small standing army, it was backed by the powerful mystical and religious authority of the kings.
pg111_n0006: Factors for the decline of Luba Kingdom
pg111_n0008: After flourishing for some time, the Luba Kingdom eventually declined in the fourteen fifties.
pg111_n0009: The disintegration was mainly due to two factors:
pg111_n0011: Slave trade: The introduction of the slave trade by Arabs and Swahili people from East African coast contributed to the decline of the Luba Kingdom.
pg111_n0012: Many people in the kingdom were taken to the coast as slaves.
pg111_n0013: This trade disrupted the Luba society leading to the weakening of the Kingdom.
pg111_n0015: Succession conflicts: Succession conflicts among members of the ruling clan also led to the decline of the Kingdom.
pg111_n0016: The struggle for power significantly weakened the kingdom.
pg111_n0017: Moreover, these conflicts forced some of the rivals to migrate to the West where they found their own kingdom, the Lunda.
pg111_n0021: The Lunda Empire was established by immigrants from the Luba Kingdom in the fifteenth century.
pg111_n0022: The Lunda people had no centralised authority apart from having a senior chief.
pg111_n0023: Moreover, they had a smaller population that lived in small villages.
pg111_n0024: They practised farming, fishing, hunting, and trading as their main activities.
pg111_n0025: Equally, their technology, arts and crafts were less developed than those of their neighbours, the Luba Kingdom.
pg111_n0026: Its foundations, as a state, were laid down from sixteen hundred C E.
pg111_n0027: Its growth and power as an empire were most evident in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries when it became one of the largest centralised states in pre-colonial Africa.
pg111_n0028: It occupied the areas now referred to as the Democratic Republic of Congo, north-eastern Angola, and north-western Zambia.
pg111_n0030: Factors for the rise of Lunda Kingdom
pg111_n0032: Three main factors led to the initial emergence and later expansion of the Lunda Kingdom.
pg111_n0035: Role of immigrants: The most important factor was the contribution of immigrants who were part of the Luba ruling clan and their followers.
pg111_n0036: One of these immigrants, known as Chibunda Ilunga, assumed and legitimised leadership power in the Lunda society by marrying a woman from among the members of the family of the Lunda senior chief.
pg111_n0037: This woman was the Lunda queen called Rweej or Lueji.
pg111_n0038: The children from this marriage and their future generations formed a new Lunda dynasty.
pg112_n0003: sixteenth century, the dynasty took the title of Mwaant Yaav or Mwata Yamvo, which meant the Lord of Vipers.
pg112_n0005: The Lunda dynasty united the previously loose and scattered Lunda chiefdoms into a single, centralised, and expanding empire.
pg112_n0006: In general, the Luba immigrants brought highly developed metalworking technology.
pg112_n0007: They also introduced among the Lunda an idea of centralised religious kingship.
pg112_n0008: This idea laid a firm base for later expansion of the Lunda Empire.
pg112_n0009: However, Lunda religious practices and chiefs were respected and maintained.
pg112_n0010: The chiefs were regarded as guardians of local spirits and owners of the land.
pg112_n0011: However, they were required to pay tribute to the king of the new empire.
pg112_n0012: The king also appointed the cilool or kilolo in each chiefdom as a royal adviser and a tax-collecting agent.
pg112_n0013: Moreover, the cilool was appointed to hold the loyalty of the confederation of the Lunda chieftaincies.
pg112_n0015: Long-distance trade: Another factor for the emergence and expansion of the Lunda Kingdom was participation in the long-distance trade.
pg112_n0016: The Lunda people played a key role in the East and Central African long-distance trade.
pg112_n0017: They mainly supplied ivory and slaves by exchanging them with weapons and textiles from the East African coast by the Arab and Swahili traders.
pg112_n0018: Both weapons and wealth obtained from the trade ensured the rise and expansion of the kingdom.
pg112_n0020: Raiding of neighbouring ethnic groups: The raiding of neighbouring ethnic groups also stimulated the rise and expansion of the empire.
pg112_n0021: The Lunda dynasty conquered many neighbouring societies and villages.
pg112_n0022: The dynasty integrated these societies into their empire.
pg112_n0023: Some of the captives were made slaves and used in agricultural production.
pg112_n0024: Others were sold to the Arab and Swahili slave traders.
pg112_n0028: By the early twentieth century, the Lunda Kingdom had collapsed completely.
pg112_n0029: There were two main reasons for the collapse of the kingdom.
pg112_n0030: The first was Chokwe invasion and the second was the partition of Africa.
pg112_n0032: Chokwe invasion: First, the empire was invaded by the Chokwe, who were armed with guns.
pg112_n0033: After the attack, the Chokwe established their own kingdom in the Lunda Empire.
pg112_n0034: Second, they introduced their own language and customs.
pg112_n0035: However, the Lunda chiefs and people continued to live in the Lunda heartland, although their previous power was highly eroded.
pg112_n0037: Partition of Africa: The European partition of Africa, which started in the eighteen eighties, ended the remnants of the Lunda Kingdom.
pg112_n0038: The area was divided among the Portuguese of Angola, King Leopold the second, who controlled the Congo Free State, and the British in the north-western Northern Rhodesia, Zambia.
pg112_n0039: This partition marked the complete disappearance of the Lunda Kingdom.
pg113_n0006: Briefly explain the lessons that modern societies in Central Africa can learn from ancient kingdoms in the region.
pg113_n0010: The kingdoms that were established in southern Africa before colonialism included Zulu and Sotho-Tswana.
pg113_n0011: This section presents the Zulu Kingdom as a case study.
pg113_n0015: The Zulu Kingdom extended from the coast of the Indian Ocean and Tugela River in the South to the Pongola River in the North of today South Africa.
pg113_n0016: The Kingdom rose in the nineteenth century under the leadership of Dingiswayo.
pg113_n0017: It lasted from eighteen hundred to eighteen seventeen.
pg113_n0018: Later on, the kingdom developed into the most powerful state under the leadership of Shaka, Chaka, who was a military leader.
pg113_n0020: Factors for the rise of Zulu Kingdom
pg113_n0022: The following were the factors that led to the rise of the Zulu Kingdom:
pg113_n0024: Centralisation of power under Shaka Zulu: Shaka took control of areas that enjoyed some freedom and placed them under his direct authority.
pg113_n0025: This had positive results since his skills in organising people strengthened the kingdom.
pg113_n0027: Influence of annual cultural festivals, Incwala: The king introduced annual cultural festivals.
pg113_n0028: People from all over the kingdom attended the festivals.
pg113_n0029: The festivals helped to build a sense of belonging, unity, and loyalty to the king.
pg113_n0031: Control of trade: The king controlled trade and all the ivory collected from the kingdom.
pg113_n0032: To the North, he kept open the trade route to Delagoa Bay where ivory was exchanged with beads and clothes.
pg113_n0033: Trade in ivory and in hides enabled the king to buy guns from the Portuguese.
pg113_n0034: These weapons helped to strengthen the army.
pg113_n0036: Standing army: Shaka established a permanent and strong army.
pg113_n0037: This meant that soldiers stayed permanently in the military camps.
pg113_n0038: They were well-trained, disciplined, equipped and ready for any emergency.
pg113_n0039: They were trained in military techniques such as using cow horn formation, short stabbing spears known as assegai, spying and using smoke signals and shields in battles.
pg113_n0040: They were not allowed to marry during the years of military service.
pg113_n0041: In addition, the soldiers depended on the state for all of their upkeep.
pg113_n0042: Shaka also used his standing army to expand his kingdom via wars.
pg114_n0003: fought many wars to achieve his purpose.
pg114_n0004: Shaka brought all the defeated clans into the Zulu kingdom.
pg114_n0005: In this way, the Zulu kingdom became more influential and powerful.
pg114_n0007: Development of agriculture: Crop production and livestock keeping were the major economic activities in the kingdom.
pg114_n0008: These activities ensured a regular and sufficient supply of food, which ensured a population increase.
pg114_n0009: The population needed a well-organised political system to create order and security in the kingdom.
pg114_n0013: The Zulu kingdom started to decline in the eighteen thirties.
pg114_n0014: This decline resulted from some factors including Boers invasion in the eighteen thirties, weak leadership and the British colonisation of South Africa.
pg114_n0016: Boer invasion in the eighteen thirties: The Boer’s invasion of Zululand contributed to the decline of the Zulu kingdom.
pg114_n0017: The Boers moved from the Cape northeastwards searching for grazing land.
pg114_n0018: Later, they reached Zululand and pushed the Zulu people outside their homeland.
pg114_n0019: These invasions weakened the economic base of the Zulu kingdom since most of their fertile land was taken by the Boers.
pg114_n0021: Weak leadership of Shaka’s successor: Shaka was succeeded by Dingane Kasenzangakhona.
pg114_n0022: However, King Dingane lacked strong leadership qualities and military abilities as commander in chief.
pg114_n0023: This weakness failed to maintain unity among the Zulu people and led to the eventual decline of the kingdom.
pg114_n0025: British colonisation of South Africa: The British colonisation of Zululand ended the power of African chiefs and established colonial rule.
pg114_n0026: The colonial government controlled the social, economic and political activities of Africans and undermined the autonomy of the kingdom.
