pg009_n0009_easy_read:
History is an important subject.
Many nations choose it for young people to study.
pg009_n0010_easy_read:
Nations choose history because it helps citizens understand themselves.
It also helps citizens understand the world around them.
pg009_n0011_easy_read:
History helps citizens study different parts of their society.
This helps them understand why society is the way it is.
It also helps them understand how these parts affect the world.
pg009_n0012_easy_read: This will help citizens become responsible for themselves, other people, and their nation.
pg009_n0013_easy_read:
In this chapter, you will learn:
- the meaning of history
- the importance of studying history
- the relationship between history and other related subjects
pg009_n0014_easy_read: You will also learn about sources of historical information.
pg009_n0015_easy_read: The skills you develop will help you use and value sources of historical information.
pg009_n0019_easy_read: History and sources of historical information
pg009_n0023_easy_read:
History is the study of events and processes from the past.
These events and processes may affect the present.
pg009_n0024_easy_read: These events and processes are about the social, political, and economic development of people and society.
pg009_n0025_easy_read: Studying history helps us answer these questions:
pg009_n0029_easy_read: What events happened in the past?
pg009_n0038_easy_read: Who took part in those events?
pg009_n0044_easy_read: How did those events affect people’s lives?
pg010_n0003_easy_read: In this case, not every event is a historical event.
pg010_n0004_easy_read: So, historical events have special qualities.
pg010_n0008_easy_read: Historical events have clear qualities that make them different from non-historical events.
pg010_n0009_easy_read: For an event to be called historical, it must have special qualities like these:
pg010_n0013_easy_read: A historical event must have a big effect on the history of a particular society.
pg010_n0014_easy_read: Historical events can strongly affect: politics; education; the economy, such as trade, industries, and agriculture.
pg010_n0015_easy_read: A good example is the Maji Maji War of nineteen oh five to nineteen oh seven.
pg010_n0019_easy_read: A historical event has effects that last a long time in the society where it happened.
pg010_n0020_easy_read: Some of these events are: the Berlin Conference of eighteen eighty-four to eighteen eighty-five; the Slave Trade; independence.
pg010_n0021_easy_read: These events can influence a society or shape it.
pg010_n0025_easy_read: Historical events are different from each other and cover many topics.
pg010_n0026_easy_read: These topics may include: social events; political events; economic events; scientific events; military events.
pg010_n0030_easy_read: A historical event happens in a specific time and place. Political, social, economic, and technological conditions can influence it.
pg010_n0034_easy_read: Historians can interpret historical events in different ways.
pg010_n0035_easy_read: Historians can have different views and stories about an event. This can lead to debate and different ideas about its causes, effects, and importance.
pg010_n0039_easy_read: Historical events give important lessons to future generations.
pg010_n0040_easy_read: By studying the past, societies learn from successes and failures. This helps them make informed decisions in the present and the future.
pg010_n0041_easy_read: For example, resistance to colonial rule in Africa gave lessons to modern nationalist leaders.
pg010_n0045_easy_read: A historical event must have a time when it happened.
pg010_n0046_easy_read: Time shows the difference between one event and another.
pg010_n0047_easy_read: Indeed, time explains when an event happened.
pg011_n0005_easy_read: Historians divide time into: days; weeks; months; years; decades; generations; centuries; millennia; periods; ages.
pg011_n0006_easy_read: A decade is a period of ten years.
pg011_n0007_easy_read: A generation is the time children need to become adults and have their own children.
pg011_n0008_easy_read: This period is usually thirty years.
pg011_n0009_easy_read: A century is a period of one hundred years.
pg011_n0010_easy_read: A millennium is a period of one thousand years.
pg011_n0011_easy_read: An age is a period when one historical event or condition is most important.
pg011_n0012_easy_read: An age may last several years, centuries, or millennia.
pg011_n0013_easy_read: Known ages in History include: the Stone Age; the Iron Age; the Industrial Age; the Nuclear Age; the Digital Age.
pg011_n0014_easy_read: A period is defined by one continuous event that lasts for some years.
pg011_n0015_easy_read: Examples include: the period of long-distance trade in East Africa; the period of the slave trade; the period of colonial rule in Africa.
pg011_n0019_easy_read: History uses a chosen starting point to divide time.
pg011_n0020_easy_read: The starting time is called year zero.
pg011_n0021_easy_read: The time from year zero onward is called the Common Era, C E.
pg011_n0022_easy_read: Before, this period was called Anno Domino, A D. It meant the years after the birth of Jesus Christ.
pg011_n0023_easy_read: The time before year zero is called Before Common Era, B C E. Before, it was called Before Christ, B C.
pg011_n0024_easy_read: For example, Julius Caesar, the ruler of the Roman Empire, died in forty-four B C E.
pg011_n0028_easy_read: There are four main ways to determine dates.
pg011_n0029_easy_read: These four ways are: recalling events; language studies; carbon fourteen; Potassium-argon.
pg011_n0031_easy_read: Recalling events: In this method, a person remembers important events.
pg011_n0032_easy_read: Examples of these events are: famines; wars; droughts; eclipses of the sun or moon; volcanic eruptions; floods; epidemics; the arrival of strangers; age groups; births; deaths.
pg011_n0033_easy_read: This method is useful for studying societies that did not keep written records.
pg011_n0035_easy_read: Language studies: People can also determine dates by studying languages.
pg011_n0036_easy_read: For example, foreign names for crops, animals, and food were introduced into Kiswahili.
pg011_n0037_easy_read: By finding when those names and words started to be used in a society, people can tell where the names and words came from. They can also tell when foreigners arrived and when the people of that society began to grow those crops.
pg011_n0038_easy_read: Other ideas may appear almost at the same time, such as: karafuu; coffee; cotton plantations.
pg011_n0040_easy_read: Carbon-fourteen dating: This is a scientific method for determining dates.
pg011_n0041_easy_read: People use this method to determine dates from the remains of plants and animals that died many years ago.
pg011_n0042_easy_read: Carbon fourteen is a carbon element that plants and other living things absorb.
pg011_n0043_easy_read: When living things die, the amount of carbon fourteen in their bodies starts to decrease at a constant rate.
pg011_n0044_easy_read: In laboratories, scientists measure how much carbon fourteen remains in a plant or animal. This helps them find how many years have passed since the plant or animal died.
pg012_n0003_easy_read: Potassium-argon: People can date archaeological materials with another scientific method called Potassium-argon.
pg012_n0004_easy_read: This technique dates archaeological remains linked to inorganic materials, especially volcanic rocks or ash, that formed millions of years ago.
pg012_n0008_easy_read: Historians use illustrations to show how historical events came one after another. These illustrations include: timelines; time graphs; family trees; time charts.
pg012_n0009_easy_read: Figures one point one, one point two, one point three, and one point four show, in this order: timelines; time graphs; family tree; time charts.

pg013_n0022_easy_read: The Mombasa Arabs set up their sheikhdom.
pg013_n0027_easy_read: Seyyid Said moved his capital from Muscat to Zanzibar.

pg013_n0082_easy_read: History is about how people try to use and change their environment for their social, economic, and political needs.
pg013_n0083_easy_read: People’s past actions are connected to their life today.
pg013_n0084_easy_read: In other words, past events made us who we are today.
pg014_n0003_easy_read: The importance of studying history includes these things:
pg014_n0007_easy_read: History helps us understand our societies and where they come from.
pg014_n0008_easy_read: It helps us feel that we belong in our community.
pg014_n0009_easy_read: In this way, History helps us love our country and its people, and also neighboring countries and their people.
pg014_n0010_easy_read: Studying History also helps us understand how and why our societies today are different from societies in the past.
pg014_n0012_easy_read: When we study History, we learn how people got their living and faced challenges in the past.
pg014_n0013_easy_read:
For example, we learn how people did these things:
- got food
- protected themselves from enemies
- treated sick people
- worshipped
pg014_n0014_easy_read: So, History helps us understand how people used their knowledge, skills, and experience to manage their environment.
pg014_n0018_easy_read: History is like a high stage. From it, we can clearly see how people lived in the past.
pg014_n0019_easy_read: History shows us these things about people in the past: their actions, their courage, their wisdom, and their unity.
pg014_n0020_easy_read: In this way, we understand other people's culture and behavior.
pg014_n0021_easy_read: We also learn to respect and accept the differences between people and societies.
pg014_n0022_easy_read: We understand that these things may be different from those of other people: ethnic groups, beliefs, customs, and traditions.
pg014_n0023_easy_read: History teaches us to accept those differences.
pg014_n0027_easy_read: History teaches us that one person's actions may affect other people.
pg014_n0028_easy_read: For example, our ancestors discovered crop cultivation and animal husbandry.
pg014_n0029_easy_read: These activities still help people today.
pg014_n0030_easy_read: Other people discovered fire and iron tools. People still use them today.
pg014_n0031_easy_read: We also learn that the things we do today may help or harm other people in the future.
pg014_n0032_easy_read: People are always affected by what other people did in the past.
pg014_n0033_easy_read: History shows that what happens in one society at one time may later affect other societies in a good or bad way.
pg014_n0037_easy_read: History is based on information from different sources.
pg014_n0038_easy_read: When we get information, we should ask these questions: Where did it come from? Can we trust it? Might someone have changed it?
pg014_n0039_easy_read: Finally, we should judge the information and make a conclusion.
pg014_n0040_easy_read: In this way, we learn that every issue can have different sources of information.
pg014_n0041_easy_read: We also learn that every problem may have several things: causes, effects, and solutions.
pg014_n0045_easy_read: History helps us understand that people develop their culture based on their environment and their contact with others.
pg014_n0046_easy_read: Through this contact, people come to understand the ways
pg015_n0004_easy_read: So, when people study History, they learn about and value the cultures of other people in the world.
pg015_n0008_easy_read: History is very important for building patriotism.
pg015_n0009_easy_read: Patriotism means love for your society or nation. It also means being willing to defend it.
pg015_n0010_easy_read: History builds this love and willingness. It teaches how past and present generations gave their lives to build the nation and defend it from enemies inside and outside the nation.
pg015_n0011_easy_read: History teaches how a nation began and how it changed over time.
pg015_n0012_easy_read: Also, History honors men and women who played important roles in building the nation as national heroes and heroines.
pg015_n0013_easy_read: Through History, learners come to value the memory and identity of their nation.
pg015_n0014_easy_read: So, History is very important. It helps people know their nation, love it, and be ready to defend it or even die for it.
pg015_n0015_easy_read: People who do not know their nation’s history often find it hard to feel proud of it or be ready to die for it.

pg016_n0004_easy_read: Read different reliable digital and non-digital sources. Identify the relationship between History and other subjects.
pg016_n0008_easy_read: History relates to some subjects, including: Geography, Mathematics, Biology, and languages such as Kiswahili, English, and Arabic.
pg016_n0009_easy_read: History also relates to Music and Theatre Arts.
pg016_n0013_easy_read: History relates to Geography because both subjects deal with ideas about the world and human beings.
pg016_n0014_easy_read: History deals with the origin of human beings. Geography deals with the origin of the universe and the places where historical events happen and where people study them.
pg016_n0015_easy_read: Another relationship is that historical events happened in certain geographical environments that supported human beings.
pg016_n0016_easy_read: For example, the remains of human civilization show that civilizations grew in environments that supported survival, mainly river valleys and forests.
pg016_n0017_easy_read: Since then, human beings have lived in such places.
pg016_n0021_easy_read: History has a close relationship with Mathematics because Mathematics helps us find the order and sequence of historical events.
pg016_n0022_easy_read: We use graphs, charts, and timelines to explain historical events.
pg016_n0023_easy_read: Mathematics is also used to find: the time when events happened, the dates of the events, and the order of the events over time.
pg016_n0024_easy_read: In this case, History uses knowledge from Mathematics to check the events that happened in the past.
pg016_n0028_easy_read: The evolution theory used in History to study the origin of human beings is also used in Biology to study the origin and existence of different species.
pg016_n0029_easy_read: So, History has a close relationship with Biology.
pg016_n0030_easy_read: The relationship between History and Biology allows more study of human existence.
pg016_n0034_easy_read: History helps us study the origin, development, and changes in human languages over time.
pg016_n0035_easy_read: History helps languages spread from one place to another through different actions and events.
pg016_n0036_easy_read: The spread of languages helps historians trace the regional movement of people and their effects on new regions.
pg017_n0005_easy_read: History studies the origin, development, and influence of music throughout human life.
pg017_n0006_easy_read: Music is not only a historical object. It also helps pass on stories about history.
pg017_n0007_easy_read: In this case, music tells about the past. It also helps history keep its meaning and pass through time.
pg017_n0011_easy_read: History and Theatre Arts are closely connected subjects. They support each other.
pg017_n0012_easy_read: History gives historical views and stories. Theatre Arts adds emotion, sympathy, and artistic explanations to historical events. This helps us understand the past and how it connects to the present.
pg017_n0016_easy_read: We gain historical knowledge by studying sources of historical information.
pg017_n0017_easy_read: People can get historical information from primary sources or secondary sources.
pg017_n0018_easy_read: Primary sources are original materials. They give first-hand information or direct evidence about a specific event.
pg017_n0019_easy_read: Primary sources are materials made by people who were directly involved in the events.
pg017_n0020_easy_read: These materials include: memos, diaries, letters, artefacts, photographs, interviews, speeches, autobiographies, and official records.
pg017_n0021_easy_read: Also, secondary sources come from primary sources.
pg017_n0022_easy_read: Secondary sources are created by people who were not directly involved in the original events.
pg017_n0023_easy_read: Secondary sources analyze, interpret, or comment on primary sources.
pg017_n0024_easy_read: Secondary source materials include: books, reviewed articles, dissertations, articles in newspapers, and academic papers.
pg017_n0026_easy_read: There are many sources for getting historical information.
pg017_n0027_easy_read: These sources include: oral sources, historical sites, written records, museums, archives, archaeology, historical linguistics, ethnographic records, and anthropology.
pg017_n0028_easy_read: However, it is important to remember that no source can do everything by itself.
pg017_n0029_easy_read: Each source can be used together with other sources.
pg017_n0033_easy_read: Oral sources are sources of historical information shared by word of mouth.
pg017_n0034_easy_read: There are two types of oral sources: oral traditions and oral testimonies.
pg017_n0038_easy_read: Oral traditions are sources of historical information passed from one generation to another by word of mouth.
pg017_n0039_easy_read: Oral traditions include: memorized stories, tales, riddles, narratives, poems, proverbs, jokes, songs, and prayers.
pg017_n0040_easy_read: Different people can present the information in oral traditions in different ways.
pg017_n0041_easy_read: For example, one Rwandese oral tradition says that the Hutu fell from heaven and met the Tutsi on earth.
pg017_n0042_easy_read: Another tradition says that the Hutu and Tutsi are brothers.
pg017_n0043_easy_read: These two oral traditions refer to one event:
pg018_n0003_easy_read: The origin of the Hutu and Tutsi.
pg018_n0004_easy_read: However, they give different views of the same event.
pg018_n0005_easy_read: In many African societies, there were professional storytellers, official storytellers, and poets.
pg018_n0006_easy_read: They used their skills to explain why important events happened in the past and how they happened.
pg018_n0007_easy_read: People still use oral traditions today in history research and writing.
pg018_n0011_easy_read: These are stories about the past from people who saw the event or the process being studied.
pg018_n0012_easy_read: Oral testimonies give information about events or processes that the narrators still remember.
pg018_n0013_easy_read: For example, soldiers who took part in the Tanzania-Uganda War of nineteen seventy-eight to nineteen seventy-nine can give valuable testimonies about the war.
pg018_n0015_easy_read: In general, oral traditions and oral testimonies have one similarity.
pg018_n0016_easy_read: Both are passed on by speaking.
pg018_n0017_easy_read: The difference is this: Oral traditions give information about the distant past. Oral testimonies give information about the recent past.
pg018_n0021_easy_read: Oral traditions and oral testimonies pass on knowledge about: cultural beliefs, traditional values, skills, and rituals.
pg018_n0022_easy_read: They teach literate and non-literate people about the past.
pg018_n0024_easy_read: Oral traditions and oral testimonies also encourage people to value and preserve their culture.
pg018_n0025_easy_read: They also entertain people during cultural activities such as: weddings, crop harvesting, initiation ceremonies, and rituals.
pg018_n0029_easy_read: Oral traditions and oral testimonies give helpful information about past events and processes when other sources are not available.
pg018_n0030_easy_read: People can also collect oral traditions and oral testimonies from literate and non-literate people.
pg018_n0031_easy_read: In addition, non-literate people can easily get historical information.
pg018_n0033_easy_read: Oral traditions and oral testimonies also help historians understand the point of view of the local people who shared the traditions.
pg018_n0034_easy_read: In the same way, oral traditions and oral testimonies express experiences, emotions, and feelings about historical events.
pg018_n0035_easy_read: This is because a person can see the emotions and feelings of the narrator.
pg018_n0039_easy_read: Oral traditions and oral testimonies are not always correct.
pg018_n0040_easy_read: Sometimes, informants leave out important information because they forget it due to age or because a long time has passed.
pg018_n0041_easy_read: They may also give different accounts of the same historical events or give exaggerated information.
pg019_n0003_easy_read: Another limit of oral traditions and oral testimonies is this: they only tell about a few past generations. They have only part of the information about the distant past because people forget over time.
pg019_n0005_easy_read: These limits sometimes make oral traditions and oral testimonies seem unreal.
pg019_n0006_easy_read: There are two ways to make oral traditions and oral testimonies more reliable.
pg019_n0007_easy_read: The first way is to collect several stories about the same event or historical process.
pg019_n0008_easy_read: This can help historians find and avoid changes in oral information.
pg019_n0009_easy_read: The second way is to talk with other people who know these traditions or testimonies.
pg019_n0010_easy_read: After the discussion, compare the different views.
pg019_n0011_easy_read: Then draw your conclusions from the findings.
pg019_n0015_easy_read: Written records are documents that give historical information.
pg019_n0016_easy_read: They include: letters, maps, magazines, legal documents, newspapers, reports, and minutes of meetings.
pg019_n0017_easy_read: These records are found in: archives, libraries, museums, offices, and the internet.
pg019_n0018_easy_read: Written records are also found in: people's homes, and religious institutions such as churches and mosques.
pg019_n0019_easy_read: Some written records are old books.
pg019_n0020_easy_read: One example of these books is The Periplus of the Erythrean Sea. A Greek trader wrote it in the first century C E.
pg019_n0021_easy_read: Another example of these books is Ptolemy’s Geography. It was written in the second century C E.
pg019_n0022_easy_read: These books describe the coastal people of East Africa and their trade activities.
pg019_n0023_easy_read: These books also tell us about the beauty of the environment and the cultures of people in cities such as Kilwa.
pg019_n0025_easy_read: In African history, there are written documents in: Arabic, Portuguese, Spanish, English, and French. Most of these documents are from the fifteenth century C E.
pg019_n0026_easy_read: These documents tell us about: people, geography, culture, and interactions among people from different regions in Africa.
pg019_n0028_easy_read: Historians read different written records to get information about the past.
pg019_n0029_easy_read: Some written records contain: pictures, tables, maps, and figures.
pg019_n0030_easy_read: These illustrations add meaning and information about the events being reported.
pg019_n0034_easy_read: Written records give historical information about past events and processes, such as: the Maji Maji War, First World War, Second World War, and European colonialism in Africa.
pg019_n0035_easy_read: They also help keep historical information for a long time.
pg019_n0036_easy_read: They also help historians write about the past so people can read it and understand it as history.
pg019_n0037_easy_read: During colonialism, people used written documents to present the achievements of colonialism as a new civilization.
pg020_n0006_easy_read: These are some of the advantages:
pg020_n0008_easy_read: Written records are easier to get and use than other sources, such as archaeological sources.
pg020_n0009_easy_read: It is also easier to find distorted information in written records.
pg020_n0010_easy_read: Written records may also last for a long time if people keep them well.
pg020_n0011_easy_read: Written records may also be reliable sources of information when people write and record them honestly.
pg020_n0012_easy_read: People can write and translate written records into different languages, such as: Kiswahili, Spanish, Arabic, and English.
pg020_n0013_easy_read: So, people in different parts of the world can use written records to write history.
pg020_n0014_easy_read: Lastly, written records are usually well organized and presented in a logical way.
pg020_n0015_easy_read: So, it is easy to find useful information in written records. Historians can use written records to write history.
pg020_n0019_easy_read: Written records also have limits, including these:
pg020_n0021_easy_read: No written record has all the detailed information about one topic.
pg020_n0022_easy_read: A person cannot learn everything from one written source.
pg020_n0023_easy_read: So, a person must read other sources of information to fill the gaps.
pg020_n0025_easy_read: Written records are also not always reliable.
pg020_n0026_easy_read: Some written records may contain wrong or distorted information.
pg020_n0027_easy_read: Written records may also support these interests: political interests, ethnic interests, religious interests, personal interests.
pg020_n0028_easy_read: For this reason, people must use written sources with great care.
pg020_n0029_easy_read: Also, during calamities or disasters, written records can be destroyed or lost.
pg020_n0030_easy_read: These calamities can be: fire, floods, earthquakes, wars.
pg020_n0031_easy_read: So, special skills and facilities are needed to keep written records safe.
pg020_n0033_easy_read: Lastly, only literate people can write written records.
pg020_n0034_easy_read: People who cannot read and write cannot use written records for any purpose.
pg020_n0039_easy_read: How will you use oral traditions and testimonies to get valid and reliable historical information?

pg021_n0011_easy_read: Historical sites give information about what people did in the past.
pg021_n0012_easy_read: Historical sites also show the level of knowledge and skills that people had in the past.
pg021_n0013_easy_read: This knowledge and these skills include: rock paintings, architecture, ironwork, irrigation systems, hunting tools, food gathering routes.
pg021_n0014_easy_read: Historical sites are also places of entertainment for interested people.
pg021_n0015_easy_read: Historical sites are also a source of income through tourism.
pg021_n0019_easy_read: Historical sites preserve evidence of ancient history because they contain different kinds of ancient information.
pg021_n0020_easy_read: For example, historical sites show: styles of buildings, utensils, working tools, settlement patterns.
pg021_n0021_easy_read: Some of the old buildings still keep their original functions today.
pg022_n0003_easy_read: Historical sites are also places where people preserve ancient objects.
pg022_n0004_easy_read: Historical sites are protected areas with important historical objects.
pg022_n0005_easy_read: Historians study and explain the historical objects found at a site. Then they write the history of the people who lived around the site.
pg022_n0006_easy_read: In Tanzania, trained workers under the National Museum of Tanzania protect and take care of these sites.
pg022_n0008_easy_read: Some historical sites also attract local and foreign tourists.
pg022_n0009_easy_read: These tourists learn about the past by looking at ancient structures.
pg022_n0011_easy_read: Historical sites are also important for historical research.
pg022_n0012_easy_read: Researchers get useful information from historical sites for research and for writing history.
pg022_n0013_easy_read: In this way, researchers use historical sites to add to information from other sources of history.
pg022_n0017_easy_read: Historical sites can be destroyed or damaged.
pg022_n0018_easy_read: Some historical sites disappear completely because of natural and human factors.
pg022_n0019_easy_read: Natural factors include: rainfall, earthquakes, wind, the sun’s heat, floods.
pg022_n0020_easy_read: Human factors include: wars, construction of different infrastructure, vandalism, grazing, farming.
pg022_n0021_easy_read: Also, some historical sites are in remote areas. These areas are hard and expensive to reach by road and other forms of transport.
pg022_n0023_easy_read: Also, preserving and managing historical sites costs a lot.
pg022_n0024_easy_read: Professionals or experts should manage these sites.
pg022_n0028_easy_read: Museums are buildings where historical objects are kept.
pg022_n0029_easy_read: For example, museums keep cultural objects linked to religious beliefs and ceremonies.
pg022_n0030_easy_read: Museums also keep collections of animal and plant fossils.
pg022_n0031_easy_read: Good examples of animal fossils are shells and bones.
pg022_n0032_easy_read: Museums also keep political objects, such as: crowns, regalia, objects used during nationalist struggles, drums.
pg022_n0033_easy_read: Museums also keep: economic objects such as coins, minerals, and cowries; technological objects such as stone tools, iron tools, canoes, and clothing.
pg022_n0034_easy_read: Museums also keep remains of artwork, such as: rock paintings, drawings, sculptures, pottery, and basketry.
pg022_n0035_easy_read: There are two types of objects kept in museums.
pg022_n0036_easy_read: The first type is artefacts. These include stone tools and iron tools.
pg022_n0037_easy_read: The second type is ecofacts. These include human, animal, and plant remains.
pg022_n0038_easy_read: Many countries have museums at the national, regional, district, and village levels.
pg022_n0039_easy_read: For example, Tanzania has: the National Museum and House of Culture; the Village Museum in Dar es Salaam; and the House of Wonders in Zanzibar, Beit al-Ajaib.
pg022_n0040_easy_read: Other museums in Africa include: the Genocide Memorial in Kigali, Rwanda; the Robben Island in South Africa; the Apartheid Museum in Johannesburg, South Africa; the National Museum of Ethiopia; the Egyptian Museum; and the Ghana National Museum.

pg023_n0007_easy_read: Museums keep many historical and cultural materials in one place.
pg023_n0008_easy_read: These materials include objects with a lot of information. These objects help people now and in the future.
pg023_n0009_easy_read: National museums also keep historical objects from all parts of the country.
pg023_n0010_easy_read: Museums make these objects available for the public to view and learn from.
pg023_n0011_easy_read: Museums preserve national heritage and historical information.
pg023_n0013_easy_read: Museums also teach people about different cultures.
pg023_n0014_easy_read: Museums are also a source of entertainment.
pg023_n0015_easy_read: People can visit museums for leisure.
pg023_n0017_easy_read: Museums also bring in income through fees that tourists pay.
pg023_n0018_easy_read: Local and international tourists visit museums to see different cultural objects and learn about the past.
pg023_n0022_easy_read: Museums help preserve the culture of society.
pg023_n0023_easy_read: Also, people do not borrow artefacts kept in museums for any purpose. This rule increases their security.
pg024_n0004_easy_read: Museums employ both professionals and other workers.
pg024_n0005_easy_read: Professional employees include: conservators, curators, and attendants.
pg024_n0006_easy_read: Another benefit of a museum is entertainment.
pg024_n0007_easy_read: Most museums entertain the people who visit them.
pg024_n0011_easy_read: Museums are very expensive to build and maintain.
pg024_n0012_easy_read: A museum needs a large space.
pg024_n0013_easy_read: Museums also need trained workers to run them.
pg024_n0014_easy_read: All these things cost a lot.
pg024_n0016_easy_read: Also, some museum objects can be damaged by: fire, moisture, heat, dust, insects, and rats.
pg024_n0017_easy_read: For example, the pages of an old book may turn yellow and tear easily because of moisture and heat.
pg024_n0018_easy_read: So, museums need a lot of care to keep the materials in good condition.
pg024_n0020_easy_read: Also, individual researchers cannot take materials out of a museum to gather historical information.
pg024_n0021_easy_read: Instead, the researchers have to visit museums several times for research.
pg024_n0022_easy_read: This can cost a lot of money and time.
pg024_n0024_easy_read: In the same way, museums cannot preserve some historical remains because of their nature and size.
pg024_n0025_easy_read: These remains include: huge commercial ships, ruins of houses, and graves.
pg024_n0026_easy_read: Also, some people cannot afford to visit museums because of cost, distance, and restrictions.

pg024_n0034_easy_read: Archives are places where people keep and maintain documents and old written records.
pg024_n0035_easy_read: These documents come from both public and private institutions.
pg024_n0036_easy_read: They include: missionaries’ records, travellers’ records, reports, photographs, some old books, colonial records, post-colonial records, and files.
pg024_n0038_easy_read: People preserve the documents carefully so they can be used for a long time.
pg024_n0039_easy_read: Some of the documents are open for public use, but others are confidential.
pg024_n0040_easy_read: National, regional, district, and village archives are in different places.
pg024_n0041_easy_read: The best-known public archives in Tanzania are: the Tanzania National Archives in Dar es Salaam, and the Zanzibar Institute of Archives and Records.
pg024_n0042_easy_read: The zonal centres include: the National Records Centre in Dodoma, the Mbeya Records Centre, and the Arusha Records.
pg025_n0003_easy_read: Centre, and the Mwanza Records Centre.

There are also church archives, such as:
- the Moravian Church Archives in Rungwe District
- the Benedictine Fathers Archives in Peramiho
pg025_n0005_easy_read:
These archives keep records from:
- the pre-colonial period
- the colonial period
- the post-colonial period
pg025_n0006_easy_read:
Right now, we can access archive information in two main ways:
- manual
- digital
pg025_n0007_easy_read:
Manual archives give written records in hard copy.
You get them by visiting the archives.
pg025_n0008_easy_read:
Digital archives give written records in soft form.
You get them by using online archives.
pg025_n0010_easy_read: A person can use manual or digital archives only after getting an official permit from the institution.
pg025_n0014_easy_read: Archives preserve historical information for public use.
pg025_n0015_easy_read:
Some archive records are confidential.
Later, they may be opened for public use.
pg025_n0017_easy_read: Archives are also the main places that keep historical information safe.
pg025_n0018_easy_read:
These places are made to reduce damage to the materials stored there from threats such as:
- fire
- thieves
- pests
- too much heat
- too much moisture
pg025_n0020_easy_read: Archives also provide a good environment for finding information from different kinds of written sources.
pg025_n0024_easy_read: Archives preserve old and recent documents.
pg025_n0025_easy_read: Documents in archives contain information from the recent past and the distant past.
pg025_n0026_easy_read: By using these documents, a person can follow how historical facts or processes continue over time.
pg025_n0028_easy_read:
Archives also organize information in a regular way.
This makes it easier for researchers to find or trace it.
pg025_n0029_easy_read:
The materials in archives can be very detailed.
They give deep information about:
- people
- places
- time
- events
pg025_n0033_easy_read: Documents kept in archives may be destroyed if people do not preserve them well.
pg025_n0034_easy_read: Archives are also expensive to set up and run.
pg025_n0035_easy_read: It is costly to set up archives because they need special buildings.
pg025_n0036_easy_read:
Archives also need:
- special facilities
- skilled personnel
- trusted people
pg025_n0037_easy_read: There may not be enough money to pay for these needs.
pg025_n0039_easy_read: Archives have strict rules for users to follow.
pg025_n0040_easy_read: This can make it hard for users to get and use records or documents at their own pace.
pg025_n0041_easy_read:
Some records are confidential.
They are not available to every researcher.
pg025_n0042_easy_read: Researchers also cannot get new documents with restricted information right away.
pg025_n0043_easy_read:
These documents can be released for use after thirty years.
This depends on negotiation with the creator of the document.
pg026_n0003_easy_read: Also, documents can be lost or put in the wrong place in the archives.
pg026_n0004_easy_read: In these cases, researchers will not get all the information they need.

pg026_n0010_easy_read: Archaeology is the study of past human activities through material remains.
pg026_n0011_easy_read:
These remains include:
- pottery
- hoes
- utensils
- bows
- arrows
- animal bones
- seeds
- ancient buildings
- irrigation canals
- iron-smelting furnaces
pg026_n0012_easy_read: These remains are also called archaeological materials.
pg026_n0013_easy_read: A person who studies archaeology is called an archaeologist.
pg026_n0014_easy_read: Examples of archaeologists are Doctor Louis Leakey and his wife, Doctor Mary Leakey.
pg026_n0015_easy_read: Doctor Louis Leakey and Doctor Mary Leakey worked at the Olduvai Gorge in north-eastern Tanzania, in Arusha Region.
pg026_n0016_easy_read: Doctor Louis Leakey and Doctor Mary Leakey discovered the oldest human skull in nineteen fifty-nine.
pg026_n0017_easy_read: They named the skull Zinjanthropus boisei.
pg026_n0018_easy_read: The skull is kept at the National Museum and House of Culture in Dar es Salaam.

pg026_n0023_easy_read: Another archaeologist is Professor Felix Chami. He is a Tanzanian scholar. He has done many archaeological studies along the coast of East Africa.
pg026_n0025_easy_read: Archaeological sites are places where people find material remains from past human activities.
pg026_n0026_easy_read:
At these sites, material remains may be found:
- above the ground
- under the ground
- in caves
pg026_n0028_easy_read: Archaeologists use survey and excavation methods to discover archaeological materials.
pg026_n0029_easy_read: In the survey method, archaeologists walk around an area in a random or planned way. They look for archaeological materials on the earth's surface.
pg027_n0003_easy_read: Excavation is used to get archaeological materials.
pg027_n0004_easy_read: Excavation means digging in a planned way and removing layers of soil to get material remains.
pg027_n0005_easy_read: Excavators use special tools: trowels, picks, shovels, and hoes.
pg027_n0006_easy_read: During excavation, archaeologists record all the objects and buildings they find.
pg027_n0008_easy_read: Archaeologists study and interpret the material remains. They do this to explain the relationship between the remains.
pg027_n0009_easy_read: For example, archaeologists may find human bones together with stone tools. This may help them explain the culture of the people who lived in that place.
pg027_n0010_easy_read: Archaeologists can also understand how the material remains were made and used.
pg027_n0011_easy_read: People use the information they gather to write the history of the people who lived there.
pg027_n0012_easy_read: That is why archaeology is seen as one of the sources of History.
pg027_n0014_easy_read: Some famous archaeological sites in Africa are: Olduvai Gorge, Arusha, Tanzania; Great Zimbabwe, Zimbabwe; Timbuktu, Mali; Fort Jesus, Mombasa, Kenya; Carthage, Tunisia; and Axum, Ethiopia.

pg027_n0021_easy_read: Archaeology gives evidence from material remains used by ancient people.
pg027_n0022_easy_read: Examples of these remains are: hoes, axes, arrows, and spears.
pg028_n0003_easy_read: This helps archaeologists and historians rebuild past events by using evidence from real objects.
pg028_n0004_easy_read: For example, people can rebuild past settlement patterns from remains found by excavation.
pg028_n0005_easy_read: It also gives historical knowledge about the past.
pg028_n0009_easy_read: Archaeology is based on real material objects.
pg028_n0010_easy_read: Archaeology uses material remains of objects that people made and used in the past.
pg028_n0011_easy_read: So, archaeology can describe people's past cultures more reliably than other sources can.
pg028_n0013_easy_read: Archaeology also helps History through its scientific methods.
pg028_n0014_easy_read: For example, historians can benefit from the carbon fourteen dating technique that archaeologists use.
pg028_n0015_easy_read: So, historians work with archaeologists to date historical events and processes.
pg028_n0016_easy_read: Archaeologists also excavate some materials and keep them in museums for future generations.
pg028_n0017_easy_read: Archaeological excavation is also important because it uncovers new findings or evidence in History.
pg028_n0018_easy_read: One example is the discovery of a human footprint in twenty sixteen at Laetoli, Tanzania.
pg028_n0022_easy_read: Some material remains cannot be recovered if they are damaged.
pg028_n0023_easy_read: Not all cultural remains stay in the ground for a long time.
pg028_n0024_easy_read: Plants and some bones decay quickly when they are buried.
pg028_n0025_easy_read: So, some material remains that could tell us about the past cannot be found for study.
pg028_n0027_easy_read: Archaeological research needs a lot of money for: excavation equipment, travel to and from the sites, camping facilities, storage, and caring facilities.
pg028_n0028_easy_read: The money needed to cover these costs may not be available.
pg028_n0030_easy_read: Archaeological work is also a long process. It involves: surveying, excavating the site to get the remains, and analyzing the materials in laboratories.
pg028_n0031_easy_read: So, archaeological work takes a long time.
pg028_n0033_easy_read: In the same way, many archaeological sites are in remote areas.
pg028_n0034_easy_read: Some sites are in very remote areas and are hard to reach.
pg028_n0035_easy_read: Sometimes, archaeologists find it difficult to locate such sites.
pg028_n0037_easy_read: A shortage of personnel and equipment is another limitation of archaeology.
pg028_n0038_easy_read: Archaeological excavations require highly trained people.
pg028_n0039_easy_read: However, these people are not always available.

pg029_n0003_easy_read: The study of languages and how they change over time.
pg029_n0004_easy_read: With this method, people can trace the origin of a group by studying its language.
pg029_n0005_easy_read: By doing this, historical linguists and historians find past human migration and interaction.
pg029_n0006_easy_read: Historical linguists and historians can even tell when contact happened between specific groups of people.
pg029_n0007_easy_read: For example, some Arabic words in Kiswahili show contact between Arabs and Swahili people along the coast of East Africa before colonialism. These words are: shukrani, shikamoo, madrasa, karafuu, and Alhamis.
pg029_n0008_easy_read: People can find the most important period of this contact by looking at when many Arabic words entered Kiswahili.
pg029_n0012_easy_read: Anthropology is a field of study about cultural practices and patterns in human societies.
pg029_n0013_easy_read: In particular, anthropology studies human societies and their: origin; development; customs; beliefs; and taboos.
pg029_n0014_easy_read: People who study these things are called anthropologists.
pg029_n0015_easy_read: Anthropologists travel around the world to study and record the cultures of existing societies.
pg029_n0016_easy_read: Anthropologists use the fieldwork method. They stay in these societies for a fairly long time.
pg029_n0017_easy_read: Anthropologists closely study existing societies. Then they give different kinds of historical information about these societies.
pg029_n0018_easy_read: This information helps historians reconstruct the past.
pg029_n0022_easy_read: Ethnographic information was created by people who lived in societies other than their own and observed them closely.
pg029_n0023_easy_read: This information includes: written records; images recorded on tapes; and images recorded on films.
pg029_n0024_easy_read: Europeans made most of these records when they traveled across the African Continent for different reasons during pre-colonial and colonial times.
pg029_n0025_easy_read: During their stay on the continent, they recorded information about subjects such as cultural practices and customs.

pg032_n0009_easy_read: Every living thing in the world develops.
pg032_n0010_easy_read: Human beings, animals, plants, insects, and bacteria have changed over time.
pg032_n0011_easy_read: Human beings came from other living creatures over millions of years.
pg032_n0012_easy_read: Changes in later generations made humans better in: appearance; mental ability; making tools

pg032_n0017_easy_read: The origin of human beings on Earth
pg032_n0021_easy_read: A theory is an explanation that many people accept. People use it to study and understand something.
pg032_n0022_easy_read: A good example of a theory is "Stoicism". It means accepting what you cannot control and focusing on what you can control to live a happy life.
pg032_n0024_easy_read: The two main theories about the origin of human beings are creation and evolution.
pg032_n0028_easy_read: Many religious groups support the theory of creation. These groups include: Judaism; Christianity; Islam; African indigenous religions
pg032_n0029_easy_read: According to the Bible, God created the world and everything in it, including human beings.
pg032_n0030_easy_read: God created human beings after He created the world, including: land; plants; water; birds
pg032_n0031_easy_read: The first human being was created on the sixth day. Then God said, "Let us make mankind in our image, in our likeness...." open parenthesis Genesis one twenty-six N I V close parenthesis.
pg032_n0032_easy_read: The Quran says: "Who made all things good which He created, and He began the creation of man from clay" open parenthesis Surah As-Sajdah thirty-two: seven close parenthesis.
pg032_n0033_easy_read: In the same way, many African societies had similar ideas about creation: the Supreme Being created everything, including human beings.
pg033_n0003_easy_read: People who support the theory of creation say that God created the Earth and everything on it, both living and non-living.
pg033_n0004_easy_read: They say that after God created the first man and woman, the human population grew through reproduction.
pg033_n0005_easy_read: They also say that people moved to different places on Earth.
pg033_n0009_easy_read: Evolution is the process in which the inherited features of a species change over many generations through natural selection.
pg033_n0011_easy_read: This theory is based on a scientific explanation of where humans came from.
pg033_n0012_easy_read: The theory says that humans and non-human primates, especially monkeys and apes, had a common ancestor more than thirteen million years ago.
pg033_n0013_easy_read: Over time, humans separated from non-human primates and changed through evolution until they became modern human beings.
pg033_n0015_easy_read: A British scientist, Charles Darwin, presented this theory in his book "On the Origin of Species," which was published in eighteen fifty-nine.
pg033_n0016_easy_read: In this book, Charles Darwin explained how evolution happened.
pg033_n0017_easy_read: Charles Darwin argued that, among the many individuals born, only the strongest or fittest survive.
pg033_n0018_easy_read: This means that only species that can adapt to the environment can live and reproduce.
pg033_n0019_easy_read: In contrast, the weak ones usually die.
pg033_n0020_easy_read: The survivors keep producing more offspring of the same type.
pg033_n0021_easy_read: In this way, new and stronger species continue to appear in each generation.
pg033_n0025_easy_read: Two pieces of evidence support the theory of evolution.
pg033_n0026_easy_read: They are: comparative studies of modern animals; fossil evidence
pg033_n0028_easy_read: Comparative studies of human evolution: Evidence from comparative anatomy shows that two groups of animals with similar features have the same ancestor.
pg033_n0029_easy_read: So, the body similarities between humans and monkeys suggest that the two groups share a common ancestor.
pg033_n0031_easy_read: Fossil evidence for human evolution: This evidence comes from animal bones that stayed under the ground for many years.
pg033_n0032_easy_read: Scientists use these bones as evidence of gradual changes in human shape and in technological development.
pg033_n0033_easy_read: Early fossil evidence has been found at different sites in Tanzania, such as: Laetoli; Olduvai Gorge; Lake Natron; Lake Ndutu; Lake Eyasi in Arusha Region
pg033_n0034_easy_read: Olduvai Gorge is the most famous site in Africa for human evolution.
pg033_n0035_easy_read: Olduvai Gorge gives evidence of the physical and technological evolution of humankind.
pg033_n0036_easy_read: Because of this, Olduvai Gorge and other sites have made Tanzania famous as the cradle, or original home, of human beings.
pg033_n0038_easy_read: Archaeologists such as Louis Leakey and his wife Mary Leakey discovered fossils in East Africa.
pg033_n0039_easy_read: Louis Leakey and Mary Leakey then studied the fossils to learn about human ancestors.
pg033_n0040_easy_read: People discovered other human remains at different sites in eastern and southern Africa.
pg034_n0003_easy_read: These places are: Koobi Fora in Kenya; Omo in Ethiopia; Hadar in Ethiopia; Sterkfontein in South Africa; and Swartkrans in South Africa.
pg034_n0004_easy_read: So, people consider eastern and southern Africa possible homes of human ancestors.
pg034_n0007_easy_read: Explain Charles Darwin's contribution to understanding human evolution.
pg034_n0011_easy_read: Fossil evidence shows three main groups of human ancestors.
pg034_n0012_easy_read: The three groups are: Ardipithecus; Australopithecus; and Homo.
pg034_n0016_easy_read: Ardipithecus is the earliest evidence of a human ancestor. It lived about five point eight to four point four million years ago.
pg034_n0017_easy_read: Ardipithecus had more ape-like features. These features include: strong teeth with small enamel; strong arms; and strong bones. These features suggest that Ardipithecus climbed trees and walked on two legs.
pg034_n0018_easy_read: Ardipithecus was found at the Omo archaeological site in Ethiopia.
pg034_n0022_easy_read: Australopithecus is another human ancestor. It lived about four point two to two point zero million years ago, after Ardipithecus disappeared.
pg034_n0024_easy_read: Raymond Dart first found it at the Taung site in South Africa. He named it Australopithecus africanus.
pg034_n0025_easy_read: Scientists found other Australopithecines at different sites in eastern and southern Africa.
pg034_n0026_easy_read: These include: Australopithecus afarensis, found in Laetoli, Tanzania, and Afar, Ethiopia; Australopithecus robustus, found in Swartkrans, South Africa; and Australopithecus boisei, or Zinjanthropus, found in Olduvai Gorge, Tanzania.
pg034_n0030_easy_read: About two point five million years ago, a creature called Homo appeared.
pg034_n0031_easy_read: People discovered this creature and named it Homo because they believed it was the first modern human being.
pg034_n0032_easy_read: Homo was different from Australopithecus. Homo had: a smaller body size; a diet that relied on meat; and a bigger brain size.
pg034_n0033_easy_read: More importantly, Homo started to make and use tools.
pg034_n0034_easy_read: The genus Homo has several species. These species include: Homo habilis; Homo erectus; Homo sapiens; and Homo sapiens sapiens.
pg034_n0036_easy_read: The following text describes the stages in human evolution from Homo habilis to Homo sapiens sapiens.
pg035_n0004_easy_read: Homo habilis were the first human beings who could make and use tools.
pg035_n0005_easy_read: That is why Homo habilis were nicknamed the "handyman."
pg035_n0006_easy_read: Fossils of Homo habilis have been found in: Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania; Koobi Fora in Kenya; and Sterkfontein in South Africa.
pg035_n0008_easy_read: Homo erectus. Homo erectus lived between one point nine million and three hundred thousand years ago.
pg035_n0009_easy_read: Homo erectus were the first to make advanced stone tools called hand axes. They could do this because their brains were more advanced than the brains of Homo habilis.
pg035_n0010_easy_read: Homo erectus was the first human to learn how to make and use fire. They used fire to roast meat and to keep warm.
pg035_n0011_easy_read: Fire also helped Homo erectus move from Africa and live in other parts of the world.
pg035_n0012_easy_read: In this case, Homo erectus was the first human to move from Africa to Asia and Europe.
pg035_n0013_easy_read: That is why fossils of Homo erectus are also found in Europe and Asia.
pg035_n0014_easy_read: Fossils of Homo erectus have been found in: Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania; Koobi Fora in Kenya; Zhoukoudian in China; and Dmanisi in Georgia.
pg035_n0017_easy_read: Some places in Africa where fossils of Homo sapiens have been found are: Laetoli, near Lake Eyasi and Lake Ndutu in Tanzania; Bodo in Ethiopia; Broken Hill in Zambia; Taung Cave in South Africa; Tangiers in Morocco; and Taramsa in Egypt.
pg035_n0018_easy_read: Examples of places outside Africa are: Tabun Cave in Israel; Krapina in Croatia; and Saccopastore in Italy.
pg035_n0021_easy_read: Their fossils are found all over the world.
pg035_n0022_easy_read: They are about one hundred fifty thousand to twenty thousand years old.
pg035_n0023_easy_read: They had a relatively larger brain than Homo sapiens.
pg035_n0024_easy_read: Fossils of these modern humans were found in: Nasera and Mumba rock shelter in Arusha, Tanzania; Middle Awash in Ethiopia; and Border Cave and Klasies River Mouth Cave in South Africa.
pg035_n0025_easy_read: Figure two point one shows the stages of human evolution from Ardipithecus to Homo sapiens sapiens.
pg035_n0027_easy_read: The stages are: Ardipithecus; Australopithecus; Homo habilis; Homo erectus; Homo sapiens; and Homo sapiens sapiens.
pg035_n0028_easy_read: Figure two point one. Stages of human evolution.
pg036_n0004_easy_read:
Read different reliable sources online and in the library about the origin of human beings from a religious point of view.
Then compare this knowledge with the theory of evolution.
pg036_n0008_easy_read: Human evolution developed together with technology.
pg036_n0009_easy_read:
This development went through two main ages.
The type of material used to make tools defined these ages.
pg036_n0010_easy_read: These ages were the Stone Age and the Iron Age.
pg036_n0014_easy_read:
Before the Stone Age, our ancestors made tools that were not made of stone.
They used softer materials such as:
- bones
- wood
- plant fibers
pg036_n0015_easy_read:
However, these tools did not last long.
Because of this, they are hard to trace.
pg036_n0016_easy_read: The Stone Age is the period in human history when stone was the main material for making tools and weapons.
pg036_n0017_easy_read: Human beings used these tools to meet their needs.
pg036_n0018_easy_read:
This period has three phases:
- the Early Stone Age, or the Old Stone Age
- the Middle Stone Age
- the Late Stone Age, or the New Stone Age
pg036_n0022_easy_read: The Early Stone Age lasted about three million to four hundred thousand years ago.
pg036_n0023_easy_read: During this period, human ancestors made and used stone tools for hunting and gathering.
pg036_n0024_easy_read:
They hunted wild animals.
They also gathered:
- fruits
- roots
- eggs from the surrounding environment
pg036_n0025_easy_read: The Early Stone Age was marked by the use of two types of tools: Oldowan tools and Acheulian tools.
pg036_n0027_easy_read:
Oldowan stone tools:
Oldowan tools were named after Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania, where people first found them.
pg036_n0028_easy_read:
People have also found Oldowan tools in these places:
- the shores of Lake Turkana in Kenya
- the Omo Valley in Ethiopia
- the Hadar Valley in Ethiopia
pg036_n0029_easy_read:
The tools were simple and rough.
People made them from hard natural rocks, sometimes with only small changes.
pg036_n0030_easy_read:
In some places, people did not change the tools.
They picked them and used them for specific tasks.
pg036_n0031_easy_read:
Oldowan tools included:
- flakes
- choppers
- cores
People used them for simple activities such as:
- killing animals
- skinning animals
- breaking bones to get marrow
pg036_n0032_easy_read:
People could also use these tools for:
- breaking nuts
- digging roots
pg036_n0033_easy_read: Homo habilis made Oldowan stone tools.
pg036_n0034_easy_read: Figure two point two shows examples of Oldowan stone tools.
pg037_n0003_easy_read: Figure two point two: Oldowan stone tools
pg037_n0005_easy_read:
Acheulian stone tools:
People first found these tools at Saint Acheul in France.
pg037_n0006_easy_read:
Acheulian stone tools were more advanced than Oldowan tools.
People made them by breaking small, sharp pieces of stone from large, hard rocks.
pg037_n0008_easy_read:
Acheulian stone tools included:
- hand axes
- cleavers
- picks
pg037_n0009_easy_read:
People used Acheulian stone tools for heavy work such as:
- cutting down trees
- killing animals
- processing meat
pg037_n0010_easy_read: Homo erectus made Acheulian stone tools.
pg037_n0011_easy_read:
People have found Acheulian stone tools in:
- Isimila in Tanzania
- Olduvai Gorge in Tanzania
- Lake Natron in Tanzania
- Laetoli in Tanzania
- around Lake Turkana in Kenya
pg037_n0012_easy_read:
Besides making stone tools, Homo erectus:
- lived together in small camps
- hunted animals
- shared food
pg037_n0013_easy_read: Figure two point three shows examples of Acheulian stone tools.
pg037_n0015_easy_read: Figure two point three: Acheulian stone tools
pg037_n0019_easy_read:
In the Early Stone Age, physical changes in human beings happened in three stages of evolution:
- Australopithecus
- Homo habilis
- Homo erectus
pg037_n0023_easy_read:
Australopithecus had:
- a hairy body that helped protect them from the cold
- large jaws and teeth
- a small brain, but larger than a chimpanzee's brain, at about four hundred cranial capacity, c c
pg037_n0024_easy_read: Their bodies were like chimpanzees' bodies.
pg037_n0025_easy_read: Their legs and pelvis were like those of human beings.
pg037_n0026_easy_read: Also, the women had smaller bodies than the men.
pg038_n0004_easy_read:
Evidence of walking on two legs is found at Laetoli in Arusha.
Australopithecus afarensis left footprints there on volcanic ash about three point five million years ago.
pg038_n0008_easy_read:
Homo habilis had a body shape like a modern human.
Its brain was large, about five hundred c c to eight hundred c c.
pg038_n0009_easy_read: This brain was bigger than the brain of Australopithecus.
pg038_n0010_easy_read:
Homo habilis also had:
- a long face
- smaller jaws
- smaller teeth
- longer arms than modern humans
- shorter legs than modern humans
pg038_n0011_easy_read: Males were heavier and taller than females.
pg038_n0015_easy_read:
During this stage of evolution, Homo erectus became fully upright.
Homo erectus could also communicate through speech.
pg038_n0016_easy_read: Homo erectus had a larger brain than Homo habilis.
pg038_n0017_easy_read: The brain size ranged from about seven hundred c c to one thousand, two hundred fifty c c.
pg038_n0018_easy_read:
Homo erectus had:
- a flat face
- thicker skull bones
- smaller teeth than Homo habilis
pg038_n0019_easy_read: Also, the arms and legs of Homo erectus were like those of modern humans.
pg038_n0023_easy_read: During this age, humans got food by: hunting wild animals with simple and rough tools; gathering roots; gathering tubers; gathering eggs; and gathering fruits from the surrounding area.
pg038_n0024_easy_read: Humans hunted: antelopes, buffaloes, and other animals.
pg038_n0025_easy_read: Animal bones from animals hunted by humans during this age have been found at Olduvai Gorge in East Africa.
pg038_n0028_easy_read: How did human beings live during the Early Stone Age?
pg038_n0032_easy_read: The Middle Stone Age was about five hundred thousand to fifty thousand years ago.
pg038_n0033_easy_read: The main difference between the Middle Stone Age and the Old Stone Age was the quality of the tools.
pg038_n0034_easy_read: During this period, tools were better and more specialized than Old Stone Age tools.
pg038_n0035_easy_read: Tools were: smaller, sharper, and easier to handle.
pg038_n0036_easy_read: Examples of Middle Stone Age tools are shown in Figure two point four: spears, arrowheads, knives, scrapers, and stone picks.
pg038_n0037_easy_read: The people who made tools in this period were Homo erectus and Homo sapiens.
pg039_n0003_easy_read: Figure two point four: Middle Stone Age tools.
pg039_n0005_easy_read: Middle Stone Age societies got food by: hunting and gathering.
pg039_n0006_easy_read: Middle Stone Age societies lived in different environments, such as: grasslands, rock shelters, river valleys, river areas, and highlands.
pg039_n0007_easy_read: Middle Stone Age societies also made rock paintings and decorated their bodies.
pg039_n0008_easy_read: Middle Stone Age societies also developed religions.
pg039_n0009_easy_read: The main technological development during this period was the discovery and use of fire.
pg039_n0010_easy_read: People made fire by striking stones against each other.
pg039_n0011_easy_read: Later, people learned how to make fire by drilling a stick by hand on dry wood, as Figure two point five shows.
pg039_n0012_easy_read: With fire and better tools, human beings controlled their environment better than before.
pg039_n0014_easy_read: This helped human beings live in thick woodland and mountain regions.
pg039_n0015_easy_read: Evidence of Middle Stone Age tools has been found in: Koobi Fora, Kenya; Chesowanja, Kenya; and Swartkrans, South Africa.
pg039_n0017_easy_read: Figure two point five: Making fire with a stick and wood.
pg040_n0005_easy_read: Using fire helped human beings roast food instead of eating raw food.
pg040_n0006_easy_read: Human beings could also burn trees and bushes to drive out or kill wild animals.
pg040_n0008_easy_read: Fire also helped human beings move to and live in the cold parts of Europe and Asia.
pg040_n0009_easy_read: This was possible because people could warm their bodies with fire.
pg040_n0010_easy_read: Lastly, people used fire to turn gums into glue. They used the glue to fix spear and arrow points onto shafts.
pg040_n0014_easy_read: During this period, human beings, that is, Homo sapiens, became more intelligent than before.
pg040_n0015_easy_read: This happened because they had bigger brains, from nine hundred c c to one thousand three hundred c c.
pg040_n0016_easy_read: Homo sapiens had features of both Homo erectus and modern human beings.
pg040_n0017_easy_read: Their physical features included large bodies and heavy muscles.
pg040_n0018_easy_read: They also had: thick chests, well-rounded foreheads, and smaller teeth than Old Stone Age people.
pg040_n0022_easy_read: During this period, human beings could make better tools from stone and wood.
pg040_n0023_easy_read: These tools helped them hunt large animals such as: buffaloes, rhinoceros, and elephants.
pg040_n0024_easy_read: They hunted animals that gave enough food for families and communities.
pg040_n0025_easy_read: Men also did other activities, such as fishing and gathering.
pg040_n0028_easy_read: Read reliable online and library sources about the Middle Stone Age. Then identify the knowledge and skills that can be used in present life.
pg040_n0032_easy_read: The Late Stone Age, also called the New Stone Age, existed from about fifty thousand years ago to about one thousand five hundred years ago.
pg040_n0033_easy_read: Tools made in this period were better and worked better than tools made in the Middle Stone Age.
pg040_n0034_easy_read: They included: different types of blades, stone axes, barbed arrows, and spears.
pg040_n0035_easy_read: The people who made these tools were Homo sapiens sapiens.
pg040_n0036_easy_read: The tools made during this time were smaller than the tools made during the Early and Middle Stone Ages.
pg040_n0037_easy_read: They were easier to use and worked better.
pg040_n0038_easy_read: Examples of these tools were spears and arrows.
pg040_n0039_easy_read: Figure two point six shows examples of these tools.
pg041_n0003_easy_read: Figure two point six: Late Stone Age tools.
pg041_n0005_easy_read: The Late Stone Age had big cultural and technological improvements.
pg041_n0006_easy_read: For example, by six thousand B C E, fishing communities had settled near: Lake Edward, Lake Rudolf, Lake Victoria, and the River Nile.
pg041_n0007_easy_read: These fishermen used barbed bone points and harpoons for fishing.
pg041_n0008_easy_read: Examples of Late Stone Age sites in East Africa are: Mumba rock shelter, Nasera rock shelter, Gambles Cave in Kenya, Enkapune ya Muto in Kenya, and Magosi in Uganda.
pg041_n0009_easy_read: The first evidence is the large amount of tool remains in those areas. There are also many fish, fowl, and animal bones.
pg041_n0010_easy_read: The second piece of evidence is drawings and paintings in caves and on rocks. They show hunting and other activities of settled communities.
pg041_n0011_easy_read: The paintings show that Late Stone Age societies: had religious beliefs, made religious symbols, and decorated their bodies.
pg041_n0015_easy_read: During the Late Stone Age, human beings had smaller teeth than in other Stone Ages.
pg041_n0016_easy_read: The teeth were suited to eating softer food. Human beings also had a large brain capacity of about one thousand three hundred to one thousand four hundred fifty c c.
pg041_n0017_easy_read: The shape of the skull was like the skull of modern human beings.
pg041_n0018_easy_read: By this time, human beings walked upright on two legs and had less body hair.
pg041_n0019_easy_read: In addition, human beings had: smaller brows, a high forehead, little facial projection, light-built jaws, and smaller limb bones.
pg041_n0023_easy_read: Late Stone Age societies depended on: hunting, gathering, fishing, and farming.
pg041_n0024_easy_read: The most important hunting weapons were bows and arrows.
pg041_n0025_easy_read: Sometimes people coated arrows with poison to kill animals such as: antelopes, buffaloes, elephants, and other animals.
pg041_n0026_easy_read: They hunted many kinds of small and large animals.
pg041_n0027_easy_read: They prepared skins and used them as clothes.
pg041_n0028_easy_read: They also fished in rivers and lakes.
pg041_n0029_easy_read: In addition, women gathered fruits and nuts.
pg041_n0030_easy_read: Women also dug up edible roots and tubers with digging sticks.
pg042_n0003_easy_read: By eight thousand B C E, some parts of Africa grew crops and kept animals. This helped hunting and gathering.
pg042_n0004_easy_read: The crops included: wheat, barley, finger millet, rice, yams, and palm oil.
pg042_n0005_easy_read: Pre-colonial African societies also kept animals such as: cattle, goats, sheep, and dogs.
pg042_n0006_easy_read: People have found evidence of the earliest food production in some parts of Africa.
pg042_n0007_easy_read: These areas are: Nile Valley, Ethiopian Highlands, regions along the Congo River, and some areas in west Africa.
pg042_n0008_easy_read: Also, Homo sapiens sapiens made art such as rock paintings and carvings.
pg042_n0009_easy_read: These artworks show activities such as: hunting, gathering, farming, and ceremonies.

pg042_n0019_easy_read: The Iron Age was a time when people used iron to make tools and weapons.
pg042_n0020_easy_read: Iron technology developed in Africa, south of the Sahara, between five hundred B C E and six hundred C E.
pg042_n0021_easy_read: Iron tools helped people control the environment better than stone tools did.
pg042_n0022_easy_read: So, iron production was an important new technology in pre-colonial Africa.
pg042_n0024_easy_read: Iron production in Africa, especially south of the Sahara, started in the basins of the Niger and Congo rivers in the first millennium B C E.
pg042_n0025_easy_read: From the basins of the Niger and Congo rivers, Bantu-speaking people spread this culture to other parts of the continent.
pg042_n0026_easy_read: The main centers of ancient ironworks in Africa included: Nsukka and Taruga in Nigeria, Meroe in Sudan, Axum in Ethiopia, Tunis in Tunisia, Cairo in Egypt, and Buganda in the interlacustrine region.
pg042_n0027_easy_read: Figure two point seven shows important Iron Age sites in Pre-colonial Africa.
pg043_n0044_easy_read: Figure two point seven: Iron Age sites in pre-colonial Africa
pg044_n0005_easy_read: People believe that humans discovered iron when they used fire to burn bushes.
pg044_n0006_easy_read: The fire melted iron ore on the surface of the earth.
pg044_n0007_easy_read:
Later, people discovered that they could smelt iron ore to get pure iron.
Then they could forge the pure iron into iron tools.
pg044_n0008_easy_read: Iron smelting means heating iron ore to change it into pure iron.
pg044_n0009_easy_read:
Iron forging means processing and shaping smelted iron into useful objects, such as:
- hoes
- axes
- knives
- machetes
- other tools shown in Figure two point eight
pg044_n0011_easy_read: Figure two point eight: Some iron tools
pg044_n0015_easy_read: Iron smelting began with collecting iron ore and charcoal.
pg044_n0016_easy_read:
Iron smelting also involved:
- building furnaces
- building blowpipes, tuyere
- making bellows
pg044_n0017_easy_read: Iron smelting furnaces in African societies had two basic types.
pg044_n0018_easy_read: The first type was a bowl-like furnace dug into the ground.
pg044_n0019_easy_read:
The second type was a ground furnace that people built.
It was about one meter or two meters high.
pg044_n0021_easy_read: People put iron ore and charcoal in the furnace.
pg044_n0022_easy_read: Then people lit the furnace and pumped air with the bellows.
pg044_n0023_easy_read: Air from the bellows entered the furnace through the tuyere.
pg044_n0024_easy_read: Many remains show that iron smelting and forging were widespread across Africa.
pg044_n0025_easy_read:
These remains include:
- furnaces
- tuyere
- bellows
- blooms
- slags
- anvils
- iron objects
pg045_n0005_easy_read: Using iron tools had many advantages.
pg045_n0008_easy_read:
Expansion of agriculture: Agriculture grew because people started to use better iron tools for production, such as:
- machetes
- axes
- hoes
pg045_n0009_easy_read: These tools helped people cultivate larger areas of land than before.
pg045_n0011_easy_read: Settled life: More farming with iron tools led to more food production.
pg045_n0012_easy_read: This led to the growth of large communities. These communities produced surplus food.
pg045_n0013_easy_read: Because of these changes, people needed a sedentary life.
pg045_n0015_easy_read: Population increase: Surplus food from the use of iron tools led to an increase in population.
pg045_n0016_easy_read: The population also increased because people moved from different regions to areas that produced iron.
pg045_n0018_easy_read: Emergence of chiefdoms and kingdoms: The use of iron weapons led to both an increase in population and wars between different groups.
pg045_n0019_easy_read: These situations needed permanent and centralized political organizations, in the form of states, to solve problems and conflicts.
pg045_n0020_easy_read: The need for a centralized political organization led to the rise of chiefdoms and kingdoms.
pg045_n0023_easy_read: Increased efficiency in hunting: Iron weapons such as arrows and spears improved hunting and made it more efficient.
pg045_n0024_easy_read: This is because iron tools were more effective than stone tools for hunting.
pg045_n0026_easy_read: Improvement of self-defense: Iron weapons such as arrows and spears helped people defend themselves against wild animals better than stone tools did.
pg045_n0028_easy_read: Emergence of specializations: Communities could produce enough food and surplus food, so not everybody had to work in agriculture.
pg045_n0029_easy_read: So, other people started to specialize in other activities, such as: basketry, pottery, pastoralism, and fishing.
pg045_n0031_easy_read: Growth of commodity exchange, trade: Iron-producing communities exchanged iron tools for other items made by communities that did not produce iron.
pg045_n0032_easy_read: In this way, the exchange of commodities between communities increased.
