pg047_n0008_easy_read: Pre-colonial African societies interacted with each other in many ways.
pg047_n0009_easy_read: These interactions helped pre-colonial African societies produce basic needs and other things they needed for life.
pg047_n0010_easy_read: These interactions and the production of needed goods influenced social and economic development.
pg047_n0011_easy_read: In this chapter, you will learn about the concepts used in social organization and economic production.
pg047_n0012_easy_read: You will also learn about these modes of production in pre-colonial Africa and their characteristics: communal, slave, and feudal.
pg047_n0013_easy_read: The skills you develop will help you tell the difference between pre-colonial African social organizations and present-day African social organizations. This will help you keep good practices and discourage inhuman social relations.
pg047_n0017_easy_read: The ownership of the major means of production
pg047_n0021_easy_read: To explain the social and economic development that Africa reached before colonialism, it is important to understand some key concepts.
pg047_n0022_easy_read: One key concept is social organization. It is about how people and groups in society interact while producing material goods.
pg047_n0023_easy_read: In this kind of organization, people get duties based on their positions in society.
pg047_n0024_easy_read: Another concept is economic production. It means the process of producing goods and services to meet human needs.
pg047_n0025_easy_read: It also includes creating economic value from raw products.
pg047_n0026_easy_read: Examples of activities related to economic production are crop cultivation and cloth-making.
pg047_n0027_easy_read: So, in economic production, social organization means how people are organized and how they relate to each other while producing goods or services.
pg047_n0029_easy_read: People need to produce different types of goods and services to survive.
pg047_n0030_easy_read: People use tools like these to produce goods and services: hand hoes, machetes, spears, axes, arrows, tractors, and computers.
pg047_n0031_easy_read: These tools together are called instruments of labour.
pg048_n0003_easy_read: So, instruments of labour are all the tools people use in the production process.
pg048_n0004_easy_read: Tools can be simple or complex. This depends on the level of technology in a society.
pg048_n0005_easy_read: These instruments help people use their natural body parts better, such as: hands, legs, eyes, and the brain.
pg048_n0006_easy_read: Means of labour help people make work easier.
pg048_n0007_easy_read: Without means of labour, work becomes difficult.
pg048_n0009_easy_read: Instruments of labour are arranged around human labour.
pg048_n0010_easy_read: Human labour is the physical and mental energy people use to produce what they want.
pg048_n0011_easy_read: Physical labour is the energy people use to produce what they want.
pg048_n0012_easy_read: Mental labour is the knowledge and skills people use during production.
pg048_n0013_easy_read: When people combine labour and instruments of labour, they are called productive forces.
pg048_n0014_easy_read: In production, productive forces act on resources such as land and forests.
pg048_n0015_easy_read: These resources are called objects of labour.
pg048_n0017_easy_read: An object of labour is anything that people work on to produce goods.
pg048_n0018_easy_read: These resources are mainly found in natural environments, such as: land, rivers, and forests.
pg048_n0019_easy_read: This means people need objects of labour to work.
pg048_n0020_easy_read: Without objects of labour, work becomes impossible.
pg048_n0021_easy_read: For example, a person may have a good fishing tool. But the person cannot fish unless there is a river, an ocean, a lake, or a water pond with fish in it.
pg048_n0022_easy_read: When people combine human labour, instruments of labour, and objects of labour, they are called means of production.
pg048_n0024_easy_read: Means of production are the combination of means of labour, human labour, and objects of labour.
pg048_n0025_easy_read: Means of production are necessary to produce goods and services.
pg048_n0027_easy_read: When the means of labour are left alone, they have no value in life.
pg048_n0028_easy_read: So, human labour must act on objects of labour to produce goods and services.
pg048_n0030_easy_read: People enter into certain relations to produce goods and services.
pg048_n0031_easy_read: Relations are either exploitative or non-exploitative. A relation is exploitative when the producers of goods and services are not paid fairly. A relation is non-exploitative when the opposite is true.
pg048_n0032_easy_read: A combination of productive forces and relations of production makes a mode of production.
pg048_n0033_easy_read: A mode of production in a society is meant to meet people's needs.
pg048_n0037_easy_read: Visit one economic production center or service provision center to study production relations. Then write a report.
pg049_n0005_easy_read: Pre-colonial African societies went through three modes of production: communalism, slavery, and feudalism.
pg049_n0006_easy_read: But not all societies went through all three modes of production.
pg049_n0007_easy_read: The change from one mode of production to another mainly depended on the environment and on the development of productive forces.
pg049_n0011_easy_read: Communalism was the first mode of production in all human societies.
pg049_n0012_easy_read: This mode was also called primitive communalism.
pg049_n0013_easy_read: People called it primitive communalism because societies had a low level of technology.
pg049_n0015_easy_read: Communalism was based on collective ownership of the means of production and on equal sharing of the gains.
pg049_n0016_easy_read: In Africa, communalism lasted much longer than any other mode of production.
pg049_n0017_easy_read: Communalism developed many years ago, when people began to live in communities.
pg049_n0019_easy_read: Some African societies still practice communal life. These include hunter-gatherer groups such as: the Mbuti of the Ituri Forest of Eastern Congo; the San of the Kalahari Desert; the Sandawe of Northcentral Tanzania; the Hadzabe of Northcentral Tanzania; the Khoikhoi of South Africa.
pg049_n0020_easy_read: Other examples are pastoralist communities such as: the Fulani of Northern Nigeria in West Africa; the Galla of north-eastern Africa; the Somali of north-eastern Africa; the Teso of Uganda and Kenya; the Karamojong of Uganda; the Ndorobo of Tanzania and Kenya.
pg049_n0021_easy_read: Some of these societies adopted new modes of production because they interacted with other societies.
pg049_n0027_easy_read: The whole society owned the main means of production, such as land, forests, and water bodies.
pg049_n0028_easy_read: All people produced goods based on gender and age.
pg049_n0029_easy_read: As a result, people shared the products of labor according to their needs.
pg049_n0030_easy_read: People did not exploit each other.
pg049_n0031_easy_read: This was because no person could own resources alone. All people worked together for a common goal.
pg049_n0032_easy_read: For example, people did hunting, farming, and fishing together.
pg049_n0033_easy_read: Communalism did not create social classes.
pg049_n0034_easy_read: Instead, people respected each other and were equal in principle.

pg062_n0004_easy_read: In addition, it led to the start and growth of centralized political systems, such as chiefdoms and kingdoms.
pg062_n0005_easy_read: Likewise, it encouraged better farming technology.
pg062_n0006_easy_read: People needed better tools to make their work easier and increase production.
pg062_n0007_easy_read: The main disadvantage of permanent crop cultivation is that it increased conflicts in society.
pg062_n0009_easy_read: These conflicts happened because resources became scarce. This was mainly about control of fertile land and iron ore sites. The increase in population caused this scarcity.
pg062_n0011_easy_read: Both shifting cultivators and permanent cultivators invented and used different techniques to improve crop yields.
pg062_n0012_easy_read: For example, the Nyakyusa, Shambaa, Sukuma, and Nyamwezi made terraces on hillsides.
pg062_n0013_easy_read: This technique kept water and prevented soil erosion.
pg062_n0014_easy_read: In the same way, people dug water canals in the gardens to keep rainwater.
pg062_n0015_easy_read: The Buganda, Ankole, Buhaya, and Ufipa grew different crops on their farms to keep moisture in the soil.
pg062_n0016_easy_read: They also made banks and planted crops such as yams and potatoes on them.
pg062_n0017_easy_read: These banks kept rainwater and prevented soil erosion.
pg062_n0018_easy_read: People buried plant remains. The plant remains decayed and became composite manure.
pg062_n0019_easy_read: People in the highlands, such as the Chagga, Pare, and Shambaa, dug irrigation furrows in their farms.
pg062_n0020_easy_read: They also made and used composite manure, as well as manure from cattle and goat.
pg062_n0021_easy_read: The people of Ukerewe and Ukara Islands made the soil richer with composite manure and animal manure.
pg062_n0022_easy_read: They also kept cattle, which gave them milk, meat, and manure.

pg063_n0005_easy_read: Pastoralism means keeping and grazing livestock.
pg063_n0006_easy_read: People who practiced pastoralism were called pastoralists.
pg063_n0007_easy_read: Ancient pastoral communities kept animals such as: cattle, sheep, camels, donkeys, and goats.
pg063_n0009_easy_read: For example, livestock provided: meat, milk, blood, manure, and hides or animal skins.
pg063_n0010_easy_read: In some societies, people used animals like camels and donkeys for transportation. They carried people and goods.
pg063_n0011_easy_read: In many societies, livestock was a source of wealth.
pg063_n0012_easy_read: People who owned many livestock were the richest in the society.
pg063_n0013_easy_read: They had prestige and enjoyed privileges because of their wealth.
pg063_n0014_easy_read: They could lend their cattle to poor people. In return, the poor people gave labor, loyalty, and patronage.
pg063_n0017_easy_read: People used cattle, goats, and sheep to pay dowry.
pg063_n0018_easy_read: Among the Zulu, Xhosa, Swazi, Shona, and Ndebele, people paid livestock as Lobola.
pg063_n0019_easy_read: Lobola is property given as livestock or other goods. A man who wants to marry, or the head of his family, gives it to the head of the woman's family. This is done in gratitude for allowing the marriage.
pg063_n0020_easy_read: People slaughtered black cattle and sheep in traditional ceremonies such as: weddings, burials, rainmaking, initiation, and the coronation of a chief or king.
pg063_n0021_easy_read: Pastoralism was common in arid, semi-arid, and savannah or tropical grassland areas in pre-colonial Africa.
pg063_n0024_easy_read: There were two types of pastoral societies: nomadic pastoralists, and sedentary or settled pastoralists.
pg063_n0028_easy_read: These pastoralists often moved from one place to another to look for water and pasture for their livestock.
pg063_n0029_easy_read: They lived on: milk, meat, and blood.
pg063_n0030_easy_read: They also ate vegetables and food grains such as maize and sorghum.
pg063_n0031_easy_read: They got these foods by exchanging with neighboring farming communities. Those communities needed livestock products.
pg063_n0032_easy_read: Nomadic pastoralists were also war-like people. They were always ready to fight to defend their wealth.
pg063_n0033_easy_read: From time to time, they raided their neighbors to take livestock.
pg063_n0034_easy_read: Examples of nomadic pastoralists were: the Tuaregs of North Africa; the Fulani of northern Nigeria; the Somali of Somalia and Kenya; the Karamajong of northern Uganda; and the Maasai of Tanzania and Kenya.
pg063_n0038_easy_read: Sedentary pastoralism was a form of animal husbandry. In this system, people kept livestock in one place.
pg063_n0039_easy_read: The livestock included: cattle; goats; sheep; camels; and donkeys.
pg063_n0040_easy_read: Herders cared for the livestock. They knew the local environment and the needs of the animals.
pg063_n0041_easy_read: Sedentary pastoralism helped pre-colonial African societies build settled communities. They depended on livestock for food and economic development.
pg064_n0003_easy_read: These communities were placed on purpose near water sources and grazing areas.
pg064_n0004_easy_read: In pre-colonial African societies, livestock were important resources. They provided food, materials for clothing, and materials for shelter.
pg064_n0005_easy_read: Some societies in the southern part of Africa practiced settled pastoralism. They included the Khoikhoi and the San.
pg064_n0006_easy_read: In the savannah regions of East Africa, the Maasai and Samburu practiced settled pastoralism.
pg064_n0007_easy_read: In West Africa, some Fulani groups were nomadic. Other Fulani groups lived in settled communities and also kept animals.
pg064_n0008_easy_read: Some animals people kept were: cattle; goats; sheep; camels; and donkeys.
pg064_n0009_easy_read: Both nomadic and settled pastoralists could identify different herbs to treat their sick animals.
pg064_n0014_easy_read: How did nomadic pastoralists in pre-colonial African societies adapt to their environment?
pg064_n0016_easy_read: Explain how sedentary pastoralists in pre-colonial African societies structured their communities.
pg064_n0020_easy_read: Some societies combined keeping animals with growing crops.
pg064_n0021_easy_read: This type of agriculture is called mixed farming.
pg064_n0022_easy_read: People practiced mixed farming in: areas with heavy rainfall; grasslands with seasonal rainfall; and woodland savannah.
pg064_n0023_easy_read: People who practiced mixed farming included: Gogo; Nyaturu; Nyiramba; Sukuma; Nyamwezi; Hutu; Ankole; Pare; and Kimbu.
pg064_n0024_easy_read: These people grew permanent and seasonal crops. These crops included: bananas; yams; beans; and cereals.
pg064_n0025_easy_read: They also kept livestock such as: cattle; sheep; goats; and donkeys.
pg064_n0026_easy_read: People kept the long-horned Ankole type of cattle in the interlacustrine region.
pg064_n0027_easy_read: People kept the short-horned cattle called zebu in the drier woodland savannah and wooded steppes.
pg064_n0028_easy_read: Other societies that practiced mixed farming in pre-colonial Africa included the Rwozi in Central Africa.
pg064_n0029_easy_read: The Rwozi used irrigation and terracing methods.
pg064_n0030_easy_read: In West Africa, these groups practiced mixed farming: Hausa; Yoruba; Ewe; Ashanti; Nupe; and Igbo.
pg064_n0031_easy_read: These societies grew different cash crops and raised livestock.
pg064_n0032_easy_read: They grew crops such as: millet; sorghum; yams; and maize. They also raised livestock such as: cattle; sheep; and goats.
pg064_n0033_easy_read: Figure four point one shows the areas that practiced: crop cultivation; pastoralism; and mixed farming, in pre-colonial Africa.

pg066_n0007_easy_read: As the population grew, social conflicts started.
pg066_n0008_easy_read: Because of this, people needed leaders to solve conflicts.
pg066_n0009_easy_read: Leaders also became more responsible for protecting important sources of wealth, such as: salt mines, pastoral lands, and iron ore.
pg066_n0010_easy_read: In the same way, leaders became responsible for sharing and using resources such as: land, water, and pastures.
pg066_n0013_easy_read: For example: some community members worked in agriculture, others made iron tools, others worked in fishing, others worked in basketry, and others worked in pottery.
pg066_n0014_easy_read: Specialisation started for two main reasons. First, not every member of society grew crops or kept animals.
pg066_n0015_easy_read: Second, there was extra food to feed people who did not produce food and who specialised in skilled craft work.
pg066_n0016_easy_read: So, some people wove baskets and mats. Others made and repaired iron tools.
pg066_n0017_easy_read: Other people specialised in trade. They exchanged their extra products to get goods they did not produce.
pg066_n0019_easy_read: Population growth and the rise of specialisation led to exchange relations. Later, these exchange relations created trading posts.
pg066_n0020_easy_read:
These trading posts grew into urban centres.
These urban centres worked as:
trading centres,
cultural centres,
and administrative centres.
pg066_n0021_easy_read:
Examples of these centres in West Africa were:
Taghaza,
Bilma,
Taoden,
and Niamey.

pg068_n0009_easy_read: Pre-colonial African societies went through many economic changes, such as in handcraft and mining.
pg068_n0010_easy_read: These changes happened mainly because people worked to improve technology to manage the environment.
pg068_n0011_easy_read: In this chapter, you will learn about the types of industries that existed in pre-colonial Africa.
pg068_n0012_easy_read: You will also learn about the different types of minerals extracted in pre-colonial African societies.
pg068_n0013_easy_read: The skills and knowledge you develop will help you appreciate the efforts our ancestors made to improve their standard of living and sustain life.
pg068_n0021_easy_read: An industry is a place where people change raw materials into finished goods.
pg068_n0022_easy_read: In pre-colonial Africa, the natural resources in a society determined the types of industries in that area.
pg068_n0023_easy_read: For example, in the iron smelting industry, people smelted iron ore and forged it into iron goods such as knives and hoes.
pg068_n0024_easy_read: In the same way, people shaped and baked clay into pots, bowls, and bricks in areas with suitable clay soil.
pg068_n0026_easy_read: Also, handcraft is the art of using skills and hands to design and make things.
pg068_n0027_easy_read: Handcraft industries were industries where people used their hands, skills, and knowledge to make products such as baskets, pots, and mats.
pg068_n0028_easy_read: Handcraft industries helped people make and get tools and other objects.
pg068_n0029_easy_read: In pre-colonial Africa, different handcraft industries developed as people specialized in activities other than agriculture.
pg068_n0030_easy_read:
These industries included:
iron making,
basketry,
spinning,
weaving,
cloth making,
carving,
and canoe making.
pg069_n0005_easy_read: Cloth making was the art of making clothes from local cotton, tree bark, and animal skins.
pg069_n0006_easy_read: Some communities in pre-colonial Africa specialized in making cloth.
pg069_n0007_easy_read: People made clothes by pounding the bark of certain trees.
pg069_n0008_easy_read: People also decorated clothes with dyes.
pg069_n0009_easy_read:
This way of making clothes was common among the Haya, Nyakyusa, and Ganda in East Africa.
They used suitable tree bark to make clothes.
pg069_n0010_easy_read:
Other societies used animal skins to make clothes, such as skins from:
sheep,
goats,
and camels.
pg069_n0011_easy_read:
Using animal skins to make clothes was common in:
Madagascar,
North Africa,
Sudan,
the Sahel belt of West Africa,
the Yoruba,
people from Malawi,
and people from Mozambique.
pg069_n0013_easy_read:
Also, making cotton cloth was common in many African societies, including:
Aksum, Sudan,
Iwelen, Nigeria,
Takrur, Ghana,
Ufipa,
Unyamwezi,
and Unyiha in East Africa.
pg069_n0014_easy_read:
Other societies were:
the Shire Valley in Malawi,
and Igombe-Ilede in South Africa.

pg069_n0021_easy_read:
People wore clothes to:
cover their bodies,
decorate themselves,
and keep warm.
pg069_n0022_easy_read:
People also wore clothes on special occasions, such as:
religious ceremonies,
traditional ceremonies,
and funeral ceremonies.
pg069_n0023_easy_read: In some societies, the colors of clothes were also important.
pg069_n0024_easy_read:
For example, rainmakers wore black clothes.
Black was a symbol of dark clouds that bring rain.
pg069_n0025_easy_read: In other societies, twins were not allowed to wear red clothes during the rainy season.
pg069_n0026_easy_read:
Clothes became important goods.
They helped trade grow in the pre-colonial period.
pg070_n0005_easy_read: Pottery is the art of making pots and other items from clay soil.
pg070_n0006_easy_read: This skill was common in places with clay soil that was good for pottery.
pg070_n0007_easy_read: In pre-colonial Africa, people who made pottery made items for home use and trade, such as: pots, pipes, and bowls.
pg070_n0008_easy_read: Pottery was common among: the Pare of northeastern Tanzania, the Kerewe of Ukerewe Island in Lake Victoria, and the Kisi on the shores of Lake Nyasa.
pg070_n0009_easy_read: Pottery was also common in the Nok area in northern Nigeria.
pg070_n0013_easy_read: Pottery was useful for making objects for cooking, storing water, storing beer, storing milk, and storing grains.
pg070_n0014_easy_read: Pottery objects also became important trade goods in local and regional trade.
pg070_n0015_easy_read: For example, Pare potters traded their objects with nearby societies, such as the Chagga, the Taveta, and the Maasai.
pg070_n0016_easy_read: Kisi potters traded their objects with the Nyakyusa, the Ndali, the Kinga, the Pangwa, the Ngoni, and other nearby societies.
pg070_n0017_easy_read: The Lozi of Zambia traded pots among themselves and with their neighbors, the Lunda and Bisa.
pg070_n0021_easy_read: Basketry is the art of weaving palm leaves and other special reeds to make items such as fish traps, mats, hats, baskets, and ropes.
pg070_n0022_easy_read: Many societies in pre-colonial Africa practiced basketry, including the Nyamwezi, the Gogo, the Zaramo, the Yao, and the Ganda.
pg070_n0023_easy_read: Basketry was also common among the Chokwe of Zambia, the Lozi of Zambia, the Tonga of Zambia, and the Buga of Guinea and Liberia.
pg070_n0024_easy_read: Other societies included the Sara of Chad, the Zulu of South Africa, the Barotse of Botswana, the Twana of Botswana, and the Bamileke of Cameroon.
pg070_n0025_easy_read: The materials used in basketry mostly came from palm trees, reeds, bamboo, and different types of grass. These materials were found in many places.
pg070_n0026_easy_read: Figure five point two shows basketry products in pre-colonial Africa.
pg070_n0028_easy_read: Figure five point two: Basketry products in pre-colonial Africa.
pg071_n0005_easy_read: Baskets were used in different ways.
pg071_n0006_easy_read: Some baskets were used to collect and carry farm products. Other baskets were used to store grain and seeds for later use.
pg071_n0007_easy_read: Basket making also produced fish traps. People used the fish traps to catch fish in rivers, lakes, and oceans.
pg071_n0008_easy_read: Mats were used for sitting, sleeping, and drying food.
pg071_n0009_easy_read: They were also used to wrap dead bodies for burial.
pg071_n0013_easy_read: Carpentry was work with wood logs and poles to make wooden products.
pg071_n0014_easy_read: This art was common in many African communities that lived in woodland areas.
pg071_n0015_easy_read: For example, artisans carved wood to make stools, mortars, pestles, doors, canoes, beehives, and wooden basins.
pg071_n0019_easy_read: Canoes were used to transport people and goods. People also used canoes for fishing.
pg071_n0020_easy_read: The Makonde of southern Tanzania and northern Mozambique carved wood to make figurines, masks, earrings, and bracelets.
pg071_n0021_easy_read: Other people made mortars to pound grains into flour and crush herbs into medicine.

pg071_n0030_easy_read: Mining is the removal of minerals from the ground.
pg071_n0031_easy_read: People in different parts of Africa practiced mining. They had knowledge and skills in taking minerals from the ground.
pg071_n0032_easy_read: Examples of these minerals in pre-colonial Africa were iron, salt, gold, copper, silver, and tin.
pg071_n0036_easy_read: Ironworking started in some African communities in the first millennium B C E.
pg071_n0037_easy_read: In East Africa, this technology started around five hundred B C E. It spread widely in the region by around seventeen hundred C E.
pg071_n0038_easy_read: The production of iron tools had these main stages: First, people mined iron ore from the ground.
pg071_n0039_easy_read: Second, people smelted the ore in furnaces to purify it.
pg071_n0040_easy_read: Third, people left the pure iron to cool and
pg072_n0004_easy_read: Fourth, people heated the solid iron until it was red hot.
pg072_n0005_easy_read: Then people hammered the iron into tools or weapons of different shapes.
pg072_n0006_easy_read: The process of hammering iron into tools is called forging.
pg072_n0007_easy_read: People who specialized in making iron into tools and weapons were called ironsmiths.
pg072_n0008_easy_read: Figure five point three shows a kiln for iron extraction used by the Fipa of Tanzania.
pg072_n0010_easy_read: Figure five point three: Kiln for iron extraction among the Fipa.
pg072_n0012_easy_read: In East Africa, ironworking developed among these groups: Meru, Kerewe, Haya, Fipa, and Baganda.
pg072_n0013_easy_read: Among the Pare, ironsmiths came from the royal Shana clan.
pg072_n0014_easy_read: Among the Zinza of Geita, anyone who paid a fee could learn iron smelting.
pg072_n0015_easy_read: In the same way, iron technology developed among the Venda people of southern
pg073_n0003_easy_read: Transvaal in South Africa and the Teso of Eastern Uganda.
pg073_n0004_easy_read: Other ironworking societies were the Mashona of Zimbabwe, the Mang’anja of Malawi, and societies around Kalambo Falls in Zambia.
pg073_n0005_easy_read: In West Africa, ironworking societies lived in the Futa Djalon plateau in present-day Guinea.
pg073_n0006_easy_read: In northeastern Africa, examples included: societies in Nubia in present-day Sudan; societies in Meroe in present-day Sudan; and Axum in present-day Ethiopia.
pg073_n0010_easy_read: The use of iron tools and weapons had many benefits.
pg073_n0011_easy_read: This improved tools. It also helped agriculture grow and increased food production.
pg073_n0012_easy_read: Iron tools also made it easier to mine iron and other minerals and to make other handcrafts.
pg073_n0013_easy_read: Also, communities could produce more different items.
pg073_n0014_easy_read: This led to the growth and development of trade.
pg073_n0015_easy_read: In some parts of Africa, people used iron bars as money.
pg073_n0017_easy_read: This happened because the technology helped people build homes and use iron weapons to defend their families and property from enemies.
pg073_n0018_easy_read: It also helped some states rise in Africa, such as: Fipaland; Buganda; and Karagwe.
pg073_n0019_easy_read: In the same way, the use of iron weapons greatly changed warfare.
pg073_n0020_easy_read: Societies with iron weapons became stronger.
pg073_n0021_easy_read: They conquered weaker societies that still used stone and wooden weapons.
pg073_n0022_easy_read: These conquests led to the growth of chiefdoms or kingdoms.
pg073_n0023_easy_read: It also made wars between rival communities happen more often.
pg073_n0027_easy_read: Salt making was one of the earliest industries in pre-colonial Africa.
pg073_n0028_easy_read: There were four main methods of getting and processing salt.
pg073_n0029_easy_read: These four methods were: taking salt from salty reeds; leaching rocky soils; mining salt from rocks; and evaporating salty water.
pg073_n0032_easy_read: People burned salty reeds, and they dissolved the ash in water.
pg073_n0033_easy_read: People filtered the solution and boiled it until all the water evaporated.
pg073_n0034_easy_read: People used the material that was left as salt.
pg073_n0035_easy_read: This method was common among the Mang’anja people along Lake Nyasa. It was also common around Lake Victoria and Lake Albert in East Africa.
pg073_n0036_easy_read: People in the interlacustrine region also commonly used this method.
pg073_n0039_easy_read: Leaching is a method where people drained water through rocky soils with a lot of salt.
pg073_n0040_easy_read: People sieved it and boiled it to get salt crystals.
pg073_n0041_easy_read: People used this method at Uvinza and Ivuna in Tanzania and at Bilma in West Africa.
pg073_n0044_easy_read: In this method, people mined salty rocks directly.
pg073_n0045_easy_read: Then people used the rock crystals as salt.
pg073_n0046_easy_read: People around Bangwelo and the Luapula rivers in Central Africa and around Lake Chad in Western Sudan used this method.
pg073_n0047_easy_read: In West Africa, people used this method at: Bilma; Taghaza; Idjil; and Taoudeni.
pg074_n0003_easy_read: Evaporation: In this method, people trapped salty ocean water in pans and left it to dry in the heat of the sun.
pg074_n0004_easy_read: After the water dried, salt crystals stayed in the pans.
pg074_n0005_easy_read: This method was common along the East African coast, and people still use it today.
pg074_n0006_easy_read: For example, salt pans are along the coast of: Tanga; Bagamoyo; Dar es Salaam; and Lindi.

pg074_n0014_easy_read: Salt had many uses in the pre-colonial period.
pg074_n0015_easy_read: Salt was used in food and to preserve food.
pg074_n0016_easy_read: Food, such as beef and fish, lasted longer when people added salt.
pg074_n0017_easy_read: Salt was also used as a medium of exchange because it was rare in many societies.
pg074_n0018_easy_read: So, salt became an important trade commodity.
pg074_n0019_easy_read: For example, people used salt from Uvinza as a medium of exchange across the Great Lakes region.
pg074_n0020_easy_read: Also, people in Ethiopia and merchants in Timbuktu, in the Sahara Desert, used salt as a medium of exchange.
pg074_n0021_easy_read: Salt was also used to treat wounds.
pg074_n0022_easy_read: In some societies, people used salt as medicine to treat wounds.
pg074_n0023_easy_read: People used sodium bicarbonate as an antacid to treat indigestion and upset stomach. It reduces stomach acid.
pg074_n0024_easy_read: Salt was also used to preserve dead bodies and stop them from decaying.
pg074_n0025_easy_read: This was common among ancient Egyptians.
pg074_n0026_easy_read: This way of preserving a dead body with salt is called mummification.

pg074_n0033_easy_read: In pre-colonial Africa, people mined and processed gold in different parts of Africa.

pg074_n0035_easy_read: In West Africa, people mined gold in: Bambuk, Bure, Lobi, and the forest area of Asante.
pg074_n0036_easy_read: The common methods used to get gold were different from place to place.
pg075_n0005_easy_read: In this method, people collected alluvial gold from streams and river beds.
pg075_n0006_easy_read: They used pans to separate the gold from sand and rocks.
pg075_n0007_easy_read: People mainly used this method along the smaller rivers of the Sabi and Zambezi Rivers in Mozambique and Zimbabwe.
pg075_n0011_easy_read: Some places had gold veins underground.
pg075_n0012_easy_read: To get the gold, people dug out rocks that contained gold.
pg075_n0013_easy_read: Then people took the rocks to furnaces and burned them to get pure gold.
pg075_n0014_easy_read: People used this method in Mashonaland in Zimbabwe and in Asante in Ghana.
pg075_n0018_easy_read: In pre-colonial Africa, people used gold as a trade item.
pg075_n0019_easy_read: People also used gold as a medium of exchange, or a form of money.
pg075_n0020_easy_read: People used gold to make symbols of power and authority for African rulers.
pg075_n0021_easy_read: For example, among the Asante of Ghana, the King's stool was made of gold.
pg075_n0023_easy_read: People also used gold to make: jewelry, ornaments, and decorative materials.
pg075_n0024_easy_read: People also used gold to make golden utensils, such as: cups, plates, handles for knives, and handles for swords.
pg075_n0025_easy_read: Gold was also a symbol of wealth and power for people who had it.
pg075_n0029_easy_read: People produced copper mainly by smelting copper ores.
pg075_n0030_easy_read: People smelted ores with copper and made them into pieces of pure metal shaped like a brick.
pg075_n0031_easy_read: People mined copper in many parts of pre-colonial Africa.
pg075_n0032_easy_read: These places included: Kafue in Zambia, Gwai River in Zimbabwe, and Katanga in Congo.
pg075_n0033_easy_read: Other places included: the Sinai Peninsula in Egypt, and the land of Igbo and Yoruba in Nigeria.
pg075_n0035_easy_read: Copper had many uses in the pre-colonial period.
pg075_n0036_easy_read: People used copper to make: ornaments, bowls, copper wire, daggers, and helmets.

pg077_n0008_easy_read: Pre-colonial African societies were active and changing. They reached different levels of social and political development.
pg077_n0009_easy_read: This development shows that African societies could: rule themselves, manage conflicts, and choose their leaders.
pg077_n0010_easy_read: By fifteen hundred C E, African societies had developed different social and political systems.
pg077_n0011_easy_read: In this chapter, you will learn about social systems, political systems, and education systems.
pg077_n0012_easy_read: You will also learn about non-centralised political systems. These systems include clan or kinship organization and the age-set system.
pg077_n0013_easy_read: You will also learn about the type of education in pre-colonial Africa.
pg077_n0014_easy_read: The skills and abilities you develop will help you use the positive parts of pre-colonial systems in the family and in society.
pg077_n0017_easy_read: Political authority without a central government
pg077_n0021_easy_read: The term "system" means a group of objects or things. They are arranged so they connect and work together for a specific function.
pg077_n0022_easy_read: Each part has a fixed place. Each part also has a clear role.
pg077_n0023_easy_read: A good example is the human digestive system.
pg077_n0025_easy_read: A political system describes power relations among people and societies.
pg077_n0026_easy_read: A political system includes: governing institutions; how leaders make decisions; how leaders deal with internal and external matters.
pg077_n0028_easy_read: A social system is a set of rules, structures, and beliefs. They guide how people interact and relate in a society.
pg077_n0029_easy_read: Education is the knowledge and skills that a society passes from one generation to another to reach a common goal.
pg078_n0003_easy_read: In pre-colonial African societies, social, political, and educational systems did not develop in the same way in all parts of Africa.
pg078_n0004_easy_read: This development was different from one society to another because of factors such as geographic location and the level of technology in each society.
pg078_n0005_easy_read: Some societies used non-centralized political systems, and others used centralized political systems.
pg078_n0006_easy_read: The two political systems were different in: how society members shared power; the kind of social relationships they had.
pg078_n0009_easy_read: Read Sections thirty-three through thirty-six of Chapter Two of the nineteen seventy-seven Constitution of the United Republic of Tanzania. Then give your views on how the Government would do its work without central authority.
pg078_n0013_easy_read: Non-centralized, or decentralized, social and political systems were a form of organization without central authority.
pg078_n0014_easy_read: Some common characteristics of a non-centralized political system were:
pg078_n0016_easy_read: These societies did not have a central ruler called a king. Their political leaders were mainly clan heads. Councils of elders helped the clan heads. The council of elders and the clan heads shared political power and authority.
pg078_n0017_easy_read: There were two forms of non-centralized social and political systems in pre-colonial Africa: clan or kinship organization; the age-set system.
pg078_n0021_easy_read: A kinship or clan organization is a type of social and political organization made up of closely related families with the same ancestor or a common ancestor.
pg078_n0022_easy_read: Kinship was the most common form used in the world, including pre-colonial Africa.
pg078_n0023_easy_read: A clan was made up of several families that were closely related.
pg078_n0024_easy_read: These families included: the husband; the wife or wives; children; grandparents; extended relatives.
pg078_n0025_easy_read: The family was the basic unit of production.
pg078_n0026_easy_read: Some examples of pre-colonial African societies that used clan or kinship organization were: the Igbo of West Africa; the Sukuma of Tanzania; the Kikuyu of Kenya.
pg078_n0027_easy_read: There were two main types of kinship in pre-colonial Africa.
pg078_n0028_easy_read: The two types were patrilineal and matrilineal.
pg078_n0029_easy_read: These groups were created for different reasons, but they served the same goals.
pg079_n0005_easy_read: This is the most common form of kinship in the world, including Africa.
pg079_n0006_easy_read: People in this system trace their family line through their fathers.
pg079_n0007_easy_read: When a woman gets married, she moves to her husband's clan and becomes part of his kin group.
pg079_n0008_easy_read: Children in this social system take the name of their father's clan and follow it.
pg079_n0009_easy_read: Examples of societies that followed the patrilineal system include: the Luo of Kenya and Tanzania; the Zulu of South Africa; the Ndebele of Zimbabwe; the Ngoni of Northern Zambia; the Tumbala of Northern Zambia.
pg079_n0010_easy_read: One characteristic of patrilineal kinship was this: men from the father's line controlled social, economic, and political decisions.
pg079_n0011_easy_read: The men from the father's line made important decisions about the welfare and interests of the family or clan.
pg079_n0012_easy_read: The men from the father's line also owned major means of production, like land, and decided how to use them.
pg079_n0013_easy_read: The men from the father's line decided the amount and sharing of the bridewealth. They also supervised marriage transactions.
pg079_n0017_easy_read: In the matrilineal social system, a married man leaves his father's family and clan to live with his wife's family.
pg079_n0018_easy_read: He may live in his wife's family compound or near it.
pg079_n0019_easy_read: Children take the name of their mother's clan and follow it.
pg079_n0020_easy_read: So, clan inheritance is based on the mother's clan.
pg079_n0021_easy_read: In pre-colonial Africa, fathers had no power over children in matrilineal societies.
pg079_n0022_easy_read: Maternal uncles made all important decisions for their nephews and nieces. This included decisions about bride wealth.
pg079_n0023_easy_read: Some societies that followed the matrilineal system were: the Luguru of Morogoro; the Yao of Lindi and Mtwara; the Makonde of Lindi and Mtwara; the Bemba of Zambia; the Mbundu of the Kingdom of Ndongo in Angola; the Herero of Namibia and Botswana; the Ashanti of Ghana; the Akan of Ghana.
pg079_n0026_easy_read: Read reliable digital and non-digital sources about patrilineal and matrilineal social systems. Then write an essay about the social-economic advantages and disadvantages of each system in modern African societies.
pg079_n0031_easy_read: These were the characteristics of the clan or kinship organization.
pg079_n0033_easy_read: A clan or kinship had: common rituals, taboos, and customs.
pg079_n0034_easy_read: These cultural characteristics helped make each clan stable, strong, and different from other clans.
pg079_n0035_easy_read: These cultural characteristics helped bring clan members together and build a sense of community.
pg080_n0003_easy_read: Clans or kinship groups governed themselves, but they had no rulers or kings.
pg080_n0004_easy_read: Because there were no rulers, clans had no central political administration and no state tools of power.
pg080_n0005_easy_read: They were also societies with no social classes.
pg080_n0006_easy_read: Because of these features, clan or kinship systems are seen as non-centralized or stateless.
pg080_n0007_easy_read: It was a social and political system with no central government to enforce laws.
pg080_n0008_easy_read: Clan leaders had limited political and military power.
pg080_n0010_easy_read: Clan or kinship communities were small and simple.
pg080_n0011_easy_read: Clan or kinship communities had small populations, and their economic and technological development was relatively low.
pg080_n0012_easy_read: They depended on simple activities: hunting, gathering, fishing, and cropping.
pg080_n0013_easy_read: They also used simple tools made of stone and wood.
pg080_n0014_easy_read: Some of these communities got simple iron tools from neighboring societies through barter trade.
pg080_n0016_easy_read: Clans had enough land and lived in clan units that were close to each other.
pg080_n0017_easy_read: There was less competition for basic resources: livestock, agricultural land, minerals, and water.
pg080_n0018_easy_read: So, there were no clear differences in wealth or property ownership.
pg080_n0022_easy_read: In clan or kinship organizations, the family was the basic unit of production.
pg080_n0023_easy_read: Land was the main means of production, and it belonged to the whole clan.
pg080_n0024_easy_read: However, the tools or instruments of labor belonged to individual families.
pg080_n0025_easy_read: The clan head and the elders did not own the main means of production.
pg080_n0026_easy_read: Their duty was to give land to other clan members to use.
pg080_n0027_easy_read: The elders also guided clan members in the production process.
pg080_n0028_easy_read: Each family in the clan received as much land as it could use.
pg080_n0029_easy_read: Clan members shared most of the products of labor based on the needs of each member.
pg080_n0030_easy_read: The main means of production and the products of labor were shared among the members of a clan.
pg080_n0032_easy_read: In politics, clan organization centered on the clan heads, who led the group.
pg080_n0033_easy_read: Clan heads were responsible for managing political, economic, and social relations in the community.
pg080_n0034_easy_read: They did these tasks: settled disputes in the community, arranged marriages for members, and performed clan rituals.
pg080_n0035_easy_read: In addition, they did these tasks: allocated land to clan members or immigrants, gave names to newly born babies, and protected all communal property, such as land, forests, and water sources.
pg080_n0038_easy_read: The close ties between family units helped the clan continue to exist and survive.
pg080_n0039_easy_read: Cultural elements made this closeness stronger.
pg081_n0003_easy_read: For example: rituals, values, customs, and taboos.
pg081_n0004_easy_read: These things connected people and united them as members of the clan.
pg081_n0008_easy_read: What were the roles of the family in pre-colonial African societies?

pg081_n0012_easy_read: Why did the clan, or kinship, organization own the main means of production together?
pg081_n0016_easy_read: The age-set system was another form of social and political organization in pre-colonial Africa.
pg081_n0017_easy_read: In this organization, work and social responsibilities were divided by age and sex.
pg081_n0018_easy_read: This social and political organization was common in: pastoral societies, agro-pastoral societies, and some agricultural societies.
pg081_n0022_easy_read: The age-set system had no central authority.
pg081_n0023_easy_read: Instead, a council of elders led the group and made decisions.
pg081_n0024_easy_read: In this system, children of the same age went through initiation together and learned the values of their community.
pg081_n0025_easy_read: They learned about: culture, history, and social responsibilities.
pg081_n0026_easy_read: After initiation, they received a group name.
pg081_n0027_easy_read: After that, they carried out special duties and responsibilities together as an age-set unit.
pg081_n0029_easy_read: Each age-set had members from one particular generation.
pg081_n0030_easy_read: Age groups were decided by: initiation, rituals, and cultural ceremonies.
pg081_n0031_easy_read: A person's rank in each age group depended on: age, wisdom, and good character.
pg081_n0032_easy_read: The leaders in each age group were older than the others, worked harder, and were more reliable.
pg081_n0033_easy_read: Obedience was an important part of life in an age group.
pg081_n0034_easy_read: The members of an age group made decisions about the day-to-day matters in their lives.
pg081_n0038_easy_read: Pastoral communities lived in places with little rain and short grass.
pg081_n0039_easy_read: These places were mainly arid and semi-arid.
pg081_n0040_easy_read: This environment allowed them to practice pastoralism as their main economic activity.
pg081_n0041_easy_read: They moved from one place to another with their herds of cattle to find good pasture and water.
pg081_n0042_easy_read: They lived in small and simple communities, not large ones.
pg082_n0003_easy_read: Pastoralists used streams and rain to get drinking water for people and livestock.
pg082_n0004_easy_read: They also depended on the plants around them for pasture.
pg082_n0005_easy_read: Pastoralists also needed safe places for people and livestock.
pg082_n0006_easy_read: Examples of pastoralists in pre-colonial Africa were: the Berbers and Tuaregs of North Africa; the Fulani and Hausa of West Africa; the Somali of North-Eastern Africa; the Karamojong of Uganda; the Maasai of Tanzania and Kenya; and the Khoikhoi of Southern Africa.
pg082_n0010_easy_read: People in pastoral societies had different responsibilities in the family and in the community.
pg082_n0011_easy_read: However, most responsibilities were given by age group and gender.
pg082_n0012_easy_read: So, men, women, children, youth, and elders had different responsibilities.
pg082_n0016_easy_read: Women and children: Women stayed at home and worked there.
pg082_n0017_easy_read: Women did these duties: cooked food, milked cows, grazed calves, and cared for the children.
pg082_n0018_easy_read: Children helped women with these duties.
pg082_n0020_easy_read: Youth: The responsibilities of youth were divided by age group.
pg082_n0021_easy_read: Youth aged nine to eighteen grazed livestock in the afternoon. When they returned home, they also helped their mothers with household duties.
pg082_n0022_easy_read: Youth aged about fifteen to twenty-five were the middle-age youth. Among the Maasai, they were called the Moran.
pg082_n0023_easy_read: The Moran had six responsibilities: defend the community from enemies; protect livestock from thieves and wild animals; raid herds of neighboring communities to get more livestock; drive cattle to new grazing land; collect tribute from traders who passed through Maasai territory; and survey neighboring areas for pasture and sources of water.
pg082_n0025_easy_read: Elders: This age group included the elderly men in the society.
pg082_n0026_easy_read: This group included elders aged forty and above.
pg082_n0027_easy_read: They were the oldest age group, so other members of the society respected them.
pg082_n0028_easy_read: The elders also owned cattle in their households.
pg082_n0029_easy_read: The most senior member of the elder group was called laibon.
pg082_n0030_easy_read: He had special respect as the highest cultural, political, and religious authority in the community.
pg082_n0031_easy_read: The laibon also led major cultural and religious ceremonies.
pg082_n0032_easy_read: People saw him as the link between his people and the gods.
pg082_n0033_easy_read: The head of a council of laibons among the Maasai was called Laigwanan.
pg082_n0034_easy_read: He was chosen from the laibons who represented different Maasai communities.
pg083_n0005_easy_read: The Maasai were one of the societies that used age-set organization.
pg083_n0006_easy_read: Draw a tree diagram. Show the different age groups and their roles.
pg083_n0010_easy_read: The Nyakyusa were one of the farming communities that used the age-set system.
pg083_n0011_easy_read: The Nyakyusa population grew very fast. This led to many people living in small areas.
pg083_n0012_easy_read: They owned large areas of fertile land. They could use this land for farming.
pg083_n0013_easy_read: The Nyakyusa did not move from place to place.
pg083_n0014_easy_read: They settled in one area and did their economic activities there.
pg083_n0015_easy_read: They adopted the age-set system to stop too many people from living in small areas.
pg083_n0016_easy_read: In this system, young people in a certain age group were given a new piece of land. They lived there and started their own settlement.
pg083_n0017_easy_read: The leaders of the age groups were called amafumu. They led each age village.
pg083_n0018_easy_read: A ceremony called ubusoka marked when a new age group became adults.
pg083_n0020_easy_read: Another farming community that used age-set organization was the Rendile of northern Kenya.
pg083_n0021_easy_read: In the Rendile community, age-set organization grouped people of similar age into separate age-sets.
pg083_n0022_easy_read: Each age-set had its own responsibilities.
pg083_n0023_easy_read: Some of these responsibilities were managing and caring for community resources.
pg083_n0024_easy_read: In the Rendile community, age-set organization was important. It helped them continue their farming practices and build unity in the community.

Pre-colonial education was a life-long process.
It passed knowledge, skills, values, norms, and experiences from one generation to another in a society.
pg084_n0006_easy_read: Pre-colonial education happened through active participation and observation.
pg084_n0007_easy_read: Each clan had its own ways to pass knowledge, skills, values, cultural norms, and taboos to young people.
pg084_n0008_easy_read: Each adult helped pass on knowledge.
pg084_n0009_easy_read: The training of young people depended on the trainer's experience in a specific field.
pg084_n0010_easy_read:
For example, some women were taught midwifery.
Later, these women taught young girls how to help each other during pregnancy.
pg084_n0011_easy_read: The young girls were also taught how to become acceptable wives and mothers.
pg084_n0013_easy_read: In the same way, adults taught young men and women about the responsibilities of marriage and parenthood.
pg084_n0014_easy_read: For example, girls were taught many home and farming duties at an early age, including: cooking, cultivation, and attending children.
pg084_n0015_easy_read: Boys were taught to be responsible husbands and fathers.
pg084_n0016_easy_read: Boys also herded cows and looked after goats and other livestock.
pg084_n0017_easy_read: Children helped with small household tasks and did light duties for relatives.
pg084_n0019_easy_read: Younger generations were taught taboos to build proper morals and protect natural resources like water, forest, and land.
pg084_n0020_easy_read:
For example, in some societies, children were not allowed to go into the forest alone.
People said they might meet dangerous creatures that could harm them.
pg084_n0021_easy_read: Young people received knowledge, values, and wisdom from their parents and relatives, especially knowledge, values, and wisdom related to the prosperity of society.
pg084_n0025_easy_read:
Pre-colonial education aimed to give young members of society knowledge, skills, and values.
It did this through spoken teaching and direct involvement in activities like fishing, carpentry, and painting.
pg084_n0026_easy_read: In most cases, people learned by doing.
pg084_n0027_easy_read: It also taught social values, good morals, and norms to younger generations to prepare them for their future work.
pg084_n0028_easy_read: For example, young people were taught economic activities such as fishing, farming, and hunting.
pg084_n0029_easy_read: At the same time, young people learned the basic knowledge and skills for particular economic activities.
pg084_n0030_easy_read:
In that way, pre-colonial education helped learners feel that they belonged.
It also encouraged learners to take an active part in family responsibilities.
pg084_n0032_easy_read: Pre-colonial education was meant to develop children's character, physical strength, and intellectual abilities.
pg084_n0033_easy_read: Children were taught practical skills and self-dependence.
pg085_n0003_easy_read: This kind of education also aimed to promote peace and security in society.
pg085_n0004_easy_read: This education trained young people to defend their societies from enemies.
pg085_n0005_easy_read: For example, in Maasai society, the Morans were responsible for keeping peace.
pg085_n0006_easy_read: The Morans also learned how to defend their community, protect their livestock from thieves, protect their livestock from wild animals, and raid neighboring communities to increase their herds of cattle.
pg085_n0008_easy_read: It also aimed to prepare young people to take over leadership when the current leaders finished their time.
pg085_n0009_easy_read: This duty was important because knowledge of administration was central to social, political, and economic development.
pg085_n0010_easy_read: Young leaders who were well prepared could make society more stable across generations.
pg085_n0012_easy_read: In addition, pre-colonial education aimed to make young people patriotic.
pg085_n0013_easy_read: Elders had the duty to teach young people patriotism so they could be proud of their people, environment, and resources.
pg085_n0014_easy_read: In pre-colonial societies, there were different conflicts between states.
pg085_n0015_easy_read: Because of this, patriotism was very important among young people. It helped stop conspiracy against the welfare of their societies.
pg085_n0020_easy_read: For example, young people were taken to seas, oceans, rivers, and lakes. There, they learned how to fish.
pg085_n0021_easy_read: Agricultural communities did something similar. They taught young people how to farm.
pg085_n0022_easy_read: Also, people who were interested in iron smithery or industries learned in a practical way how to make iron or other industrial goods.
pg085_n0024_easy_read: Pre-colonial education was not the same everywhere.
pg085_n0025_easy_read: It was different from one society to another, depending on that society's economic, social, and environmental conditions.
pg085_n0026_easy_read: Each society had its own customs and traditions.
pg085_n0027_easy_read: For example, the customs and traditions of societies living in arid and semi-arid environments were different from those of societies living around rivers and lakes.
pg085_n0031_easy_read: You are one of the students chosen to take part in the debate on the motion "Pre-colonial education was better than formal education".
pg085_n0032_easy_read: Give clear arguments to support or oppose the motion.
pg086_n0003_easy_read: Pre-colonial education was useful and important for the societies where people practiced it.
pg086_n0004_easy_read: It had positive parts that helped shape the culture of societies at that time.
pg086_n0005_easy_read: The education did not favor one social class over another, so it was not discriminatory.
pg086_n0006_easy_read: All members of society received this education, no matter their wealth or status.
pg086_n0007_easy_read: The only difference was that sometimes boys learned military skills, but girls did not.
pg086_n0008_easy_read: This happened because of the way informal education was given.
pg086_n0009_easy_read: As a result, this education did not create social classes in society.
pg086_n0010_easy_read: Instead, it encouraged specialization. This showed in the work of diviners and healers.
pg086_n0012_easy_read: This type of education was not driven by money.
pg086_n0013_easy_read: During the pre-colonial era, every member of society saw themselves as having important responsibilities in society.
pg086_n0015_easy_read: To encourage instructors, the community gave them gifts. These gifts were domestic animals or crops, depending on what was available at the time.
pg086_n0017_easy_read: Pre-colonial education stressed good morals and good social behavior.
pg086_n0018_easy_read: The learners were taught to have good character.
pg086_n0019_easy_read: Elders made sure learners received good values and behavior, such as hard work. Elders strongly condemned bad behavior, such as theft or prostitution.
pg086_n0021_easy_read: Pre-colonial education had a few weaknesses.
pg086_n0022_easy_read: For example, the education included some customs and traditions that were unnecessary.
pg086_n0023_easy_read: In many cases, it weakened the rights of women.
pg086_n0024_easy_read: For example, a woman whose husband died was not allowed to inherit the wealth he left behind.
pg086_n0025_easy_read: In some societies, women were not allowed to eat some foods: eggs, milk, and some parts of animal flesh, such as the liver.
pg086_n0026_easy_read: In the same way, women were not allowed to learn iron-working in iron-working societies.

pg088_n0008_easy_read: The way states formed in pre-colonial Africa was different in different regions and at different times.
pg088_n0009_easy_read: Some regions became centralised states. Other regions stayed decentralised.
pg088_n0010_easy_read: This chapter continues the discussion about state organization from Chapter Six.
pg088_n0011_easy_read: In this chapter, you will learn about the centralised states in: western Africa, central Africa, southern Africa, and eastern Africa.
pg088_n0012_easy_read: The skills and knowledge from this chapter will help you value and keep good African historical ways of creating and maintaining good governing institutions.
pg088_n0020_easy_read: A state is a centralised political organization. It makes and enforces rules over resources and people in a territory.
pg088_n0021_easy_read: The main parts of a state are: people, territorial boundaries, sovereignty, which means freedom from foreign rule, and government.
pg088_n0022_easy_read: Centralised states in pre-colonial Africa developed slowly. Different factors influenced this development.
pg088_n0023_easy_read: In African history, political centralisation started with Ancient Egypt around the third millennium B C E.
pg088_n0024_easy_read: However, this process became more common and more regular from about the fifth century. It continued through the nineteenth century.
pg088_n0025_easy_read: Pre-colonial African states in eastern, western, central, and southern Africa had different characteristics and different ways of organizing themselves.
pg088_n0029_easy_read: Several centralised states developed in East Africa.
pg088_n0030_easy_read: The centralised states included: Buganda, Bunyoro, Karagwe, and Ruanda-Urundi.
pg088_n0031_easy_read: Other states were semi-centralised, for example: Nyamwezi, Chagga, Hehe, Sangu, Sukuma, Pare, Shambaa, and Kamba.
pg088_n0032_easy_read: Figure seven point one shows some centralised and semi-centralised states in East Africa.
pg088_n0033_easy_read: Among these states, Buganda and Bunyoro are used as case studies.
