pg090_n0005_easy_read: The Bunyoro Kingdom goes back to the kingdom of Bunyoro-Kitara. The Bachwezi people founded Bunyoro-Kitara in the thirteenth century.
pg090_n0006_easy_read: By the sixteenth century, Bunyoro-Kitara had started to decline. It led to new and smaller kingdoms.
pg090_n0007_easy_read: Bunyoro was one of the new kingdoms that emerged.
pg090_n0008_easy_read: The title of the king of Bunyoro was Omukama.
pg090_n0012_easy_read: There were clear reasons for the rise of the Bunyoro Kingdom.
pg090_n0015_easy_read: Influence of traditions: Traditions had a strong influence on the choice of the Omukama.
pg090_n0016_easy_read: The Omukama was chosen from the chiefs of the ruling family, or the royal dynasty of Babito.
pg090_n0017_easy_read: This practice helped reduce disputes about who would take power among the provincial chiefs called Saza.
pg090_n0019_easy_read: Role of strong kings: The Bunyoro Kingdom needed strong leadership to keep its position.
pg090_n0020_easy_read: Famous kings like Omukama Kabarega gave this leadership. They helped Bunyoro grow into a powerful kingdom in the nineteenth century.
pg090_n0021_easy_read: Kabalega Kamurasi created Bunyoro's standing army. It had about twenty thousand soldiers.
pg090_n0023_easy_read: He divided his army into ten divisions. Each division had a commander.
pg090_n0024_easy_read: The army divisions were then sent to the provinces. They defended the empire from outside attacks.
pg090_n0025_easy_read: They also stopped internal revolts against the central government.
pg090_n0026_easy_read: The army kept law and order. It was also used to raid neighboring states during wars of conquest and expansion: Toro, Ankole, and Busoga.
pg090_n0028_easy_read: Influence of geographical conditions: Bunyoro was one of the most fertile areas in the Great Lakes region.
pg090_n0029_easy_read: The climate was good. It helped the people of Bunyoro grow different crops and raise livestock.
pg090_n0030_easy_read: The people produced enough food. This food supported their society, including rulers and soldiers.
pg090_n0032_easy_read: Strong and efficient political system: The kingdom was divided into provinces.
pg090_n0033_easy_read: Provincial chiefs called Saza ruled these provinces. The Omukama appointed them.
pg090_n0034_easy_read: The Saza controlled land for the Omukama.
pg090_n0035_easy_read: These chiefs were loyal to the king.
pg090_n0036_easy_read: In their provinces, the chiefs gave land to peasants and cattle herders. In return, they received loyalty, services, and tributes.
pg090_n0037_easy_read: They helped promote peace and unity among the people of Bunyoro.
pg090_n0041_easy_read: The Bunyoro Kingdom declined in the sixteenth century for several reasons, including the following:
pg091_n0003_easy_read: Expansion in the size of the kingdom: The kingdom became larger. This made it hard for the king to control it well.
pg091_n0004_easy_read: Sometimes, provincial chiefs, especially chiefs near the borders, rebelled against the central government and broke away.
pg091_n0005_easy_read: Examples of provinces that broke away were: Buddu, Toro, Busoga, and Koki.
pg091_n0006_easy_read: This caused Bunyoro to decline because it lost important provinces that produced grain and iron tools.
pg091_n0008_easy_read: Disputes in the ruling family: Members of the ruling family sometimes argued about who should become king.
pg091_n0009_easy_read: A good example of disputes and conflicts about who should become king happened during the rule of Omukama Kyebambe Nyamutukura the third.
pg091_n0010_easy_read: One of his sons, Kaboyo Omuhanwa, rebelled against his father and started the Toro kingdom.
pg091_n0012_easy_read: Limited control over regional chiefs: Provincial chiefs had some independence from Omukama.
pg091_n0013_easy_read: For example, the provincial chiefs could raise their own armies.
pg091_n0014_easy_read: This was dangerous to the unity of the kingdom because some leaders built their own armies and rebelled against the central government.
pg091_n0018_easy_read: The Buganda Kingdom was in the southwest of modern Uganda.
pg091_n0019_easy_read: The Buganda Kingdom started as a small political unit in the sixteenth century. It began to expand in the seventeenth century.
pg091_n0020_easy_read: The Buganda Kingdom reached its highest level of prosperity in the middle of the nineteenth century.
pg091_n0021_easy_read: The Buganda Kingdom was one of the most centralized states in East Africa.
pg091_n0023_easy_read: Buganda came into existence after the Bunyoro-Kitara Kingdom collapsed.
pg091_n0024_easy_read: By the second half of the nineteenth century, Buganda became one of the strongest and largest kingdoms in the interlacustrine region.
pg091_n0025_easy_read: Buganda grew larger by conquering and controlling small neighboring kingdoms.
pg091_n0026_easy_read: The conquered territories were put under chiefs called Batongole.
pg091_n0027_easy_read: The Batongole were responsible to the Kabaka as the territorial leader.
pg091_n0031_easy_read: The Buganda Kingdom was one of the best political systems in the interlacustrine region.
pg091_n0032_easy_read: At the top of the leadership structure was the Kabaka.
pg091_n0033_easy_read: The Kabaka was the main political leader and the final decision maker.
pg091_n0034_easy_read: Below the Kabaka was an administrative structure with a number of chiefs.
pg091_n0035_easy_read: The chiefs helped the Kabaka spread his authority across the kingdom.
pg091_n0036_easy_read: The Kabaka governed his kingdom with the help of his advisory council, called the Lukiiko.
pg091_n0037_easy_read: The council was made up of: the prime minister, called Katikiro; the treasurer general, called Omuwanika; and the chief justice, called Mugema.
pg091_n0038_easy_read: The Kabaka appointed the members of the Lukiiko.
pg091_n0039_easy_read: The Lukiiko did not make laws, but it advised the Kabaka.
pg092_n0005_easy_read: Several factors led to the rise of the Buganda Kingdom.
pg092_n0008_easy_read: Development of agriculture: Buganda grew in an area with a good climate and fertile soil for farming.
pg092_n0009_easy_read: People grew banana as the main food crop.
pg092_n0010_easy_read: The kingdom produced extra food. This helped the population grow, and the growing population needed to be governed.
pg092_n0011_easy_read: There was also a clear division of labor among the Baganda.
pg092_n0012_easy_read: Women focused on food production. Men did other duties, including warfare, to expand the kingdom.
pg092_n0014_easy_read: Formation of a strong and stable army: At its peak, Buganda had one of the strongest armies in pre-colonial African societies.
pg092_n0015_easy_read: This helped the Baganda strengthen and expand their kingdom.
pg092_n0016_easy_read: The army also protected the wealth of the society and conquered neighboring societies.
pg092_n0018_easy_read: Clear system of leadership succession: Buganda had a centralized system of administration.
pg092_n0019_easy_read: Kabaka and his subordinate leaders used a hereditary system.
pg092_n0020_easy_read: In this system, leadership passed from father to son.
pg092_n0021_easy_read: This helped prevent and solve disputes over succession.
pg092_n0022_easy_read: The situation was different in the Bunyoro and Ankole states, where disputes over succession were common.
pg092_n0024_easy_read: Control of trade: Buganda took part in long-distance trade in East and Central Africa.
pg092_n0025_easy_read: This trade allowed Kabaka to collect tributes. These tributes were used to strengthen his kingdom.
pg092_n0026_easy_read: Trade also gave the kingdom weapons, especially guns.
pg092_n0028_easy_read: Strong link between the state and clans: Buganda's political system reduced conflict and kept peace in the state.
pg092_n0029_easy_read: Kabaka married wives from several clans.
pg092_n0030_easy_read: Marriage alliances with different clans helped Kabaka create unity and harmony within the kingdom.
pg092_n0032_easy_read: Religious beliefs and practices: Religious beliefs and practices helped the Buganda Kingdom grow and expand.
pg092_n0034_easy_read: As a clan head, Kabaka was a spiritual leader. He led religious functions, and people saw him as a semi-divine person.
pg092_n0035_easy_read: As a spiritual leader, Kabaka was surrounded by religious leaders from different clans.
pg092_n0036_easy_read: So, religion was one of the pillars that encouraged social and political unity and maintained power relations within the kingdom.
pg092_n0038_easy_read: Development of iron technology: People used iron to make weapons and tools. These helped Buganda conquer weaker states and carry out production activities.
pg092_n0039_easy_read: Both conquest and high production helped the kingdom expand.
pg093_n0005_easy_read: Many factors helped the Baganda Kingdom rise, but in the end it became weak.
pg093_n0006_easy_read: These were the factors that weakened the Buganda Kingdom.
pg093_n0008_easy_read: Establishment of colonialism: Colonial rule reduced the political power and authority of the Kabaka.
pg093_n0009_easy_read: The Buganda Agreement of nineteen hundred allowed the Governor to control Buganda.
pg093_n0010_easy_read: Under this agreement, Kabaka Mwanga unwillingly accepted British control and became part of the British protectorate.
pg093_n0011_easy_read: As part of the British protectorate, the Kingdom was no longer free.
pg093_n0012_easy_read: This greatly reduced the power of the Kabaka and weakened the Kingdom.
pg093_n0014_easy_read: Religious differences and conflicts: There were three religious groups in conflict: Christianity, Islam, and the indigenous religion.
pg093_n0015_easy_read: These conflicts happened in the second half of the nineteenth century.
pg093_n0016_easy_read: These religious groups divided the Buganda Kingdom through different religious beliefs.
pg093_n0017_easy_read: Buganda slowly lost its internal unity and stability as a socio-political group, and this weakened it.
pg093_n0019_easy_read: Introduction of colonial economy: British colonial officials introduced a peasant economy. This changed the production system in Buganda and caused the kingdom to break apart.
pg093_n0020_easy_read: People started to grow cash crops. This reduced the production of food crops.
pg093_n0021_easy_read: As a result, the available food was not enough to feed the whole population in the kingdom.
pg093_n0023_easy_read: Conflicting administrative interests: Many Batongole ruled Buganda. Some provincial chiefs tried to gain complete power and authority over their subjects.
pg093_n0024_easy_read: These efforts caused administrative misunderstandings and conflicts between the Batongole and the Kabaka.
pg093_n0025_easy_read: This situation caused administrative problems across the whole kingdom and finally weakened it.
pg093_n0028_easy_read: Compare the administrative systems of the Buganda and Bunyoro Kingdoms and their influence on the rise of state formation.
pg093_n0032_easy_read: The earliest centralised states in the western Sudanic zone were: Ghana, Mali, and Songhay. Figure seven point two.
pg094_n0003_easy_read: Figure seven point two: Western Sudanic states.
pg094_n0007_easy_read: The Ghana Empire was in the southern border area of modern-day Mauritania and Mali. It was between the bend of the Niger River and the Senegal River.
pg094_n0008_easy_read: This empire grew in the fifth century. It formed after war joined several small states together.
pg094_n0009_easy_read: The Soninke people founded the empire.
pg094_n0010_easy_read: The capital of the Ghana Empire was Kumbi Saleh. The king's title was Tunka or Ghana.
pg094_n0011_easy_read: The towns near the Ghana Empire were: Walata, Awdaghust, also known as Audoghast, Timbuktu, Tichitt, and Jenne.
pg094_n0015_easy_read: The factors that helped the Ghana Empire rise were very similar to the factors in Buganda, in East Africa.
pg094_n0016_easy_read: The following factors led to the rise of the Ghana Empire.
pg094_n0018_easy_read: Good geographical position: Ghana was where many Trans-Saharan trade routes met.
pg094_n0019_easy_read: The Ghana Empire played a middle role in this trade.
pg095_n0003_easy_read: Trade routes from the southern, northern, and eastern regions passed through Ghana.
pg095_n0004_easy_read: Ghana’s location also supported farming. This gave people enough food.
pg095_n0006_easy_read: Availability of gold: Ghana produced a lot of gold. Gold was the main trade item and a form of money.
pg095_n0007_easy_read: Gold trade made the empire politically strong and economically rich.
pg095_n0009_easy_read: Efficient administrative system: The Ghana Empire was divided into provinces.
pg095_n0010_easy_read: The king appointed provincial chiefs in each province.
pg095_n0011_easy_read: Those chiefs supported the king in their own areas.
pg095_n0012_easy_read: In this way, the king controlled the whole kingdom.
pg095_n0014_easy_read: Military strength: The king of Ghana created a strong standing army of about two hundred thousand soldiers.
pg095_n0015_easy_read: The army fought weaker chiefdoms and defended the kingdom from outside attacks.
pg095_n0017_easy_read: Development of iron technology: Iron technology produced farming tools.
pg095_n0018_easy_read: These tools helped farming. They increased food production and improved food security.
pg095_n0019_easy_read: Food security led to population growth. This made the empire stronger.
pg095_n0020_easy_read: Weapons made of iron also increased military power. State security also helped the territory expand.
pg095_n0024_easy_read: The Ghana Empire declined and finally collapsed in the eleventh century for these reasons:
pg095_n0026_easy_read: Attacks by Almoravids: The Almoravids from North Africa attacked Ghana many times from ten seventy-six to ten seventy-seven.
pg095_n0027_easy_read: The attacks aimed to take back Awdaghust. Awdaghust was a major source of salt and gold.
pg095_n0028_easy_read: These attacks weakened the empire and caused its decline.
pg095_n0030_easy_read: Dissatisfaction of traders: Gold traders in Ghana complained about the king’s control of the gold trade and the heavy taxes. This made trade unprofitable.
pg095_n0031_easy_read: So, many traders moved their activities to other growing states, such as Mali.
pg095_n0032_easy_read: This weakened the empire and contributed to its decline.
pg095_n0034_easy_read: Dissatisfaction of vassal states: Some vassal states refused to pay tribute. Other vassal states declared themselves independent from the kingdom.
pg095_n0035_easy_read: This weakened the empire and contributed to its decline.
pg095_n0037_easy_read: Vastness of the empire: The Ghana Empire was too large to control.
pg095_n0041_easy_read: The Mali Empire rose after the Ghana Empire declined.
pg095_n0042_easy_read: The Mali Empire began as a small Mandinka kingdom at the upper bend of the Niger River.
pg095_n0043_easy_read: Between the eleventh century and twelfth century, Sundiata Keita and some rulers of Mali brought a number of
pg096_n0003_easy_read: Malinke chiefdoms were under their control.
pg096_n0004_easy_read: In the thirteenth century, Sundiata led a Malinke army against Sumanguru of Sosso. He defeated him in the Battle of Kirina, near the modern city of Bamako.
pg096_n0005_easy_read: After Sumanguru's defeat, Sundiata took control of all the Soninke people.
pg096_n0006_easy_read: Sundiata built a large Mali Empire. Its capital was at Niami.
pg096_n0007_easy_read: The kings of Mali used the title Mansa.
pg096_n0008_easy_read: The most famous ruler of the empire was Mansa Kankan Musa.
pg096_n0012_easy_read: These factors led to the rise of the Mali Empire:
pg096_n0014_easy_read: Strong standing army: Mansa Musa kept a large standing army with a battalion of commanders.
pg096_n0015_easy_read: The army protected the empire from outside attacks.
pg096_n0016_easy_read: The army also patrolled trade routes. It also made sure district chiefs paid tribute to the king.
pg096_n0018_easy_read: Role of Islam: Mansa Musa used Islam as the state religion.
pg096_n0019_easy_read: He used Islam to unite the people and to gain their respect.
pg096_n0020_easy_read: Islamic laws, Sharia, were used to control people's behavior and attitudes.
pg096_n0021_easy_read: This brought discipline and unity to the people.
pg096_n0023_easy_read: Development of agriculture: Mali had rich farmland.
pg096_n0024_easy_read: The fertile land helped people grow many kinds of grains and other crops.
pg096_n0025_easy_read: They also kept livestock such as cattle, goats, and sheep.
pg096_n0026_easy_read: Farming and cattle keeping made sure there was enough food.
pg096_n0027_easy_read: This led to an increase in population.
pg096_n0029_easy_read: Control of gold mines and trade routes: The empire controlled gold mines at Bambuk, Bundu, and Wangara.
pg096_n0030_easy_read: The empire also controlled gold trade routes that passed through its territory.
pg096_n0031_easy_read: Because of this trade, these places became major trade centers in the empire: Niami, Jenne, Timbuktu, and Gao.
pg096_n0032_easy_read: Gold trade linked the empire with Morocco, Tripoli, and Egypt.
pg096_n0033_easy_read: Trade also attracted traders from Europe and the Middle East.
pg096_n0034_easy_read: This development strongly helped the rise of Mali.
pg096_n0036_easy_read: Strong leadership: Sundiata Keita and Mansa Musa were good leaders.
pg096_n0037_easy_read: They divided the empire into provinces. They appointed leaders to be in charge of each province.
pg096_n0038_easy_read: They did not want to have total power.
pg096_n0039_easy_read: They left the administration of the region to loyal chiefs they valued.
pg096_n0040_easy_read: This style of leadership promoted loyalty and understanding between the king and his vassals.
pg096_n0044_easy_read: The Mali Empire started to decline in the second half of the 14th century.
pg096_n0045_easy_read: Several factors led to the decline of the empire.
pg096_n0047_easy_read: Internal struggles for succession: The empire faced many conflicts and struggles over succession.
pg096_n0048_easy_read: These struggles created divisions and separation, and they weakened the state.
pg097_n0003_easy_read: Attacks from trade rivals: The Mosi Kingdom in the south and the Tuaregs in the north attacked the Mali Empire. They wanted to control the Trans-Saharan Trade routes and trade goods such as gold, slaves, and salt.
pg097_n0004_easy_read: These attacks made the empire weaker and led to its collapse.
pg097_n0006_easy_read: The rise of the Songhay Empire: Sunni Ali created the Songhay Empire.
pg097_n0007_easy_read: Sunni Ali's soldiers attacked and destroyed Jenne. They also took its wealth.
pg097_n0008_easy_read: This made the Mali Empire weaker because Jenne was the backbone of its economy.
pg097_n0009_easy_read: The attack and looting helped cause the decline of the Mali Empire.
pg097_n0013_easy_read: The Songhay Empire was the largest empire among the western Sudanic states.
pg097_n0014_easy_read: Gao was the capital city of the empire.
pg097_n0015_easy_read: Gao was also one of the great centers of trade during the Trans-Saharan Trade.
pg097_n0017_easy_read: Under Sunni Ali's leadership, Gao conquered nearby kingdoms.
pg097_n0018_easy_read: By the 15th century, Gao had become the center of a large empire called Songhay.
pg097_n0019_easy_read: Another important leader of the Songhay Empire, besides Sunni Ali, was Askia Mohamed.
pg097_n0023_easy_read: The factors that led to the rise of the Songhay Empire were not very different from those of the Mali Empire.
pg097_n0024_easy_read: The differences were in the context.
pg097_n0025_easy_read: The following factors led to the rise of the Songhay Empire.
pg097_n0027_easy_read: Control of trade routes: Some important Trans-Saharan Trade routes passed through Gao.
pg097_n0028_easy_read: Gao used this chance to tax traders who passed through the area.
pg097_n0029_easy_read: The empire used the money from taxes to build and support a large permanent army.
pg097_n0031_easy_read: Strong leadership of Sunni Ali and Askia Mohamed: Sunni Ali and Askia Mohamed helped the empire expand successfully.
pg097_n0032_easy_read: By the late 15th century, the empire had expanded across the whole area between Kebbi in the east and Jenne in the west.
pg097_n0033_easy_read: In the north, the empire had reached Timbuktu. In the south, it had reached Hombori.
pg097_n0035_easy_read: The role of Islam: Another important factor was making Islam the state religion.
pg097_n0036_easy_read: Rulers used Islam to unite the people and to justify wars of conquest, called Jihads.
pg097_n0037_easy_read: They also used Islam to justify making non-Islamic believers into slaves.
pg097_n0039_easy_read: Strength of the army: Sunni Ali had a strong army. It helped him protect and expand the empire.
pg097_n0040_easy_read: His army included well-armed horse-riding forces. They were used to conquer and defend the kingdom.
pg098_n0003_easy_read: Development of agriculture and industry: More farm production gave enough food to civilians and soldiers.
pg098_n0004_easy_read: Industries made tools. These tools helped increase the production of different goods and weapons.
pg098_n0005_easy_read: All these activities were very important for the growth of the empire.
pg098_n0009_easy_read: The Songhay Empire reached the height of its power in the early sixteenth century.
pg098_n0010_easy_read: After that, the Songhay Empire started to decline.
pg098_n0011_easy_read: These were the reasons for the decline of the Songhay Empire:
pg098_n0013_easy_read: Succession disputes after the death of Askia Mohamed: The death of Askia Mohamed caused misunderstandings in the ruling family.
pg098_n0014_easy_read: After Askia Mohamed died, a time of weak and unskilled leadership followed.
pg098_n0015_easy_read: This caused frequent unrest. This unrest weakened the stability of the Songhay Empire.
pg098_n0017_easy_read: Resistance to heavy tributes: Peasants and artisans resisted the heavy tributes demanded by the king.
pg098_n0018_easy_read: The peasants and artisans disobeyed the king. They refused to carry out his decisions.
pg098_n0021_easy_read: Change of trade routes: During the sixteenth century, trade routes changed direction toward the Atlantic coast, where European merchants had settled.
pg098_n0022_easy_read: This change caused Trans-Saharan Trade to decline. Trans-Saharan Trade was the backbone of the Songhay Empire.
pg098_n0024_easy_read: Moroccan invasion in the sixteenth century: The Sultan of Morocco wanted to control the West African gold trade by himself.
pg098_n0025_easy_read: His army attacked and conquered the Songhay Empire.
pg098_n0026_easy_read: This invasion weakened the Songhay Empire and led to its collapse.
pg098_n0030_easy_read: How did trade and commerce help state formation in the Western Sudanic States?
pg098_n0034_easy_read: In pre-colonial Africa, several states also developed in the Forest Zone of West Africa.
pg098_n0035_easy_read: The most important forest states were: Asante, Oyo, Benin, and Ife.
pg098_n0036_easy_read: Most of these states were founded by the Yoruba people.
pg098_n0037_easy_read: State formation among the Yoruba began in the eleventh century.
pg098_n0038_easy_read: Figure seven point three shows the Forest States.
pg099_n0003_easy_read: Figure seven point three: Forest States.
pg099_n0007_easy_read: The Oyoko people, one of the Akan clans, founded the Asante Kingdom in the seventeenth century.
pg099_n0008_easy_read: First, the Oyoko founded five small chiefdoms. Later, the five chiefdoms joined together to form the powerful Asante Kingdom.
pg099_n0009_easy_read: The chiefdoms were: Kumasi, Nsuta, Kokofu, Bwekai, and Dwaben.
pg099_n0010_easy_read: By sixteen seventy, Kumasi was the greatest and most powerful kingdom.
pg099_n0011_easy_read: Obiri Yeboa was the first ruler of the Asante Kingdom.
pg099_n0012_easy_read: Obiri Yeboa made Kumasi the center that united the Asante Kingdom.
pg099_n0013_easy_read: Obiri Yeboa also made Kumasi the capital of the kingdom.
pg099_n0014_easy_read: The title of the king of the Asante Kingdom was Asantehene.
pg099_n0018_easy_read: The reasons why the Forest Zone states rose were the same as in other areas.
pg099_n0019_easy_read: The reasons for the rise of the Asante Kingdom were:
pg099_n0021_easy_read: Soil fertility: The Asante Kingdom developed in an area with fertile soil.
pg099_n0022_easy_read: Fertile soil supported agriculture. Agriculture was the main economic activity in the kingdom.
pg099_n0023_easy_read: The development of agriculture made sure there was enough food for the people, rulers, and soldiers.
pg099_n0024_easy_read: The Asante people grew crops such as grains and palm.
pg100_n0003_easy_read: Military strength: The kingdom built a strong military force. It had a well-trained army with modern weapons, such as guns.
pg100_n0004_easy_read: The kingdom got these weapons from the Trans-Saharan Trade and the Atlantic Slave Trade.
pg100_n0005_easy_read: The army fought wars to conquer other places. This made the kingdom larger.
pg100_n0006_easy_read: The army also kept peace and security in the kingdom.
pg100_n0008_easy_read: Long-distance trade: The kingdom took part in long-distance trade in West Africa. It also set up trading centers along the Atlantic coast.
pg100_n0009_easy_read: Trade was mainly based on exporting slaves and gold from the forest region.
pg100_n0010_easy_read: The kingdom imported: beads, clothes, and firearms.
pg100_n0011_easy_read: The kingdom used these firearms for security and war.
pg100_n0012_easy_read: In some cases, war produced slaves. Slaves were important goods for trade.
pg100_n0013_easy_read: The kingdom used the wealth from this trade to make the kingdom stronger.
pg100_n0015_easy_read: Strong leadership: The Asante Kingdom grew because of the strong leadership of Asantehene Obiri Yeboa, Osei Tutu, and Opokwu Ware.
pg100_n0016_easy_read: Yeboa brought together the rulers of these states into one Oyoko clan: Nsuta, Kokofu, Bwekai, and Dwaben.
pg100_n0017_easy_read: This brought unity among the people of the kingdom.
pg100_n0018_easy_read: Obiri Yeboa used this unity to conquer the nearby states.
pg100_n0019_easy_read: Those states accepted Yeboa as the Asantehene of Asante.
pg100_n0020_easy_read: Obiri Yeboa died in the late sixteen seventies, but he had already built the foundation of the Asante Kingdom.
pg100_n0022_easy_read: Osei Tutu became very important in the growth of the kingdom.
pg100_n0023_easy_read: Osei Tutu was a charming, strong, and brave leader.
pg100_n0024_easy_read: He expanded the kingdom and built a highly centralized kingdom.
pg100_n0025_easy_read: He used the Golden Stool as a symbol of unity. All the Asante people respected it.
pg100_n0026_easy_read: He introduced a royal family line. Asante rulers had to come from the descendants of Obiri Yeboa and Osei Tutu.
pg100_n0027_easy_read: He also made Kumasi the capital of the empire.
pg100_n0028_easy_read: He introduced a traditional yearly religious festival called Odwira.
pg100_n0029_easy_read: He also required every adult in the empire to pay tribute.
pg100_n0030_easy_read: All these actions helped strengthen political unity and the economy of the empire.
pg100_n0032_easy_read: Military conquest of neighboring states: Osei Tutu and his successors successfully conquered neighboring states.
pg100_n0033_easy_read: Osei Tutu created a federation. It conquered Denkyira and other Akan states.
pg100_n0034_easy_read: By the eighteenth century, Osei Tutu controlled most of the goldfields in the Forest zone.
pg100_n0035_easy_read: His successors, Opukwu Ware and others, expanded the borders of Asante from the coast to the Savannah in the North.
pg100_n0037_easy_read: Traditional belief: At the start of Osei Tutu’s rule, Okomfo Anokye, a traditional priest, made Osei Tutu the occupant of the Golden Stool.
pg100_n0038_easy_read: This action strengthened the Asante Kingdom in different ways.
pg100_n0039_easy_read: Osei Tutu then became both a religious leader and a political leader.
pg100_n0040_easy_read: He became a link between the people and the gods.
pg100_n0041_easy_read: The Golden Stool replaced all earlier symbols of authority.
pg100_n0042_easy_read: The Golden Stool became the symbol of unity and the soul of the people of Asante.
pg101_n0005_easy_read: By the first half of the nineteenth century, the Asante Kingdom had started to decline.
pg101_n0006_easy_read: This happened for several reasons, including these:
pg101_n0008_easy_read: British imperial activities: The British often attacked the Asante Kingdom between eighteen seventy-one and nineteen oh-one.
pg101_n0009_easy_read: This harmed peace and security in the Asante Kingdom. It also harmed trade in the region.
pg101_n0010_easy_read: The imperial activities reduced the prosperity of the Asante Kingdom.
pg101_n0011_easy_read: As a result, the Asante Kingdom declined.
pg101_n0013_easy_read: Abolition of the slave trade: From about the middle of the nineteenth century, the British led a campaign to end the slave trade.
pg101_n0014_easy_read: This campaign ended the slave trade in West Africa. This ruined most forest states, including the Asante Kingdom.
pg101_n0015_easy_read: This happened because the power of these states depended on the slave trade.
pg101_n0016_easy_read: When the slave trade ended, the Asante Kingdom lost important sources of revenue. As a result, it declined.
pg101_n0018_easy_read: Vastness of the kingdom: In the first half of the nineteenth century, the Asante Kingdom became larger.
pg101_n0019_easy_read: This growth partly caused the decline of the Asante Kingdom.
pg101_n0020_easy_read: The conquered territories gradually rebelled against the central government in Kumasi. Then they became self-governing states. These territories were: Gonja, Kong, Bonchiku, Baule, and Anyi.
pg101_n0024_easy_read: Investigate the role of important leaders in the formation of states in the Forest States of West Africa.
pg101_n0028_easy_read: Ife was a Yoruba state. It was formed around the fourteenth century.
pg101_n0029_easy_read: Oduduwa founded Ife. His origin is explained by two myths.
pg101_n0030_easy_read: The first myth is the creation myth.
pg101_n0031_easy_read: According to this myth, Oduduwa was brought to earth from heaven by his father, Olorun. The Yoruba regarded Olorun as their supreme god.
pg101_n0032_easy_read: The second myth says that Oduduwa came to Ife from the eastern part of the region.
pg101_n0036_easy_read: These factors influenced the rise of the Ife Kingdom: good climatic conditions, revenues, and good leadership.
pg101_n0038_easy_read: Good climatic conditions: The Ife Kingdom was in an area with good climatic conditions.
pg101_n0039_easy_read: This helped the people produce surplus food.
pg101_n0040_easy_read: Because of this, the kingdom could support rulers and officials who were not directly involved in production.
pg102_n0003_easy_read: Collection of revenues: The rulers of Ife collected taxes from traders and tributes from peasants.
pg102_n0004_easy_read: The people of Ife had trade links with the people of the Sahel. The Sahel people were known for mining copper and salt.
pg102_n0005_easy_read: The Kingdom collected taxes from traders in copper and salt from the Sahel.
pg102_n0006_easy_read: In addition, the Kingdom collected tributes from its peasants. The peasants exchanged food and kola nuts for copper and salt from the Sahel region.
pg102_n0008_easy_read: Good leadership: Oduduwa's good leadership was another important reason for the rise and growth of this state.
pg102_n0009_easy_read: Oduduwa united his people and built a strong, well-organized state.
pg102_n0010_easy_read: In addition, Oduduwa's subjects respected him greatly. This was partly because they believed he was the son of Olorun.
pg102_n0014_easy_read: The Ife Kingdom became weaker because the Oyo Kingdom grew stronger in Yorubaland.
pg102_n0015_easy_read: The Oyo Kingdom invaded Ibadan. Ibadan was an important town in Yorubaland, and Ife controlled it at that time.
pg102_n0016_easy_read: After the invasion, Ife lost control of Ibadan and became weak.
pg102_n0017_easy_read: Later, Oyo invaded Ife and settled in Ife territory.
pg102_n0018_easy_read: This marked the complete collapse of Ife.
pg102_n0022_easy_read: Benin was in the southern part of Ife, near the Niger Delta.
pg102_n0023_easy_read: Benin was deep in the forest.
pg102_n0024_easy_read: The Kingdom was in the area that is now southwestern Nigeria.
pg102_n0025_easy_read: So, the present-day country of Benin is not connected to the ancient Benin Kingdom.
pg102_n0026_easy_read: Edo-speaking people developed this state in the thirteenth century.
pg102_n0027_easy_read: The title of the King of Benin was Oba.
pg102_n0028_easy_read: The kings of Benin, called oba, claimed that they descended from Oduduwa, the founding ancestor of the Yoruba.
pg102_n0029_easy_read: The first Oba of Benin was Oranmiyan, the son of Oduduwa. People say that the early inhabitants brought him to Benin to solve conflicts among the chiefs.
pg102_n0030_easy_read: By the fifteenth century, Benin had grown into a huge centralized state with a wall around it.
pg102_n0031_easy_read: When Europeans came to Benin, they called it the Great City of Benin because of its size and its decorative buildings.
pg102_n0035_easy_read: The factors that helped the Benin Kingdom rise were similar to those of other states.
pg102_n0036_easy_read: The only difference was the context.
pg102_n0037_easy_read: The following were the factors for the rise of the Benin Kingdom:
pg102_n0039_easy_read: Strong leadership: The Kingdom had strong leaders such as Ewuare, also called Ewuare the Great.
pg102_n0040_easy_read: He changed Benin from a city-state into a kingdom.
pg102_n0041_easy_read: Under his leadership, the kingdom became well organized and stronger.
pg102_n0042_easy_read: Oba Ewuare appointed royal district chiefs. These chiefs helped keep the empire stable.
pg102_n0043_easy_read: He created a good oba succession system. In this system, his oldest son was officially recognized as the next ruler of the kingdom.
pg103_n0003_easy_read: Strong army: The leaders of Benin built a strong army in the middle of the fifteenth century.
pg103_n0004_easy_read: The army protected the state from outside threats.
pg103_n0005_easy_read: The army kept peace, security, and stability in the state.
pg103_n0006_easy_read: The army also helped the territory grow by conquering weaker neighboring states.
pg103_n0008_easy_read: Involvement in trade: The oba of Benin and some people in the empire traded with the Portuguese.
pg103_n0009_easy_read: They took trade goods from Benin to the coast, such as: ivory, gums, pepper, and cotton cloth.
pg103_n0010_easy_read: They sold those goods to Portuguese traders.
pg103_n0011_easy_read: Also, Benin artists made items that Europeans bought, such as: saltcellars, ivory carvings, and bangles.
pg103_n0015_easy_read: The empire declined in the eighteenth century for several reasons.
pg103_n0018_easy_read: Civil wars and dynastic disputes: Later, the kingdom of Benin faced civil wars and dynastic disputes.
pg103_n0019_easy_read: These disputes were sometimes caused by conflicts over who would succeed to power.
pg103_n0020_easy_read: The disputes finally led to wars. These wars weakened the state.
pg103_n0021_easy_read: So, internal disputes were an important reason for the decline of the Benin Kingdom.
pg103_n0023_easy_read: Slave trade: The obas sold their people and war captives to the Portuguese as slaves.
pg103_n0024_easy_read: The slave trade was one source of Benin's wealth. But it also harmed the empire's production capacity.
pg103_n0025_easy_read: This happened because the slave trade took productive people away from their areas.
pg103_n0026_easy_read: This caused a shortage of labor.
pg103_n0027_easy_read: In the end, this led to the decline of the state.
pg103_n0029_easy_read: British invasion: In eighteen ninety-seven, British troops invaded Benin and took sculptures made of: brass, bronze, and copper. These sculptures were symbols of power in the kingdom.
pg103_n0030_easy_read: The invasion also led to the signing of several treaties with the people of the Niger Delta.
pg103_n0031_easy_read: These treaties declared the whole Niger Delta region a British protectorate.
pg103_n0032_easy_read: With this declaration, Benin lost its independence and autonomy.
pg103_n0033_easy_read: This marked the decline of Benin.
pg103_n0037_easy_read: The Oyo Kingdom was established in the fourteenth century.
pg103_n0038_easy_read: Like other Forest states, the Oyo Kingdom came from the Ife Kingdom.
pg103_n0039_easy_read: People believe the founders of the Oyo Kingdom were descendants of Oduduwa, the founder of the Yoruba states.
pg103_n0040_easy_read: Other Forest states in Yorubaland were in the south. Oyo was north of the tropical forests, in the Savannah.
pg103_n0041_easy_read: Oyo occupied the southwestern corner of present-day Nigeria.
pg103_n0042_easy_read: The title of the ruler of the Oyo state was Alaafin.
pg104_n0005_easy_read: Several factors helped the Oyo Kingdom rise.
pg104_n0008_easy_read: Invasion by the Bariba and Nupe: The Oyo Kingdom rose because the Bariba and Nupe invaded the Ife Kingdom.
pg104_n0009_easy_read: This invasion made the people move from the Ife Kingdom to Oyo Ile, Old Oyo.
pg104_n0010_easy_read: In Oyo Ile, the people built outlying towns. These towns formed the new Oyo Kingdom.
pg104_n0012_easy_read: Military strength: The rulers of Oyo built a centralized state with a standing army.
pg104_n0013_easy_read: Also, the Kingdom was in an area without tsetse flies. This made it possible to use horses.
pg104_n0014_easy_read: During this time, horses helped make the army more effective because soldiers used them in war.
pg104_n0016_easy_read: Involvement in trade: The Kingdom took part in the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade and in other trade with neighboring areas.
pg104_n0017_easy_read: The Kingdom got access to this trade after it invaded the coastal kingdom of Allada.
pg104_n0018_easy_read: The Kingdom was one of the main protectors of trade between the coast and Hausa land. This helped the Kingdom a lot.
pg104_n0019_easy_read: Through this trade, Oyo rulers collected many tributes and taxes from: villages, towns, and transit traders.
pg104_n0020_easy_read: This money benefited the rulers and the state in general.
pg104_n0022_easy_read: Strong and organized leadership: The kingdom had strong leaders such as Alaafin Orompoto and Abiodun.
pg104_n0023_easy_read: These leaders organized the state well and stabilized its economy.
pg104_n0024_easy_read: The council of seven chiefs, called Oyo Mesi, chose these leaders. The leaders came from the lineage that traced its origin to Oduduwas or to Oduduwas’ son, Oronyan.
pg104_n0025_easy_read: The Basorun led the Oyo Mesi.
pg104_n0026_easy_read: The system of checks and balances also helped make sure there were good leaders.
pg104_n0027_easy_read: Oyo Mesi could also force the Alaafin to leave the throne and commit suicide if he did not perform well.
pg104_n0031_easy_read: The Oyo Kingdom collapsed in the nineteenth century.
pg104_n0032_easy_read: Some of the reasons for its decline were:
pg104_n0034_easy_read: Leadership problems: The decline of the Oyo Kingdom started when some leaders failed to rule the state well.
pg104_n0035_easy_read: Some of these leaders lacked wisdom and ruled against the established norms of the kingdom.
pg104_n0036_easy_read: One such leader was Aole, also called Awole. He took the throne in seventeen eighty-nine.
pg104_n0037_easy_read: Aole ordered an attack on Apomu, one of the towns of Ife. This went against the oath he had taken.
pg104_n0038_easy_read: Ife was seen as the ancestral home of the people of Oyo. So this action caused embarrassment and chaos in the kingdom.
pg104_n0039_easy_read: After this incident, the king was forced to commit suicide.
pg105_n0003_easy_read: The people who followed Aole brought more problems. These problems caused some chiefdoms to break away.
pg105_n0004_easy_read: Egba was one of the chiefdoms that broke away. It became independent in seventeen ninety-seven.
pg105_n0006_easy_read: Fall of the Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade: In eighteen oh seven, the slave trade ended along the coast of West Africa. This made the empire's economy unstable.
pg105_n0007_easy_read: This happened because Oyo depended a lot on selling slaves for revenue. Oyo used this revenue for its own development.
pg105_n0008_easy_read: When the slave trade ended, the Oyo Kingdom lost this important source of revenue. So, the empire declined.
pg105_n0010_easy_read: The weakening of the Oyo army: Internal conflicts weakened the Oyo army. They also reduced its ability to face later military attacks.
pg105_n0011_easy_read: For example, Benin invaded Oyo in seventeen eighty-three, and Nupe invaded Oyo in seventeen ninety-one. The army was too weak to resist. As a result, the empire declined.
pg105_n0013_easy_read: Disintegration of the central authority: Because of internal conflicts, some chiefdoms stopped paying tribute.
pg105_n0014_easy_read: This reduced the revenue of the central government.
pg105_n0015_easy_read: For example, in eighteen seventeen, Dahomey, under King Ghezo, refused to pay tribute.
pg105_n0016_easy_read: One year later, Dahomey took its independence.
pg105_n0018_easy_read: Conflicts between the council of chiefs, Oyo Mesi, and kings: The council of chiefs played an important role in the rise and growth of the Oyo Kingdom. The council elected the king and removed his leadership.
pg105_n0019_easy_read: However, by the early nineteenth century, conflicts of interest developed between the council and the kings.
pg105_n0020_easy_read: For example, between seventeen fifty-four and seventeen seventy, there was a conflict between Gaha, the leader, Basorun, of the council of chiefs, and the Alafins.
pg105_n0021_easy_read: As a result, the leader of chiefs, Basorun, was involved in the murder of four kings during his time in the council.
pg105_n0022_easy_read: These conflicts made the state less stable and led to its fall.
pg105_n0025_easy_read: Briefly explain the role of religion in helping the Asante Kingdom grow.
pg105_n0029_easy_read: Pre-colonial Central African kingdoms included: Kongo, Mwenemutapa, Luba, Lunda, Malavi, and Lozi.
pg105_n0030_easy_read: Four kingdoms are discussed in Figure seven point four: Kongo, Mwenemutapa, Luba, and Lunda.
pg106_n0052_easy_read: Figure seven point four: Some centralized states in Central Africa
pg107_n0005_easy_read: The Kongo Kingdom was one of the most important kingdoms in Central Africa.
pg107_n0006_easy_read: The Kongo Kingdom started near the end of the fourteenth century.
pg107_n0007_easy_read: By fourteen eighty-two, when the Portuguese arrived, the Kongo Kingdom had a strong central government.
pg107_n0008_easy_read: The king's title was Mani Kongo.
pg107_n0009_easy_read: The capital of the kingdom was called Mbanza.
pg107_n0010_easy_read: The Portuguese later called the capital San Salvador.
pg107_n0011_easy_read: The first Mani Kongo of the kingdom was Nzinga Nkuwu.
pg107_n0015_easy_read: The Kongo Kingdom became powerful for several reasons.
pg107_n0018_easy_read: Development of arts and crafts: The Bakongo were very skilled in arts and crafts.
pg107_n0019_easy_read: The Bakongo were skilled: metal workers, potters, and weavers.
pg107_n0020_easy_read: People traded fine clothes made from raffia palm fiber along the Atlantic coast.
pg107_n0021_easy_read: People exchanged the clothes for salt and seashells. Salt and seashells were used as local money.
pg107_n0023_easy_read: Frequent movement of the people: People often moved in and out of the Kongo Kingdom.
pg107_n0024_easy_read: This movement led to new villages with different clans.
pg107_n0025_easy_read: Those clans needed a political organization to unite them.
pg107_n0026_easy_read: The Kongo state gave strong central leadership to those clans.
pg107_n0028_easy_read: Religious beliefs: The king's power and authority partly depended on religious beliefs.
pg107_n0029_easy_read: The people saw the Mani Kongo as a semi-god.
pg107_n0030_easy_read: He used spiritual powers to unite the people in his kingdom.
pg107_n0031_easy_read: These powers made all provinces pay tribute to the king.
pg107_n0032_easy_read: The tributes helped the king strengthen the central government.
pg107_n0034_easy_read: Monopoly of trade: The king of Kongo controlled trade in the kingdom, including the slave trade.
pg107_n0035_easy_read: He made traders who passed through the kingdom pay taxes.
pg107_n0036_easy_read: He also collected tributes from vassal states.
pg107_n0037_easy_read: The taxes and tributes helped strengthen and unite the kingdom.
pg107_n0039_easy_read: Favorable climatic conditions: The Kongo Kingdom was in a dense forest region.
pg107_n0040_easy_read: The area had enough rain and fertile soil. This helped agriculture grow.
pg107_n0041_easy_read: Agriculture provided enough food for the growing population in the kingdom.
pg107_n0043_easy_read: Population increase: As the number of people grew, they needed to organize themselves under a strong political authority.
pg107_n0044_easy_read: This helped keep law and order in society and protect people from outside threats.
pg107_n0048_easy_read: The Kongo Kingdom declined in the seventeenth century.
pg107_n0049_easy_read: The reasons for the decline include the following:
pg108_n0003_easy_read: Introduction of Christianity: Portuguese Catholic priests introduced Christianity.
pg108_n0004_easy_read: The priests taught Bakongo Christians that Jesus Christ is the only King of the Earth.
pg108_n0005_easy_read: This meant that Mani Kongo Nzinga Nkuwu was not the king.
pg108_n0006_easy_read: This teaching encouraged the Bakongo Christians to stop being loyal to Nzinga Nkuwu.
pg108_n0007_easy_read: This caused division and conflict between Christians and traditionalists.
pg108_n0008_easy_read: As a result, Nzinga Nkuwu and his son Mpanzua Kitima left Christianity.
pg108_n0009_easy_read: However, Nzinga Nkuwu’s mother and son Nzinga Mbemba stayed Christian.
pg108_n0010_easy_read: This division made the kingdom weaker.
pg108_n0012_easy_read: Resistance from provincial governors: Divisions in the royal family led the provincial governors to declare independence.
pg108_n0013_easy_read: The provincial governors refused to pay tribute to the central authority at Mbanza, San Salvador.
pg108_n0014_easy_read: This forced Mani Kongo to find other ways to get money for the government.
pg108_n0015_easy_read: Mani Kongo started trading relations with the Portuguese. This weakened the kingdom.
pg108_n0017_easy_read: Introduction of the slave trade: The Portuguese started and supported local wars to increase the supply of slaves.
pg108_n0018_easy_read: However, Nzinga Nkuwu did not want the slave trade in his kingdom.
pg108_n0019_easy_read: Different views about the slave trade brought the king into conflict with the Portuguese slave traders.
pg108_n0020_easy_read: These conflicts weakened Mani Kongo’s power and led to the fall of the kingdom by the second half of the eighteenth century.
pg108_n0024_easy_read: The Mwenemutapa Kingdom was founded around the fifteenth century.
pg108_n0025_easy_read: The Mwenemutapa Kingdom was in the north of Mashonaland, in present-day Zimbabwe.
pg108_n0026_easy_read: The name Zimbabwe comes from the Shona language. It means stone buildings known as Great Zimbabwe.
pg108_n0027_easy_read: Nyatsimba Mutota founded the Mwenemutapa Kingdom. He belonged to the Karanga clan of the Mashona ethnic group.
pg108_n0028_easy_read: The capital of Mwenemutapa was called Great Zimbabwe.
pg108_n0029_easy_read: Under Nyatsimba Mutota’s leadership, the Mwenemutapa Kingdom fought wars and conquered the Tonga and Tawara of the Zambezi Valley.
pg108_n0030_easy_read: Mutota’s victories gave him the title Mwenemutapa. This title meant master of the conquered land.
pg108_n0031_easy_read: Mutota died in fourteen fifty. His son Matope took the throne. Matope also died in fourteen eighty.
pg108_n0032_easy_read: After Matope died, there were disputes about who would take the throne. These disputes lasted until fourteen ninety, when Changamire took over.
pg108_n0036_easy_read: The kingdom of Mwenemutapa became powerful for the following reasons.
pg108_n0038_easy_read: Trading activities: The Mwenemutapa Kingdom was famous for: gold, copper, and ivory.
pg108_n0039_easy_read: These goods attracted many traders from: Swahili areas, Portugal, and Arab areas. They came to the kingdom to trade.
pg108_n0040_easy_read: Mwenemutapa charged duties on all goods imported into the kingdom.
pg108_n0041_easy_read: The wealth from these duties was used to strengthen the kingdom.
pg109_n0003_easy_read: Rise of ambitious leaders: Mwenemutapa rose and grew because ambitious leaders wanted to expand the kingdom.
pg109_n0004_easy_read: These leaders included Nyatsimba Mutota, his son Matope, and Changamire.
pg109_n0005_easy_read: They wanted land where their people could: settle, graze livestock, and grow crops.
pg109_n0006_easy_read: So, he took control of the area from Great Zimbabwe to Dande, from the Zambezi to Limpopo, and from the Kalahari Desert to the Indian Ocean.
pg109_n0008_easy_read: Role of indigenous religion: The Mashona worshipped a supreme god called Mwari.
pg109_n0009_easy_read: People could only approach their powerful god through priests called Svikiro.
pg109_n0010_easy_read: This strong religious system made people obey their kings.
pg109_n0011_easy_read: The Mwari cult was an important spiritual institution. It helped the Mwenemutapa Kingdom rise and grow.
pg109_n0013_easy_read: Strong and well-equipped army: Creating a strong and well-equipped army helped protect the Kingdom.
pg109_n0014_easy_read: Also, the strong army helped the king gain the support of village leaders.
pg109_n0015_easy_read: This made local village leaders pay tribute to the king regularly.
pg109_n0019_easy_read: The Mwenemutapa Kingdom began to decline in the first half of the sixteenth century.
pg109_n0020_easy_read: The reasons for this decline included the following.
pg109_n0022_easy_read: Resistance against payment of tributes: Some clans started to refuse to pay tribute to the king. These clans included: Uteve, Barwe, and Manyika.
pg109_n0023_easy_read: This weakened the kingdom because it lost one of its most important sources of revenue.
pg109_n0025_easy_read: Arrival of Portuguese: Portuguese merchants took part in the gold trade from Mwenemutapa in the Indian Ocean trade. This partly caused the decline of the Kingdom.
pg109_n0026_easy_read: Between fifteen oh two and fifteen oh seven C E, the Portuguese attacked and captured Kilwa and Sofala. These places were trading centers for gold from Mwenemutapa.
pg109_n0027_easy_read: When the Portuguese conquered these centers, the amount of gold from the Mwenemutapa Kingdom went down.
pg109_n0028_easy_read: As a result, the economy of Mwenemutapa fell.
pg109_n0029_easy_read: So, Mwenemutapa began to lose its strength and later declined.
pg109_n0030_easy_read: After conquering Kilwa and Sofala, the Portuguese attacked the Mwenemutapa Kingdom to control the gold mines.
pg109_n0031_easy_read: This invasion allowed the Portuguese to remove the king of Mwenemutapa and place their own appointee on the throne.
pg109_n0032_easy_read: As a result, the Mwenemutapa Kingdom declined in the seventeenth century.
pg109_n0036_easy_read: The Luba Kingdom was one of the important centralized states in Central Africa.
pg109_n0037_easy_read: It was on the upper Lualaba River valley, around Lake Kisale, in the southeast of the present-day Democratic Republic of Congo, D R C.
pg109_n0038_easy_read: By thirteen hundred C E, people in the
pg110_n0003_easy_read: The people in the Lake Kisale region organized themselves into many farming and trading chiefdoms.
pg110_n0004_easy_read: These chiefdoms joined into one centralized kingdom between thirteen hundred C E and fourteen hundred C E, under a dynasty called Nkongolo.
pg110_n0005_easy_read: Later, in the fifteenth century, Ilunga Kalala overthrew the Ngongolo dynasty. People believed he was a brave hunter with magical powers.
pg110_n0006_easy_read: Ilunga Kalala started the Ilunga dynasty. This dynasty centralized government power and expanded the kingdom to the west of Lake Kisale.
pg110_n0010_easy_read: Several factors helped the Luba Kingdom begin and expand.
pg110_n0014_easy_read: The kingdom was in a good environment.
pg110_n0015_easy_read: The area was good for farming because it had fertile soil and enough rainfall.
pg110_n0016_easy_read: This environment supported the growing of cereal crops.
pg110_n0017_easy_read: Also, the woodlands had many animals, including elephants. People hunted elephants for ivory.
pg110_n0018_easy_read: All these activities helped the state develop.
pg110_n0021_easy_read: Another important reason for the rise and expansion of the Luba Kingdom was better iron and copper technology.
pg110_n0022_easy_read: People did not mine iron and copper in the Luba region. They imported them from the north.
pg110_n0023_easy_read: Even so, peasants around Lake Kisale developed knowledge and skills in metalworking.
pg110_n0024_easy_read: They worked iron to make tools for farming, such as hoes and axes.
pg110_n0025_easy_read: They also made iron weapons. These weapons helped strengthen the army.
pg110_n0026_easy_read: People imported copper from the present-day border of Zambia and Congo, the Copper Belt.
pg110_n0027_easy_read: The people around Lake Kisale used copper to make items such as fine wire for rings, bracelets, and necklaces.
pg110_n0028_easy_read: They also made copper into bricks shaped like crosses.
pg110_n0029_easy_read: They exchanged all these items for other goods from neighboring societies.
pg110_n0030_easy_read: As a result, wealth increased in the area. This increase led to the formation and expansion of the state.
pg110_n0033_easy_read: Fishing was another factor in the rise of the Luba Kingdom.
pg110_n0034_easy_read: The land had lakes and rivers that were rich in fish.
pg110_n0035_easy_read: The people of Luba developed important tools for fishing.
pg110_n0036_easy_read: These tools included fishing nets, harpoons, and dugout canoes.
pg110_n0037_easy_read: They also developed different ways to dry fish.
pg110_n0038_easy_read: They sold a large amount of fish to other societies in the region and beyond.
pg110_n0039_easy_read: The wealth from this trade was used to develop and expand the kingdom.
pg110_n0042_easy_read: Good leadership also helped the Luba Kingdom begin and expand.
pg110_n0043_easy_read: Luba kings created a well-organized leadership system.
pg110_n0044_easy_read: The Luba kings appointed provincial governors. These governors were often from the royal family.
pg110_n0045_easy_read: These governors were responsible for collecting tribute from the chiefs under them.
pg111_n0003_easy_read: The royal family controlled the central court.
pg111_n0004_easy_read: The kingdom had a small standing army. But the kings also had strong mystical and religious authority.
pg111_n0008_easy_read: The Luba Kingdom grew strong for some time. Then it declined in the fourteen fifties.
pg111_n0009_easy_read: The main causes of the breakup were two factors:
pg111_n0011_easy_read: Slave trade: Arabs and Swahili people from the East African coast brought the slave trade. This helped cause the decline of the Luba Kingdom.
pg111_n0012_easy_read: Many people in the kingdom were taken to the coast as slaves.
pg111_n0013_easy_read: This slave trade disrupted Luba society. It weakened the kingdom.
pg111_n0015_easy_read: Succession conflicts: Conflicts over who would rule, among members of the ruling clan, also led to the decline of the kingdom.
pg111_n0016_easy_read: The struggle for power greatly weakened the kingdom.
pg111_n0017_easy_read: These conflicts forced some rivals to move west. There, they started their own kingdom, called the Lunda.
pg111_n0021_easy_read: Immigrants from the Luba Kingdom established the Lunda Empire in the fifteenth century.
pg111_n0022_easy_read: The Lunda people did not have a centralized authority. They only had a senior chief.
pg111_n0023_easy_read: They also had a smaller population. The people lived in small villages.
pg111_n0024_easy_read: Their main activities were farming, fishing, hunting, and trading.
pg111_n0025_easy_read: Their technology, arts, and crafts were less developed than those of their neighbors, the Luba Kingdom.
pg111_n0026_easy_read: The Lunda state's foundations were laid from sixteen hundred C E.
pg111_n0027_easy_read: The Lunda Empire grew most in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. At that time, it became one of the largest centralized states in pre-colonial Africa.
pg111_n0028_easy_read: The Lunda Empire occupied areas that are now the Democratic Republic of Congo, northeastern Angola, and northwestern Zambia.
pg111_n0032_easy_read: Three main factors led to the early rise and later expansion of the Lunda Kingdom.
pg111_n0035_easy_read: Role of immigrants: The most important factor was the contribution of immigrants from the Luba ruling clan and their followers.
pg111_n0036_easy_read: One of these immigrants was Chibunda Ilunga. He gained and made his leadership power accepted in Lunda society by marrying a woman from the family of the Lunda senior chief.
pg111_n0037_easy_read: This woman was the Lunda queen called Rweej or Lueji.
pg111_n0038_easy_read: The children from this marriage, and the generations after them, formed a new Lunda dynasty.
pg112_n0003_easy_read: In the sixteenth century, the dynasty took the title Mwaant Yaav or Mwata Yamvo. This title meant the Lord of Vipers.
pg112_n0005_easy_read: The Lunda dynasty brought the scattered Lunda chiefdoms together into one central empire that kept growing.
pg112_n0006_easy_read: In general, the Luba immigrants brought advanced metalworking technology.
pg112_n0007_easy_read: They also gave the Lunda the idea of a central religious king.
pg112_n0008_easy_read: This idea gave a strong base for the later growth of the Lunda Empire.
pg112_n0009_easy_read: However, the Lunda kept their religious practices and chiefs.
pg112_n0010_easy_read: People saw the chiefs as guardians of local spirits and owners of the land.
pg112_n0011_easy_read: However, the chiefs had to pay tribute to the king of the new empire.
pg112_n0012_easy_read:
The king also appointed the cilool or kilolo in each chiefdom.
The cilool or kilolo was a royal adviser and a tax collector.
pg112_n0013_easy_read: In addition, the cilool was appointed to keep the loyalty of the Lunda confederation of chiefdoms.
pg112_n0015_easy_read: Long-distance trade: Another reason for the start and growth of the Lunda Kingdom was taking part in long-distance trade.
pg112_n0016_easy_read: The Lunda people had an important role in long-distance trade in East and Central Africa.
pg112_n0017_easy_read: The Lunda mainly traded: ivory and slaves. They exchanged them for: weapons and textiles. These goods came from Arab and Swahili traders on the East African coast.
pg112_n0018_easy_read: The weapons and wealth from trade helped the kingdom rise and grow.
pg112_n0020_easy_read: Raiding of neighbouring ethnic groups: Raiding nearby ethnic groups also helped the empire rise and grow.
pg112_n0021_easy_read: The Lunda dynasty conquered many nearby societies and villages.
pg112_n0022_easy_read: The dynasty brought these societies into the empire.
pg112_n0023_easy_read: Some captives became slaves and worked in agriculture.
pg112_n0024_easy_read: Other captives were sold to Arab and Swahili slave traders.
pg112_n0028_easy_read: By the early twentieth century, the Lunda Kingdom had completely collapsed.
pg112_n0029_easy_read: There were two main reasons for the collapse of the kingdom.
pg112_n0030_easy_read:
The first reason was the Chokwe invasion.
The second reason was the partition of Africa.
pg112_n0032_easy_read: Chokwe invasion: First, the Chokwe, who had guns, invaded the empire.
pg112_n0033_easy_read: After the attack, the Chokwe set up their own kingdom inside the Lunda Empire.
pg112_n0034_easy_read: Second, the Chokwe brought in their own language and customs.
pg112_n0035_easy_read: However, the Lunda chiefs and people continued to live in the Lunda heartland, but they had lost much of their earlier power.
pg112_n0037_easy_read:
Partition of Africa: The European partition of Africa began in the eighteen eighties.
It ended what was left of the Lunda Kingdom.
pg112_n0038_easy_read: The area was divided among: the Portuguese of Angola; King Leopold the second, who controlled the Congo Free State; and the British in north-western Northern Rhodesia, Zambia.
pg112_n0039_easy_read: This partition marked the complete end of the Lunda Kingdom.
pg113_n0006_easy_read: Briefly explain what lessons modern societies in Central Africa can learn from ancient kingdoms in the region.
pg113_n0010_easy_read: Before colonialism, kingdoms in southern Africa included the Zulu and Sotho-Tswana kingdoms.
pg113_n0011_easy_read: This section uses the Zulu Kingdom as a case study.
pg113_n0015_easy_read: The Zulu Kingdom stretched from the coast of the Indian Ocean and the Tugela River in the south to the Pongola River in the north of present-day South Africa.
pg113_n0016_easy_read: The kingdom rose in the nineteenth century under Dingiswayo's leadership.
pg113_n0017_easy_read: The kingdom lasted from eighteen hundred to eighteen seventeen.
pg113_n0018_easy_read: Later, the kingdom became the most powerful state under Shaka, or Chaka, who was a military leader.
pg113_n0022_easy_read: The following factors led to the rise of the Zulu Kingdom:
pg113_n0024_easy_read:
Centralization of power under Shaka Zulu:
Shaka took control of areas that had some freedom. He put them under his direct authority.
pg113_n0025_easy_read: This had good results because his skill in organizing people made the kingdom stronger.
pg113_n0027_easy_read:
Influence of annual cultural festivals, Incwala:
The king started annual cultural festivals.
pg113_n0028_easy_read: People came to the festivals from all parts of the kingdom.
pg113_n0029_easy_read: The festivals helped people feel: that they belonged, united, and loyal to the king.
pg113_n0031_easy_read:
Control of trade:
The king controlled trade and all the ivory collected in the kingdom.
pg113_n0032_easy_read: In the north, he kept the trade route to Delagoa Bay open. There, people exchanged ivory for beads and clothes.
pg113_n0033_easy_read: Trade in ivory and hides helped the king buy guns from the Portuguese.
pg113_n0034_easy_read: These weapons helped make the army stronger.
pg113_n0036_easy_read:
Standing army:
Shaka set up a permanent and strong army.
pg113_n0037_easy_read: This meant that soldiers stayed in military camps all the time.
pg113_n0038_easy_read: The soldiers were: well trained, disciplined, equipped, and ready for any emergency.
pg113_n0039_easy_read: The soldiers trained in military methods such as: using the cow horn formation, using short stabbing spears called assegai, spying, using smoke signals, and using shields in battle.
pg113_n0040_easy_read: The soldiers could not marry during their years of military service.
pg113_n0041_easy_read: Also, the soldiers depended on the state for all their upkeep.
pg113_n0042_easy_read: Shaka also used his standing army to expand his kingdom through wars.
pg114_n0003_easy_read: Shaka fought many wars to achieve his goal.
pg114_n0004_easy_read: Shaka brought all the defeated clans into the Zulu kingdom.
pg114_n0005_easy_read: In this way, the Zulu kingdom became more powerful and more important.
pg114_n0007_easy_read: Development of agriculture: Growing crops and keeping livestock were the main economic activities in the kingdom.
pg114_n0008_easy_read: Growing crops and keeping livestock gave the kingdom a regular and enough supply of food. This helped the population grow.
pg114_n0009_easy_read: The growing population needed a well-organized political system to create order and security in the kingdom.
pg114_n0013_easy_read: The Zulu kingdom started to decline in the eighteen thirties.
pg114_n0014_easy_read: The Zulu kingdom declined for several reasons: Boer invasion in the eighteen thirties, weak leadership, and British colonization of South Africa.
pg114_n0016_easy_read: Boer invasion in the eighteen thirties: The Boer invasion of Zululand helped cause the decline of the Zulu kingdom.
pg114_n0017_easy_read: The Boers moved from the Cape to the northeast to look for grazing land.
pg114_n0018_easy_read: Later, the Boers reached Zululand and forced the Zulu people out of their homeland.
pg114_n0019_easy_read: These invasions weakened the economy of the Zulu kingdom because the Boers took most of its fertile land.
pg114_n0021_easy_read: Weak leadership of Shaka's successor: Dingane Kasenzangakhona became king after Shaka.
pg114_n0022_easy_read: However, King Dingane did not have strong leadership qualities or strong military ability as commander in chief.
pg114_n0023_easy_read: This weakness did not keep the Zulu people united. It led to the final decline of the kingdom.
pg114_n0025_easy_read: British colonization of South Africa: The British colonization of Zululand ended the power of African chiefs and set up colonial rule.
pg114_n0026_easy_read: The colonial government controlled the social, economic, and political activities of Africans. It also weakened the kingdom's independence.
